Maratha activist Jarange refuses to end fast, gives Sept 11 deadline
Maratha reservation activist Manoj Jarange refused to end his hunger strike after talks with the Maharashtra government failed. He set a September 11 deadline, asked eligible Marathas to seek Kunbi certificates, and warned of a Mumbai protest.
Maratha reservation activist Manoj Jarange on Thursday refused to call off his indefinite hunger strike, saying he would continue the protest until the community's demands were accepted.
He also issued an ultimatum to the Maharashtra government, saying he would take the agitation to Mumbai on September 12 if the demands were not implemented by September 11.
The announcement came after talks between Jarange and a Maharashtra government delegation failed to produce a breakthrough. Jarange urged members of the Maratha community to start applying for Kunbi caste certificates from September 4, claiming that nearly 58 lakh Kunbi records had been identified.
He also asked eligible families to begin the process of obtaining both Kunbi certificates and validity certificates, saying applications could be based on family, blood and clan links with people whose Kunbi records had been traced, including records found in the Hyderabad Gazette.
Jarange has been on an indefinite hunger strike for the past week at Antarwali Sarati village in Maharashtra's Jalna district, demanding reservation for Marathas.
A government delegation comprising Ministers Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil and Uday Samant, MLC Prasad Lad and MLA Makarand Patil met him on Thursday.
Vikhe Patil appealed to Jarange to end or postpone his fast, citing his worsening health, and said the government was committed to resolving the issues raised by the Maratha community.
According to Vikhe Patil, the government has traced nearly 58 lakh Kunbi records and will expedite the issuance of Kunbi certificates.
He said nodal officers would be appointed to monitor the process and assist applicants facing difficulties.
Kunbi, an agrarian community, is included in the Other Backward Class (OBC) category and is eligible for reservation in government jobs and education.
Jarange has been demanding Kunbi certificates for eligible Marathas to enable them to claim reservation under the OBC quota.
Jarange, however, rejected the government's appeal to end his fast. He said those eligible to apply for Kunbi certificates should begin the process immediately and approach the concerned district collector if they faced any difficulties.
"I will not withdraw my hunger strike until all the demands of the Maratha community are accepted. If Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde genuinely wants to support the Maratha community, he should take a sincere and concrete stand and extend his support," Jarange said.
"I will drink and take IV fluids, but I will not break my fast," he added.
Late on Thursday night, Jarange set a September 11 deadline for the government to act and warned of a fresh escalation in Mumbai the following day.
"This is my last hunger strike. My body will not support me anymore. If I protest again, I will die. I will give you time until September 11. However, if our demands are not implemented by September 11, I will go to Mumbai and protest on September 12," he said.
With the talks failing to yield a resolution, Jarange has continued his fast, called on eligible Marathas to seek Kunbi certificates and set September 11 as the deadline for the government to implement the community's demands.

Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton, Oprah Winfrey and others pay tribute to Gloria Steinem
Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton and Oprah Winfrey are among a slew of politicians, celebrities, writers and activists who are lauding Gloria Steinem as a revolutionary and inspiring figure
Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton and Oprah Winfrey are among a slew of politicians, celebrities, writers and activists who are lauding Gloria Steinem as a revolutionary and inspiring figure.
The celebrated author and activist, who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the U.S. women’s movement, died Wednesday at her home in New York City. She was 92.
Kamala Harris
“To know her as a person is to know someone who was kind, sharp, and witty. She was invested in young women and keeping the door open for the next generation of leaders, and her advocacy was always about fighting for the strength, intelligenc, and dignity of women everywhere. She showed incredible support for women running for office, and I will always be grateful for her encouragement and support in my campaign for the presidency.” — the former vice president, on Facebook.
Hillary Clinton
“Gloria Steinem was, at heart, an optimist. Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice she made every day. Even though we’ve faced setbacks to women’s full participation and equality in America and around the world, I want Gloria’s voice to remain in our heads.” — the former secretary of state, on social media.
Oprah Winfrey
“Every woman who has ever walked into a room knowing she belongs there; every woman who has demanded equal pay, equal respect, ownership of her own body, and the right to make her own choices; every girl who has grown up assuming that her dreams are hers to pursue — whether she knows Gloria Steinem’s name or not — is living, in some measure, inside the progress Gloria helped create.” — the media mogul and television producer, on social media.
Nancy Pelosi
“May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward.” — former Speaker of the House, on X.
Jane Fonda
“For decades, she trudged through every airport in the country, in sandals and a trench, carrying her own suitcase, packed with a few black clothes, hair curlers, and steam iron, in order to speak to women — at conferences, town halls, consciousness raising groups. No group was too small to deserve Gloria’s time. This is how she built the new women’s movement.” — actor and activist, on Instagram.
Barbra Streisand
“From the first moment I met Gloria in the 1970s, I was deeply impressed by her. She stood for everything I believed in: equality for women in the workplace, a woman’s right to choose, greater political representation for women, and a thoughtful, determined response to every form of gender-based discrimination. She gave voice to these issues with fierce intelligence and steely determination, but also with wit, empathy, and humility. What made her so extraordinary was not only the strength of her convictions, but the humanity and grace with which she expressed them.” — singer and actor, on social media.
Jill Biden
“Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures. For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls. She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward.” — the former first lady, on social media.
Melinda French Gates
“Generational change doesn’t happen by accident or fate — it takes leaders like Gloria Steinem who work hand in hand with so many others to build a lasting movement.. What a light she was for me and so many others. What a debt we owe her.” — the philanthropist and businesswoman, on social media.
Julie Taymor
“She got tremendous joy out of being with other people, with other women, and improving their lives. ... She understood about working from the bottom up — and she never really wanted credit for any of it. She always said if she wasn’t alive, there would still be a women’s movement. I think she underestimated her power. She was very modest. She had not an ounce of, you know, narcissism or ‘me, me, me’ about her. And she was able to really make change.” — the director of “The Glorias,” a 2020 biopic of Steinem, in an interview with The Associated Press.
Julianne Moore
“The time I spent studying Gloria Steinem in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life. Everything I watched, everything I read, everything I observed about her gave me a template for how I wanted to behave.” — the actor, who played Steinem in the 2020 film “The Glorias,” on Instagram.
Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex
“Privately, she was even better than you would imagine — spending Thanksgiving with our family, introducing me to one of my best friends (forever the champion of female friendship), loving our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit.” — Duchess of Sussex, on Instagram.
Roxane Gay
“Gloria was one of a kind. Genuine, generous, curious, thoughtful. She lived a staggering life and her passing is a staggering loss tempered only by the ferocity of her legacy.” — the writer, on Instagram.
Abigail Disney
“Everything Gloria did was rooted in kindness. It flowed through her political activism.” — her friend and fellow activist, to the AP.
Rachel Cargle
“Gloria, you changed my life. You seeded a fire in me that would result in my own activism. I am forever grateful to have learned from what you offered the world.” — the author and social justice activist, commenting on Instagram.
Harvey Fierstein
“An unstoppable visionary who demanded an equal role for females in a male dominated world and worked tirelessly, for decades, to bring that change about. The greatest irony was how many women she had to battle as they cowered behind their male owners. But battle she did. Equal rights! Freedom to choose! Access to political power! Equal pay for equal effort.” — the actor and playwright, on social media.
Jill Filipovic
“I have done what I wanted to do with my life. That would not have been possible without Steinem and the scores of other feminists who it is no exaggeration to say radically reshaped America and the world.” — the author and feminist, in her Substack newsletter.

We want Fury v Joshua at Wembley - London mayor
- Published
London Mayor Sadiq Khan says he is "really keen" to host the proposed Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight at Wembley Stadium and has urged promoters to get in touch.
BBC Sport understands Saudi organisers Sela have contacted the mayor's office in recent weeks about bringing the long-awaited contest to the national stadium.
However, with organisers and broadcaster Netflix understood to favour New York's Madison Square Garden for a November bout, sources close to the discussions say talks over a London venue have not progressed, with no detailed talks over dates or timings.
"A message to the promoters - we want to host it in London. Talk to us, we're really keen to have it," Khan told BBC Sport on Thursday.
Wembley Stadium's usual curfew is 23:00, although Khan has previously indicated he would support efforts to bring the fight to London.
A late-night fight in London - potentially in the early hours - could mean it draws a larger television audience in the US.
Brent Council, the local authority involved in any approval, has said a potential extension of the curfew would need to be assessed by Wembley's safety advisory group.
It remains unclear how late that curfew could be pushed back.
"Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are two great British boxers. Both have been world champions," Khan said.
"They both recognise and love the fans in this country who have supported them throughout their careers, amateur and professional.
"Wembley has hosted many fantastic events, including bouts involving Tyson and Anthony. We, the fans, want to see them box live in London."
There is hope that the venue will be finalised in the coming days. Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn has said he wants an announcement this week, with a news conference to follow next week.
BBC Sport has contacted Sela for comment.

Hearn says his side signed a contract for the bout to take place in the United Kingdom, while Sela and Netflix's preference would be the United States, to cater for American audiences.
Matchroom Boxing's Hearn has previously said Joshua's contract specifically stipulated a UK venue and would need to be renegotiated for the fight to take place Stateside.
Hearn says he has since set out terms under which Matchroom would agree to the change, with negotiations continuing over a possible move to New York.
The contact from Sela represents a significant development from the end of July, when sources close to the mayor told BBC Sport there had been no approach from the fight's organisers.
But the lack of progress since that initial contact underlines the uncertainty still surrounding Wembley's chances of hosting the contest.
"I'm hoping the promoters understand that not only will you get 100,000 people watching this bout live, you'll get millions watching it across the globe, where both boxers are cheered on by their loyal fans," Khan said.

Tiranga Yatra at 13000 Feet- National Pride Celebrated in Tawang’s Border Villages
The spirit of patriotism reached the high frontiers of Arunachal Pradesh as the Chuna and Mago Sector Vibrant Villages in Tawang district hosted a Tiranga Yatra at an altitude of nearly 13,000 feet. The event brought together local communities, the civil administration, Panchayati Raj representatives, and security forces in a celebration of national unity and pride.
The program was organized as part of the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign and commemorated 150 years of Vande Mataram, connecting the national celebration with the people living in one of India’s most remote border regions.
A Community Celebration at the Frontier
The Tiranga Yatra was organised by the Jang Sub-Divisional Administration in collaboration with the Indian Army, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), BJP Mandal 3-Mukto, and residents of Chuna and Mago.
The yatra was flagged off by the Zilla Parishad Chairperson, in the presence of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Assistant Commissioner, Panchayat representatives, Heads of Offices, senior personnel of the Indian Army and ITBP, and local residents.
The participation of people from different sections of the community reflected the spirit of collective responsibility and the strong bond between frontier communities, the administration, and the forces serving in the region.
A 300-Meter Tricolour Across the Mountains
The highlight of the celebration was the carrying of a 300-meter-long National Tricolour from Chuna to Mago village.
Against the backdrop of the Eastern Himalayas, the Tricolour made its way through the high-altitude terrain, turning the yatra into a memorable expression of national pride. The event was further enriched by a band performance by students of Higher Secondary School Jang, whose participation brought the enthusiasm of the younger generation to the celebrations.
Honouring India’s Frontier Communities
Events such as the Tiranga Yatra also highlight the important role of Arunachal Pradesh’s border communities in the country’s frontier landscape. Villages such as Chuna and Mago are located in challenging high-altitude terrain, where communities continue to live, work, and contribute to the social and economic life of the region.
The participation of villagers alongside the Indian Army, ITBP, civil administration, and Panchayati Raj representatives demonstrated the importance of community participation in strengthening the social fabric of the border areas.
The event also complemented the broader objective of the Vibrant Villages Programme, which seeks to improve infrastructure, connectivity, livelihoods, and public services in strategically located border villages while strengthening their connection with the rest of the country.
The Tricolour at the High Frontiers
The Tiranga Yatra at Chuna and Mago was more than a ceremonial event. It brought the national spirit directly to communities living at one of India’s highest and most remote frontiers.
The sight of a 300-meter Tricolour moving through the Himalayan landscape served as a powerful reminder of the unity that connects every part of the country, from its cities and towns to its most distant border villages.
At nearly 13,000 feet, the celebration reflected the resilience of Arunachal Pradesh’s frontier communities and the enduring spirit of national unity.

Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.
The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.
“I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.
Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.
Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.
But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.
In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”
As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.
On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.
Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.
In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”
It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.
However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

Medical groups offer vaccine guidance to fill federal vacuum
The latest COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines remain very safe and highly effective for protecting people against severe complications from the potentially life-threatening respiratory viruses, according to independent analyses released Wednesday.
As a result, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the American College of Family Physicians and the Infectious Diseases Society of America simultaneously issued guidelines recommending Americans continue to get immunized.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
The advice aims to fill the void created by the failure of the administration to issue updated recommendations for how Americans should use the vaccines to best protect themselves against these respiratory illnesses.
The groups continue to recommend the vaccines more broadly than the Trump administration. For example, they recommend routine COVID vaccines for healthy younger adults, young children and pregnant people. Current federal advice doesn't recommend those groups routinely get vaccinated.
"Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared," said Bruce Gelin of the Vaccine Integrity Project, an independent initiative based at the University of Minnesota, to counter questions being raised about vaccines by the Trump administration. "We cannot allow the breakdown of the federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance."
The analyses of the COVID, RSV and flu immunizations come as the newest versions of the vaccines are starting to become available. Meanwhile, flu and COVID infections are on the rise, students are returning to school, and the fall and winter respiratory season is approaching.
"Americans are hearing conflicting messages about vaccines right now, and it's understandable that people are asking whom they should trust," Gelin told reporters at a briefing before the new research and updated guidelines were released publicly. "Americans should have access to the best available scientific evidence."
Federal vaccine guidelines in limbo
In a typical year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would have issued updated guidelines for how immunizations should be best used to fight the infections.
But the CDC's process for issuing those guidelines was frozen by a lawsuit that blocked the Trump administration's efforts to reduce the number of vaccines children routinely receive.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic, tried to cut the number of federally recommended routine vaccines, a move Trump recently tried to revive.
Trump and Kennedy claim children get too many vaccines at the same time and that those immunizations are linked to autism. Most doctors, public health authorities and infectious disease experts strongly dispute that, arguing vaccines are very safe and highly effective.
"For decades physicians like me have relied on federal vaccine recommendations because they were based on science and careful review," Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, the American Medical Association's president-elect, said at the briefing. "But with the massive changes at the federal level, trust is waning."
Despite the litigation, many independent experts hoped the CDC would nevertheless issue some kind of advice before the next wave of respiratory infections. On Tuesday, the CDC extended the 2025 recommendations for the flu vaccines to this year. But so far, the administration has been silent on other vaccines. Neither the Department of Health and Human Services nor the CDC responded to NPR's request for comment on the status of federal guidance.
"The problem is that silence at this point is complicit with trying to not make sure people know about the importance of vaccines," Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned last year as director of the CDC's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases to protest the agency's policies under Trump, told NPR in an interview. "The bottom line is that this is dangerous."
Insurance coverage for vaccines appears intact
In addition to providing guidance for doctors and patients, the CDC's recommendations also influence whether insurance companies pay for the immunizations, pharmacists can administer them, and federal programs will supply them free.
The lack of federal guidance, conflicting messages and potential barriers to immunizations worry public health officials because vaccination rates are already falling, leading to resurgences of dangerous diseases like measles.
"It's unprecedented that we're in this situation," Jennifer Kates, who studies vaccine policies at KFF, a nonpartisan health research group, told NPR in an interview. "It creates confusion about what the current status is. And vaccination rates have already been going down because it's hard for people to get good information and understand who they should trust."
That raises fears that even fewer people will get vaccinated, increasing the risk of sickness, hospitalization and death. Even though the annual summer and winter COVID surges have been getting milder, last year's flu season was unusually severe. Both diseases still claim tens of thousands of lives in the U.S. each year.
Despite the absence of new guidelines this year, most people should still be able to get the immunizations for free because private insurers are pledging to continue covering them. Federal programs like Medicare will still pay for them and the Vaccines for Children Program, which provides vaccines for about half of U.S. children for free, is still expected to supply them.
In addition, most states have decoupled the ability of pharmacists to administer the shots from federal guidelines and are instead often relying on the recommendations of medical groups, such as those releasing guidance now.
"We're anticipating that this year for the fall respiratory virus season for flu and for COVID there will be far less challenge than there was last year this time," Brigid Groves of the American Pharmacists Association told NPR. "It should be business as usual. The vast majority of patients across the nation should be able to access these vaccinations with very little barriers, very little hiccup."
Some pharmacists may, however, demand a prescription if they are in one of the handful of states that still require that.
A group effort to analyze vaccine data
For the new analyses, which were published in the journal JAMA, the Vaccine Integrity Project worked with the American Medical Association to review thousands of the latest studies of the vaccines. Those analyses helped the medical groups update their guidelines.
The federal government last year made it more difficult for some people to get the COVID vaccines by limiting the approvals to people who are at high risk for serious disease because they are age 65 or older or have other health problems. The administration also dropped the recommendation that all healthy young children and pregnant women routinely get vaccinated against COVID, even though they are at increased risk, too.
But in the updated independent recommendations, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists continues to urge COVID vaccination for pregnant women, as well as those considering getting pregnant or breastfeeding.
"These vaccines not only protect mom's health and reduce the risk of adverse outcomes during pregnancy, but they also protect the newborn when they are unable to get vaccinated," Dr. Christina Davidson, ACOG's chief medical officer, said during the briefing.
The American Academy of Pediatrics' latest guidelines recommend COVID vaccination for:
- All infants and children ages 6 months through 23 months,
- Children ages 2 to 18 at risk for serious complications,
- Anyone ages 2 to 18 who isn't at risk but whose parents or guardian wants them to get a shot.
"We are committed and continue to be committed to the health and the well-being of the children of this country," Dr. Andrew Racine of the pediatrics academy said during the briefing. "Every recommendation that you are hearing today begins with one simple question: What best protects children from preventable children and helps them to thrive? And what you are hearing from us today is an answer to that simple question."
The pediatrics academy also broadened its recommendation for RSV immunization from just infants under 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season if their mothers weren't vaccinated during pregnancy. It now also recommends immunization for infants and children ages 8 to 19 months entering their second season. Anyone age 6 months and older should also get an annual flu shot starting at 6 months, the academy recommends.
The American Academy of Family Physicians' latest guidelines recommend:
- All adults 19 years and older get one of the updated COVID vaccines, which received Food and Drug Administration approval Aug. 27;
- Adults ages 65 and older should get a second dose six months after the initial shot;
- Anyone age 6 months and older should also get a flu shot. 
For the first time this year, people ages 50 and older will be able to get a new kind of flu shot that uses the same mRNA technology as the COVID vaccines. It may provide stronger protection than traditional flu shots, though it can cause more mild side effects.
"The bottom line is that vaccines are one of the country's greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness and death," Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said during the briefing. "Making sure families get recommended vaccines during respiratory illness season not only keeps individuals healthy, but also helps protect entire communities."
The timing of when people should get a COVID or flu shot varies. Those at high risk for serious complications or planning to travel or attend large gatherings might consider getting their shots sooner, such as two weeks ahead of those events. Others may want to wait until later in the fall to ensure they have the strong protection during the winter holidays and when infections tend to peak.
"You're going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine," the AMA's Fryhofer says. "So if you have a big event, if you have to go to a wedding or you're going on some fabulous trip or are going to a fabulous birthday party or just any birthday party or get-together, think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that even so you can remain healthy and well."
While the Vaccine Integrity Project's efforts drew praise from medical groups, the lack of federal guidance is still likely to create confusion that will lead to some people forgoing vaccination.
"There is no substitute for the kind of clear, coherent messages and communication that the CDC has provided for decades. And in its absence I expect that we will see more confusion, more uncertainty about how best to make use of vaccines as we approach this respiratory virus season," said Jason Schwartz, who studies vaccine policies at Yale University.

Two teenagers killed as Palestinian villagers resist ‘theft’ of sheep by Israeli settlers
A 16-year-old student was shot dead by an army sniper, while it was unclear if a 19-year-old was shot by a soldier or a settler
Two Palestinian teenagers have been shot dead in the West Bank as the military razed an entire village near Hebron in the latest escalation of violence in the occupied territory.
Khalil Abu Alia, 16, a high school student, and Omar al-Nassan, 19, were shot after a group of settlers under police and army escort entered the al-Mughayyir village near Ramallah on Wednesday to take sheep from a Palestinian home, local residents said.
The army claimed its troops were providing security to police officers and Israeli settlers who had gone to take sheep claimed by them. The military offered no evidence of ownership of the livestock.
Snipers climbed on rooftops and shot Abu Alia while he was on the doorstep of his house, his teacher Waheed Abu Naim told the Guardian.
They also shot Al-Nassan twice, the second time in the back, the villagers said. Both died before they could reach hospital.
Abu Alia was killed by a soldier but it wasn’t clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler, the paper reported.
The Israeli army claimed its soldiers fired on "key instigators" of a “violent disturbance”, apparently referring to an attempt by the Palestinians to resist the settlers by throwing stones and cinder blocks.
The killings at al-Mughayyir come amid intensifying settler violence in the West Bank, where a siege by settlers of Qusra village in August drew international condemnation.
At least 79 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed in the West Bank by Jewish settlers or Israeli forces since the beginning of 2026, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
Israeli soldiers and settlers had previously killed three students from the al-Mughayyir boys school, where Abu Alia was due to start his grade 11, Mr Abu Naim, who taught all five boys killed in recent weeks, said. “We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” he told the Guardian. “This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester which starts in three days."
The Benjamin Netanyahu government has spearheaded a rapid expansion of Jewish settlements in the West Bank, which was captured by Israel in the 1967 war, establishing dozens of new settlements and settler outposts.
Rights groups say the increasing settler presence on the edge of Palestinian villages, like Qusra, is part of a wider effort to seize more land from Palestinians, further eating into territory where Palestinians aim to establish a state.
The latest killings of the Palestinian teenagers came after foreign secretary Ed Miliband stated on Tuesday that the UK would “reset” its policy on Israel in the coming weeks, as one of his ministers suggested goods coming out of Israeli settlements in the West Bank could be subject to sanctions.

Vance's Antichrist comments are a 'common belief', his friend tells BBC
- Published
Recent remarks by US Vice-President JD Vance about the Antichrist and "the end times" are a "very, very common belief", one of his friends says.
Vance recently mused on his religious views while responding to a question on a Christian podcast. He said he would "not [be] shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us" and speculated on whether the end of the world was nigh.
His friend Rod Dreher, a conservative writer, rejected any suggestion that the comments would harm the vice-president. He told the BBC's Today programme: "Most Americans who are inclined to vote Republican already believe this stuff."
In his podcast comments, Vance also clarified that such thoughts did not preoccupy him.
In Christianity, the "end times" phrase refers to theories about what will happen at the end of the world. Many churches believe God has a divine plan for the end of everything.
Meanwhile, the Antichrist is seen as the enemy of God who appears during the final phase of the world's existence and takes it over.
Vance, who became a Catholic as an adult, reflected on these topics during a recent podcast discussion with Bryce Crawford, a US Christian podcaster.
"Do I think that we're in the end times? I don't know," he said in response to a Crawford question on the subject. "And I think that it's probably bad for me spiritually to focus too much on it, because there are, like, things you gotta do.
"I gotta be good to my wife. I gotta be good to my kids. I have to be as good of a leader as I can for the United States of America."
The vice-president continued by saying: "I think that there are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us."
But Vance reiterated that he was preoccupied with being vice-president, explaining: "What I'm trying to focus on is doing as much of God's work as possible right now."
Reacting to Vance's comments about the Antichrist, Dreher said: "This might sound bonkers to someone who is outside the Christian religion, but it is a very, very common belief within Christianity."
He said his friend was simply reflecting that the world appeared to be going "crazy" through the rapid development of AI and ongoing conflicts.
Dreher, who was present when Vance was received into the Catholic Church, said Ronald Reagan had made similar comments when he was the US president, and that this was seen as "perfectly normal" by his voters.
Vance converted to Catholicism in 2019, then in his mid-30s, and has described how the Church resonated with his family and social values and his conservative politics.
Since becoming vice-president, he has occasionally tangled with Pope Leo and his papal predecessor Francis, on issues including the Trump administration's immigration policy.
Vance is due to appear behind the lectern on Thursday afternoon to deliver the first White House press briefing since the departure of Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.

He also informed that the state government will set up a Tamil Nadu Olympic City and a Motor Sports City in Chennai.
These three major developmental initiatives aim to boost the state's infrastructure and global standing.

New Secretariat-Assembly complex
The proposed Secretariat-cum-Assembly complex will span 20 lakh square feet and will consolidate all state government departments, news agency PTI reported. The complex will be established at an estimated cost of ₹1,200 crore. The "eco-friendly" facility will feature:
- It will have conference halls and public service centers.
- Advanced facilities such as fire safety systems and accessibility infrastructure for persons with disabilities.
- The complex will feature ample vehicle parking and modern facilities for government staff.
The historical buildings within Fort St. George will be preserved as a heritage site for future generations.
"The new project, estimated at ₹1,200 crore, will span 20 lakh square feet in Chennai, integrating all government departments into a modern, accessible, and eco-friendly facility while preserving the heritage of the existing Fort St. George," Vijay said.
The chief minister added, "The government has control only over a small portion (approximately 4 acres) of the 107-acre Fort St. George campus, as the rest is managed by the Defence and the Archaeological Survey of India."
He also explained that in order to ensure efficient administration, it is necessary to consolidate all government departments into one modern and accessible complex.
"To ensure efficient, world-class administration for the coming century, it is necessary to consolidate all government departments into one modern, accessible, and eco-friendly complex," Vijay stated.
A precise location for the construction site within the city was not specified.

Vijay announced the establishment of a Tamil Nadu Olympic City in Chennai and said that it will be developed by the Tamil Nadu Sports Development Authority.
The Olympic City aims to create an integrated sports hub that provides athletes with advanced training and support facilities, news agency ANI reported.
Key highlights will include:
- The Olympic City will feature world-class sports arenas.
- It will have state-of-the-art sporting equipment
- The facility will also include dedicated Sports Science and Sports Medicine centres.
- It will also have a High Performance Training Centre.
The facility will feature modern infrastructure like accommodation for sportspersons and coaches.

While warning that breaching the 1.5°C global warming limit would bring irreversible losses that no adaptation initiatives could undo, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) on Wednesday (September 2, 2026), for the first time, set out a detailed “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway.
This is a route under which the world overshoots the 2015 Paris Agreement’s central goal — limiting the rise in average global temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels — which a UNEP report said was now unavoidable, but holds the peak as low as possible and then brings temperatures back down below the limit by the end of the century.
The report, Limiting Overshoot, released in Nairobi, said global warming would cross 1.5°C “in the next few years”. Even a scenario in which every country delivers on its national climate plan and net-zero target puts peak warming at 1.8°C, it said. According to the report, current policies point to a rise of about 2.6°C by 2100, with a range of 1.9–3.6°C. The pathway, the report said, "is by no means an acceptable or preferred pathway; it is simply the best remaining option."
The diplomatic grounds for that framing were laid at the 30th UN Climate Change Conference, COP30, held in 2025 in Brazil’s Belém, where the consensus “Global Mutirão” decision became the first COP text to concede that a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C limit was likely, given how fast the remaining carbon budget was being spent. At the conference, countries also committed, for the first time, to limiting the size and duration of the overshoot and to closing adaptation gaps, which would require deep, rapid and sustained emission cuts.
Given that cuts alone will no longer suffice, a steep scaling up of nature-based removals such as large reforestation programmes was needed, COP30 CEO Ana Toni said in a statement. UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres also released a statement, saying, “This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead. We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition."
Compounding costs
The UNEP report suggested that time spent above 1.5°C carries compounding costs such as faster sea-level rise, coral reef collapse, glacier loss exceeding a quarter of global mass by 2100, declines of up to 14% in global food production by 2050 without effective adaptation, and rising odds of irreversible tipping points in the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and the Amazon.
Moreover, it gets harder to roll back the effects of a tonne of emitted carbon. The report computed that every five years of continued high emissions adds roughly 0.1°C to peak warming. Reversing that same 0.1°C afterwards means pulling about 220 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide back out of the atmosphere over and above whatever is still being emitted. Very broadly, a single large tree growing for about 30 years can cut out only a tonne of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide removal, the report stresses, is needed in addition to, not instead of, emission cuts, and can credibly cool temperatures back to the 1.5°C limit only if peak warming stays well below 2°C. Even the most optimistic scaling up of emission cuts is unlikely to reverse more than a few tenths of a degree this century, the report underlined.
UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen was explicit that the report is not a concession. “Let’s be very clear, the 1.5 target is still the goal. But now we need to approach it differently from above,” she said.
The report arrives at a moment of uncertainty over whether countries will cut emissions at all. The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, formally exited the Paris Agreement earlier this year and has also announced its withdrawal from the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the Green Climate Fund. Separately, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the conflict in West Asia has produced what the International Energy Agency calls the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, with output from affected countries down more than 14 million barrels a day. Sustained high energy prices could push governments toward coal and other short-term fossil responses.
Methane targets
The report, in a first for the UN, placed significant stress on methane, which currently contributes about 0.5°C of warming. Cutting it is described as the most effective way to slow warming in the near term. Human activity currently puts out roughly 350–400 million tonnes of methane a year, mostly from fossil fuel operations, livestock, rice paddies, landfills and wastewater. When modellers build the pathways that underpin net-zero targets, they typically assume that about half of this gets cut by mid-century through “cheap, technically easy” interventions such as plugging leaks and venting from oil and gas. But the other half, roughly 150–200 million tonnes a year still being emitted in 2050 from agriculture and waste, is harder to cut; though shaving 60–70 million tonnes from it could reduce temperature rise to the same extent as removing 220 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Over 155 countries have joined the Global Methane Pledge to cut anthropogenic methane at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030. India, China, Russia and Iran remain outside it.
The UNEP report co-author Richard Betts of the University of Exeter said, “It is a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world."

The Bombay High Court has dismissed all petitions filed by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) on Friday (August 14, 2026) against an order that recognised community health volunteers as workers eligible for minimum wages under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
The court held that although the volunteers are designated as “swayamsevaks,” their functions align with those of municipal employees. They perform public health duties, maintain attendance, work fixed hours, follow medical staff instructions, and receive a fixed monthly payment.
AIUTUC demands immediate implementation of revised minimum wages
The BMC had challenged the September 7, 2020 order of the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Mumbai). The order had ruled that these volunteers are entitled to the notified minimum wage and directed the corporation to pay the difference between the existing honorarium and the statutory minimum wage.
The corporation argued that no employer-employee relationship exists. It submitted that the volunteers work five hours daily and receive ₹14,000 as an honorarium. It contended that the term “honorarium” exempts them from the purview of the Minimum Wages Act.
Justice Sandeep Marne, in a single-judge bench, rejected these submissions. He noted that the nature of the volunteers’ work and the degree of control exercised over them establish an employment relationship.
The court observed that these volunteers have been associated with the municipality for decades. They assist in health awareness campaigns, support government health programmes, and act as a link between health centres and local communities, particularly in slum areas. The programme has been operational for approximately 38 years.
The volunteers perform assigned duties for remuneration. They are required to report to duty, work specified hours, and follow instructions from medical staff. The court stated that describing their payment as an “honorarium” does not exclude them from the purview of the Minimum Wages Act.
Justice Marne upheld the Assistant Labour Commissioner’s order. He ruled that denying social security protections to these workers would not be justified. The judgment states that they are entitled to the notified minimum wage applicable to the employment category under the Act.
The court also clarified that the volunteers render service to the corporation and are not just doing volunteer work. The petitions filed by the municipal corporation against the Labour Commissioner’s order were dismissed.

The poster of the former Prime Minister was put up, in which the ex-PM said, “Israel must return the lands of Arabs it has occupied. The lawful rights of the Palestinians must be established”
Students of Jadavpur University on Thursday (September 3, 2026) put up a poster in the campus of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s remark on the territorial integrity of Palestine.
Only a day before, the administration whitewashed all the graffiti from the walls of the university after Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari directed the university administration to take action against the ‘anti-national’ graffiti painted on the walls, including the ones demanding freedom of Palestine and Kashmir, and also slogans on shooting the fascists.
The poster of the former Prime Minister was put up at the green zone area of the university, in which the ex-PM said, “Israel must return the lands of Arabs it has occupied. The lawful rights of the Palestinians must be established.”
The statement was made by Mr. Vajpayee in 1977 at a public meeting in Delhi shortly after the Janata Party government came to power for the first time. He was then given the charge of the External Affairs Ministry.
At the bottom of the poster, credit was given to the “nationalist students of Jadavpur University”. A QR code linked to Mr. Vajpayee’s full speech was also included in the poster.
After the State CM’s directive on August 26, 2026, the university administration whitewashed all the graffiti across the main building, Aurobindo Bhaban, the Arts Hostel, and the Open-Air Theatre. However, the graffiti was repainted, which students claimed was an attempt to ‘reclaim’ the walls of the university.
One of the freshly painted graffiti on Monday (August 31, 2026) quoted Karl Marx, saying, “We have no compassion, and we ask no compassion from you. When our turn comes, we shall not make excuses for the terror.”
A day later, a group of police personnel and officials from the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) arrived at the university at around 12:30 a.m. on Tuesday (September 1, 2026) and whitewashed all the graffiti on the walls of the JU campus. This included a portrait of artist Chittaprosad Bhattacharya, a painting on climate change, as well as the aforementioned statement of Marx, quotes from Ho Chi Minh, Urdu couplets, and more.
However, the graffiti and the poster were back on the walls across the campus once again on Thursday (September 3, 2026).
Apart from the former PM’s poster, a sarcastic graffiti on Italian dictator Benito Mussolini and the RSS was also painted to justify the ‘Azadi’ slogan, which was also termed as ‘anti-national’. This graffiti said, “Mussolini ko de di Azadi, RSS ko bhi de denge Azadi” (Mussolini was given freedom, so will be given to RSS as well).
A few more sarcastic graffiti on Vinayak Damodar Savarkar was also seen on Thursday (September 3, 2026).
To counter the graffiti and posters by the Left students, the ABVP also put up photos and posters on Rabindranath Tagore, Vidyasagar, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and Vande Mataram across the campus on Thursday (September 3, 2026).
However, on Thursday (September 3, 2026), the State CM further launched a scathing attack on the dissident voices within the university.
“Bengal is the land of Netaji and Shyamaprasad. Swami Vivekananda was born in Kolkata. And on this land you will say ‘Kashmir maange azaadi’! There are no rallies when Pahalgam happens, but during Operation Sindoor, you say, Stop the war. Do we have to tolerate these things? You will write ‘Free Palestine’ on the walls of Jadavpur? Write ‘Free PoK’. I will support it,” he said, addressing the annual programme of Vivekananda Vidya Bharati Vikas Parishad, an RSS-affiliated organisation, at Ramakrishna Mission in Kolkata’s Golpark.
Rallies by ABVP and Left students
Meanwhile, the Left students took out a rally against the invitation of several BJP leaders, including Rahul Sinha, Swapan Dasgupta, and Tapas Roy, and also the Jadavpur MLA Sarbori Mukherjee at a ‘Nationalist Conference’ that took place at the Triguna Sen auditorium in the university. The event was organised by an organisation, Haripada Bharati Smritiraksha Samiti, in the afternoon.
The students opposed the invitation of the BJP leaders inside the campus days after the clash erupted between the ABVP and Left students on August 20.
Jadavpur University had emerged as the flashpoint of the right versus left politics after a group of Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad Supporters forced themselves inside the university premises on August 19 and tried to tear posters and burn flags of the left student’s union. The university has been on the boil since then.
“Ms. Mukherjee sent outsiders inside the campus who vandalised the university and set fire to the main building late at night. Why was she invited?,” asked the general secretary of the Students’ Federation of India, Srijan Bhattacharya, during the protest rally at 8B Bus Stand opposite to the University.
He also added that the graffiti made by the students reflects the opinions of the public. “CM cannot decide which one of them is nationalist and anti-nationalist. If he thinks those are not the opinions of the common people, why doesn’t he conduct the students’ union election and let the students decide it through voting?”
The ABVP supporters also held another rally inside the campus, carrying the national flag and uttering ‘Vande Mataram’.
Calling the left students spoiling the environment of the university, they said that they have been pushing an anti-national mentality and don’t allow any other voices to be raised democratically.

'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
- Published
More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.
The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.
"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.
His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.
Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.
The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.
They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.
In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.
At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.
"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.
He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.
Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.
Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.
Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.
He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.
On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.
Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.
"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.
In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.
"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.
I came to realise it was not true"
Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."
This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.
Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."
Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.
The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.
Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.
Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.
"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.
TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.
With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.
Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.
Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.
His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.
People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.
Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.
The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.
Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.
The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.
The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.
As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.
The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.
After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".
"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.
He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.
Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.
Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.
"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.
"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyage
- Published
Far from hitting the bars and fleshpots of the Thai beach resort of Pattaya, in their first hours onshore most of the nearly 5,000 sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln seemed determined to go shopping.
At the Hard Rock Hotel – one of two beachside hotels where they were able to stay off the ship – they hung around clutching their recent purchases. But perhaps, after a record 250 days confined inside a grey steel warship, the normality of a trip to the mall might have been just what they needed.
With their military haircuts, moustaches and navy t-shirts, they stood out against the usual Pattaya crowd in flip-flops and beachwear.
Night, though, is when this resort city comes into its own, putting on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars.
Pattaya's tourism industry has been hit by conflict in the Middle East, where the USS Abraham Lincoln was last operating, with many of the tourists the city depends on choosing to stay at home.
Local establishments have been hoping American sailors, arriving with nine months of unspent salary while at sea, will provide a much-needed boost. On Wednesday night, the city's most famous promenade, Walking Street, was very much open to them, with a huge, illuminated sign at its entrance welcoming the crew of the US carrier.
They have, however, been reminded the sex industry is off-limits, as prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand.
But alcohol was flowing. By midnight some of the younger sailors were so inebriated they had to prop each other up. Others edged nervously into the red-lit caverns of the go-go bars, with their gyrating and barely-clothed pole dancers.
Conversation over the pounding music was challenging. One older crew member told us they really needed the break.
"The news says we've been at sea for nine months. To be honest I've lost track of time," he said.
"It got boring. It's never big enough on board. It's big but it still feels like a boat, especially when you're sharing it with thousands of people." How long would it take them to get home to California? "Too long," he said.
Restaurant owner Kosol Homkhunthod said the American sailors had "created a buzz" in town and among his staff - business had been "really slow" lately.
And a passing tourist described seeing "tonnes of people sitting on the beach", with soldiers in good spirits. "It's not like that every day."
But bar owner Kanta Saenkla complained many of the sailors appeared to simply be roaming around rather than enjoying the local bars.
"They haven't really come in for drinks or anything," she said. "Mostly they just walk around. They're not spending money like they did in previous years."
Out partying or not, Pattaya is a welcome respite for the crew.
Shakeira Fairfax, mother of 25-year-old sailor Jada Fairfax, told Reuters there had been moments over the past few months when "morale was low".
She described the period after hostilities broke out in the Middle East as an "uncertain" and "scary" time.
"I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'mum', I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," Fairfax added.
The crew have been well-drilled not to talk about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln during its long combat deployment in the operation against Iran, which have been the subject of criticism back in the US.
Some sailors were wary of making any conversation at all. Others referred journalists' questions to their media teams. Visible everywhere in Pattaya were the men wearing t-shirts emblazoned with the letters SLG, or Shore Liaison Group.
It is their job to maintain discipline on land, to watch out for the crew members, some of whom are very young and inexperienced, and to co-ordinate with the local authorities during port calls.
US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson did not answer questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing while in Pattaya, saying that "we're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can".
US personnel, he added, would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".
The decision by the USS Abraham Lincoln to stop in Pattaya makes a lot of sense. Port calls by the US Navy in Thailand, a long-standing treaty ally, are routine with well-established protocols.
It is also on the ship's route from the Gulf to California, giving the crew a chance to let off steam, and enjoy a break from the demands of life on board a warship.
If their stop in Thailand does the trick, any frustration they may feel over their unexpectedly long and tough mission may have dissipated by the time they get home.

Breaking down Chelsea's staggering 39 summer exits
- Published
Chelsea have had a few remarkable transfer summers since their forced sale from Roman Abramovich's control in May 2022.
Once again they were big spenders, outlaying £349m on 11 signings such as Morgan Rogers, Maxence Lacroix and Emiliano Martinez.
But there was something different this time.
Chelsea actually made a trading profit after selling 17 players.
Another 22 were loaned out, four of those with either sell-on options or obligations totalling more than £140m.
It meant a staggering 39 players left the club - and that is not including the four young players who were released.
And, remarkably after all that, the Chelsea website, external still lists a first-team squad on their books of 30 players.
Here, we break down the Blues' remarkable summer of 50 deals, focusing on their 39 sales.
Who left on permanent deals
Chelsea's internal figures suggest the club generated more than £500m in player departures during the summer window.
This includes loan fees and is a total that would represent a world record.
Earlier this week BBC Sport's calculations, carried out by FootballTransfers.com founder Paul Macdonald, put the incomings at £349m and the outgoings at £382m.
That figure did not include any potential loan option/obligation fees, or future clauses which are dependent on achieving certain targets.
Chelsea estimate they have made a profit of about £120m on transfer activity.
Whichever way you add it up, their summer represents a staggering, record-breaking period of player trading in European football.
Among the 39 players sold or loaned out were Enzo Fernandez, whose £125m move to Manchester City matched the British transfer record, and Senegal striker Nicolas Jackson, who joined Aston Villa for £65m.
Spain full-back Marc Cucurella moved to Real Madrid for £51.8m, while Liam Delap and Andrey Santos were each sold in deals worth around £50m.
In fact Chelsea had five sales above £40m, or seven if you include two loans that have a £75m option (Mykhailo Mudryk to Tottenham) and a £43m obligation (Alejandro Garnacho to Villa).
To put that into context, there were four £40m-plus signings in the whole of Serie A, two in La Liga and four in the German Bundesliga.
Who left on loan
What has been stark is Chelsea's willingness to do business with Premier League clubs, including their rivals.
Arsenal are the 'big six' club to have signed the most Blues players under the current ownership, recruiting Noni Madueke, Kai Havertz and Kepa Arrizabalaga among others.
Chelsea have also completed eight deals with Aston Villa in four years - a figure matched only by the number of Brighton players who have moved to Stamford Bridge during the same period.
They also did business with Tottenham for the first time in 17 years when winger Mudryk joined Spurs on loan.
It was also the first loan move between the clubs in 34 years.
Yet again there were more deals with sister club Strasbourg this summer - two transfers and three loans.
Has Chelsea's strategy finally started to pay off?
Does this all show Chelsea's recruitment strategy, which has attracted significant criticism over the years, has finally started to deliver, at least financially?
Or has it been a sign of sorting out the transfer chaos of the first four years under Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital?
For most of their tenure, the strategy centred on signing young players to long-term contracts and rapidly rebuilding a squad largely inherited from the Abramovich era - a process that initially came at considerable expense.
Spending on transfer fees has overall significantly exceeded income from player sales - and the club subsequently breached Uefa's financial controls, resulting in a fine and a settlement agreement.
Chelsea also controversially remained within Premier League financial regulations after selling assets, including two hotels and the women's team, to companies within the club's ownership structure.
Since then, they have increasingly focused on trying to balance their spending by generating significant transfer income.
Before this summer, Chelsea had already recorded sales total of £236m, £178m and £289m in successive summers.
What does that mean?
Put simply, Chelsea have spent almost £2bn across nine transfer windows, but have generated more than £1bn through player sales in this time.
A new approach after season of turmoil
Chelsea's chastening 8-2 Champions League defeat by Paris St-Germain last season was a turning point.
The discontent that had simmered behind the scenes - and in the stands - became harder to ignore.
Players, including Fernandez and Cucurella, publicly questioned aspects of the club's direction, while supporter protests reflected a growing sense of frustration during a difficult period on and off the pitch.
A 10th-placed Premier League finish last season only intensified scrutiny amid a growing acknowledgement within the club that change was needed.
Senior figures began speaking to experienced players to gather feedback with the aim of addressing some of the concerns.
Some like Fernandez were unconvinced and pushed to leave, but Moises Caicedo, Reece James and Joao Pedro renewed their contracts.
Influential co-owner Behdad Eghbali also publicly acknowledged the need to "tweak the model", improve decision-making and learn from mistakes.
Chelsea appointed Xabi Alonso as manager, believing he had the profile and authority to command the dressing room.
Recruitment was also reassessed.
Previous managers had highlighted shortcomings within what had been the Premier League's youngest squad for two consecutive seasons.
Those concerns ranged from a poor disciplinary record and difficulties defending set-pieces to lapses in concentration, inconsistent finishing and, ultimately, inconsistent results.
Sources around the club have also described a dressing-room culture affected at times by high turnover, with some feeling the pace of change became too rapid and relationships too transactional.
The arrivals of Jordan Henderson, Danny Welbeck and Argentina keeper Martinez, the oldest players Chelsea have signed since Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang in 2022, are intended to bring experience and leadership to a youthful group.
Rogers and Lacroix have also arrived with proven Premier League pedigree and physical presence, although the club's commitment to recruiting elite young talent remains unchanged.
The adjusted approach amounts to an acknowledgement that elements of the previous strategy fell short, while retaining the principles that have enabled Chelsea to generate significant transfer profits.
Whether it leads to success on the pitch this season remains to be seen.
