After country music legend and philanthropist Dolly Parton died in August 2026, rumors spread online about supposed public spending cuts to her Imagination Library, which sends free books to children until their 5th birthdays.
Posts online claimed that Missouri or Indiana Republicans cut funding for the child literacy program. Some claims were vaguer, merely stating that "Republicans" ended financial support for the Imagination Library. Readers asked us whether the Imagination Library was "defunded" after Parton's death or in the past year and whether U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, Congress, Republicans or other various entities were the culprit.
Here's the truth: In about two dozen states, the Imagination Library receives state government funding. In the year before Parton's death, two states with Republican-controlled governments — Indiana and Missouri — and two with Democrat-controlled governments — Maine and Washington — ended or reduced financial support for the Imagination Library.
At least one state with a Republican governor and Democrat-controlled Legislature, Nevada, also did not renew several grants that supported local partners of the Imagination Library.
The federal government does 
Dollywood Foundation spokesperson Tracy Long declined via email to answer any questions about funding for the Imagination Library; The New York Times reported on Aug. 25 that the Imagination Library was overwhelmed following Parton's death.
At least one state, Oregon, passed bipartisan legislation in 2026 that codified the Imagination Library as an official state program.
According to the Imagination Library's website, 
Here's everything we know about the Imagination Library's funding and why some states and other organizations stopped providing 
How is the Imagination Library funded?
The Imagination Library uses a mix of private and public funding at the state and local levels. The organization itself covers all of the administrative and overhead costs. Local partners who work with the Imagination Library are asked to enroll children in the coverage area and pay an average of $2.60 per child per month toward wholesale books and mailing costs, according to a 2024 infographic from the library.
(Imagination Library)
According to Courtney Vashaw, director at a New Hampshire library that partners with Parton's foundation, in at least some cases, like hers, the Imagination Library pays for the books, too.
"Where does local funding come into it? The postage," she said in a phone call. "There has to be some kind of partnership that allows for that money to be raised."
As of June 2026, the Imagination Library has full coverage in 21 states, according to a fact sheet the organization released. State governments often support those statewide programs through a 50/50 funding match, where the state pays for half of the local partners' costs.
Many of the Imagination Library's local partners — which are all nonprofit organizations — also heavily rely on federal or state grant funding.
Did state Republicans cut funding?
Missouri and Indiana Republicans cut funding after reportedly facing budget deficits. Kentucky lawmakers also reportedly considered cutting funding but reversed the move after public backlash.
Missouri
In November 2023, under Republican Gov. Mike Parson, Missouri became the first state to cover all costs for the Imagination Library. (Tennessee, Parton's home state — which Republicans control — was the first to introduce a statewide program involving partial public funding support.)
In lieu of local nonprofit partners, Missouri had school districts partner with the initiative, and the schools did not have to pay for the books or postage.
But in June 2026, under Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers cut state funding for the program for the upcoming fiscal year — reportedly from $6 million to $2 million.
"The Governor is a strong supporter of children's literacy. Given the seriousness of Missouri's budget imbalance, tough decisions are being made to restore responsible spending across the entirety of state government," Gabby Picard, Kehoe's spokesperson, said in an email.
According to the Missouri Department of Education, the planned cuts mean it can't support adding more children to the program. However, Missouri children already enrolled in the program will continue receiving books "as funding allows."
Indiana
Indiana began supporting the Imagination Library statewide through the 50/50 funding match model in 2023 under Republican Gov. Eric J. Holcomb, who championed the program. Lawmakers allotted $6 million to the program over two years.
In 2025, under Republican Gov. Mike Braun, GOP lawmakers cut the funding from the state budget entirely. Facing public backlash, the Indiana governor tasked his wife, Maureen Braun, with fundraising for the state-level match.
"In March, Mrs. Braun announced that fundraising for the state-level match for the program through June 30, 2027 is nearly complete," Griffin Reid, a spokesperson for Indiana's governor, said in an email. "The program is successfully delivering books to young Hoosiers in all 92 counties in Indiana."
According to the Indiana Capital Chronicle, the program was on hiatus while Maureen Braun fundraised.
News outlets have reported that the governor's office has consistently declined to share how much the first lady has raised. Reid also did not respond to our questions asking for specific numbers.
Did state Democrats cut funding?
Yes, in Washington, which was facing budget issues, and Maine, for unclear reasons. Nevada, which has a Republican governor but a Democratic state Legislature, also failed to renew several grants to help fund local partners of the Imagination Library.
Washington
Washington established its statewide program in 2022 through bipartisan legislation under Democratic leadership. The state also used the 50/50 match model.
In 2025, while facing a $12 billion shortfall, Washington cut all state funding to the Imagination Library under Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson and a Democrat-controlled Legislature.
State Superintendent Chris Reykdal, a Democrat, kept the program running through "limited discretionary funds" until June 2026. Reykdal has called on the Legislature and Ferguson to restore funding.
On July 31, 2026, the Imagination Library of Washington announced grants from two private foundations "expected to ultimately restore access for approximately 40,000 children and return the program to full statewide coverage."
Ferguson's office did not return an inquiry about restoring state funding.
Maine
Maine's Imagination Library program launched in late 2023 using the 50/50 match model after the Democratic state Legislature approved a $200,000 proposal from Democratic Gov. Janet Mills.
During Maine's budget process for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, both Mills and the Maine State Library requested funding to continue operating the program and to expand it into all of Maine's counties, according to emails from Beth Crist, director of special projects at Maine State Library, and Ben Goodman, a spokesperson with Mills' office.
The final budget the Legislature approved provided only $100,000 a year, however, which was not enough to expand the program, nor to support the existing nonprofit partners who administered it across seven counties at the time, Crist and Goodman said.
Maine's budget chairs, both Democrats, did not return an inquiry as to why the Legislature did not fully fund the program. Crist said the Legislature did not provide an explanation to Maine State Library.
Some chapters still operate in Maine without state funding.
Nevada
Nevada does not have a statewide Imagination Library program. However, in October 2025, Storied, a local partner serving Clark County, announced that the Nevada Legislature did not renew a grant that started in 2023, as the Nevada Current reported (and Storied confirmed).
Meredith Helmick, executive director of Storied, said in an email that the organization was able to resume its program in July 2026, "but on a much smaller scale."
"Kids will start receiving books in September," Helmick said.
Helmick said Storied spent the 10-month hiatus applying for local and state grants and receiving donations from local private foundations and individuals. She hopes to "find a path towards statewide coverage or to at least bring the program in Clark County back to its previous levels."
The Nevada Independent also reported that United Way Northern Nevada and the Sierra, a partner in Nevada's Washoe County, lost state grant funding in 2025.
However, a United Way Northern Nevada and the Sierra spokesperson, Daniel Amaya, said in an email that it was "changes in federal funding and resources being allocated elsewhere" that resulted in a pause in its partnership with Imagination Library.
"The loss of federal funds to the State of Nevada directly impacts the amount of money the state can allocate," Amaya said.
According to the Imagination Library's website, Washoe County no longer has an operating Imagination Library presence. United Way is seeking donations to resume the program.
"Our hope and goal is to restart Dolly Parton's Imagination Library in Northern Nevada as soon as we secure the funding needed," Amaya said. "We look forward to the day we can turn the page and begin this important work again."
Did Trump or the federal government cut funding?
Federal funding indirectly provided support to local partners who worked with the Imagination Library, even though the federal government doesn't directly fund the program.
Aside from Washoe County in Nevada, the Trump administration's 2025 cuts to federal grant funds affected at least one other area: New Hampshire's North Country, which is effectively the top half of the state.
Whitefield Public Library — the Imagination Library's local partner in the North Country — first launched the program in 2025 after months of work, said Vashaw, the director of Whitefield Public Library.
Part of that work involved finding a financial partner who could cover the local partner costs for the program: an organization called the Education Alliance for New Hampshire.
After just a "handful of months" of that group running the program, however, the Trump administration rescinded federal grant funding that the Education Alliance relied on. The Education Alliance closed down.
"Their doors were shuttered, their programs closed with very little notice and that meant we had no funding," Vashaw said. "We literally weren't sure we were going to be able to pay the bills come January."
The Department of Education declined to answer questions about these funds on the record.
After emergency fundraising, the Whitefield Public Library was able to keep the program going. As of this writing, 620 kids are enrolled, Vashaw said.
Vashaw said private fundraising isn't on track for 2027. However, she's hoping a bipartisan effort from New Hampshire lawmakers to make the Imagination Library available statewide will help keep the program going.

As the Hyderabad edition of The Hindu celebrates its Golden Jubilee, attention naturally turns to its editors, landmark stories and the newsroom leadership that helped build one of India’s most respected newspapers. Equally important, though far less celebrated, is the contribution of the district correspondents who served as the newspaper’s eyes and ears across united Andhra Pradesh.
When the Hyderabad edition was launched in September 1976, The Hindu had only a handful of staff reporters in the State, supplemented by part-time stringers in a few towns. In the early years, reporters from Hyderabad frequently travelled to districts, spending several days gathering stories and understanding local issues. The extensive use of local datelines reflected a growing recognition that readers wanted news from beyond the State capital.
As circulation expanded, The Hindu realised that sustained district coverage required a permanent presence on the ground. The newspaper gradually built a network of dedicated district correspondents, beginning with journalists such as Mahesh Vijapurkar in Warangal and Dasu Keshava Rao in Kurnool. Both would go on to occupy senior positions in the organisation, illustrating the importance attached to district journalism. Keshava Rao eventually became Chief of Bureau for united Andhra Pradesh, while Vijapurkar retired as Chief of Bureau of The Hindu’s Mumbai Bureau.
Even before the Hyderabad edition, The Hindu maintained footholds in Andhra Pradesh through reporters based in Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam. Late R.J. Rajendra Prasad, who retired as Chief of Bureau, A.P. was one among the most notable faces of The Hindu in Andhra Pradesh. He had the distinction of serving as the team leader for over three decades, a record. Among the pioneers was veteran journalist V. Ramachandran, who worked in Kurnool during the period when it served as the capital of the Andhra State carved out of the erstwhile Madras State. These early journalists laid the foundation for what would eventually become one of the strongest district reporting networks among English-language newspapers in the State.
The real expansion occurred during the 1990s. Responding to growing readership and the increasing importance of district-level news, The Hindu began appointing correspondents across almost every district of united Andhra Pradesh. By the early 2000s, dedicated representatives were present in nearly all districts. Their influence often extended beyond journalism. Some correspondents jokingly recalled being regarded as third in importance after the District Collector and Superintendent of Police. Politicians frequently preferred to begin major interactions only after the arrival of The Hindu correspondent, a reflection of the newspaper’s credibility and standing.
This network transformed the newspaper. District correspondents brought rural concerns into the mainstream, reporting on governance, agriculture, education, health care, irrigation projects, social movements and grassroots politics. Their work helped bridge the gap between villages and policymakers, ensuring that voices from Telangana, Rayalaseema and Coastal Andhra found a place in a newspaper known for its national outlook.
The evolution of district reporting was accompanied by rapid technological change. In the early years, stories were dictated over trunk-call telephone lines, sent through telegrams or dispatched by post. Filing a report could be a cumbersome and time-consuming exercise. Coverage itself remained largely centred on district administration, official announcements, major crimes and political visits.
Technology dramatically altered that landscape. Computers replaced typewriters, while fax machines, email, mobile phones and digital photography transformed the speed and efficiency of reporting. For district correspondents, these innovations represented a revolution. This writer, then posted in Nizamabad, was among the first two district correspondents in The Hindu to receive a Wipro Acer laptop in 1997, then a rare and prized possession. Stories could now be filed directly from remote locations using public STD booths. By connecting the laptop’s modem to a telephone line, reports could be transmitted to the newsroom within seconds. What once took hours or even days could now be accomplished almost instantly.
The Hyderabad edition played a crucial role in this transformation. For the first time, district journalists had a nearby editorial centre. Instead of routing stories through Madras, they could work directly with editors in Hyderabad. The result was quicker decision-making, stronger coordination and more contextual coverage of the State affairs.
The 1990s are often remembered as the golden age of district reporting in united Andhra Pradesh. Correspondents were no longer confined to covering official events. They became chroniclers of social and economic change, documenting droughts, agrarian distress, irrigation projects, rural development programmes, education initiatives and shifting village economies.
The period also coincided with the rise of the Naxalite movement across Telangana and parts of north coastal Andhra. Reporting from districts such as Warangal, Karimnagar, Adilabad, Khammam and Nizamabad demanded courage and balance. Correspondents frequently travelled into remote, conflict-prone regions to understand the reality. behind the headlines. Their reports helped readers comprehend not only incidents of violence but also the social and economic conditions that fuelled the insurgency. This writer himself went into the forests six times to interview the outlawed People’s War Group (now CPI -Maoists) naxalite leaders including three key Central Committee members.
District correspondents also played a pivotal role during the Telangana movement and the years leading to the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh. Long before the issue dominated national politics, correspondents were documenting changing public sentiment in villages, universities, government offices and public gatherings across the region. The history of The Hindu in united A.P. cannot be told solely through headlines, editorials or bureau exclusives. It is equally a story of district correspondents who travelled on dusty roads, attended village meetings, covered disasters and conflicts, reported elections and social movements, and chronicled the changing fortunes of a State.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction as rivers, including the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli, overflowed and swept away homes, roads, bridges, hydropower projects, and other infrastructure. Experts attributed the disaster to a glacial collapse near the Nepal-China border, which triggered a massive ice-and-rock avalanche and debris flow, sending huge amounts of water, mud, and debris into downstream river systems. As of 02 September 2026, the floods and landslides had killed more than 1,000 people across Nepal and Tibet, while more than 4,400 people remained missing. Search and rescue operations continued, particularly at hydropower projects where hundreds of workers were believed to be trapped in tunnels (here, here, and here).
Amid this, several videos are being shared on social media, claiming to show the actual visuals of the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The video shows real visuals of the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026.
Fact: None of these videos show the actual visuals of the August 2026 floods in Nepal. While the rescue of a girl and the destruction of bridges and buildings were real incidents, the videos circulating on social media are AI-generated and falsely linked to the Nepal floods. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows Nepal’s security forces rescuing a girl trapped under mud and debris.
Our investigation found that Nepal’s security forces did rescue a girl during a search and rescue operation. On 29 August 2026, the Facebook page of Nepal’s Armed Police Force posted a video of the rescue operation. According to the post, on 28 August, the Timore Rasuwa team of the Nepal Armed Police Force, in coordination with the Nepal Army, rescued a girl named Manisha Magar from a flood- and landslide-affected area and airlifted her to a hospital by helicopter.
However, the video going viral on social media is AI-generated and does not show the actual rescue operation.
Video 2
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows an elephant saving two children during floods in Nepal.
In our investigation, we found that the viral video is AI-generated and does not depict a real incident. The Hive AI Detection tool gave the video a score of 90.2%, indicating that it is likely AI-generated.
Video 3
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a real incident in Nepal in which a bridge collapses, causing people and vehicles on it to seemingly fall into a river and get swept away.
Our investigation found that several bridges were indeed swept away by the devastating floods in Nepal. However, the video going viral on social media is AI-generated and does not show a real incident.
Video 4
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a real incident in Nepal where a huge amount of water rushes towards a settlement, flooding it and destroying buildings.
In our investigation, we found that the viral video is AI-generated and does not depict a real incident. The Hive AI Detection tool gave the video a score of 65.2%, indicating that it is likely AI-generated.
Video 5
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a real incident in Nepal where a shark was spotted in floodwaters.
In our investigation, we found that the viral video is AI-generated and does not depict a real incident. The Hive AI Detection tool gave the video a score of 99.7%, indicating that it is likely AI-generated.
Video 6
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a real incident in Nepal where a multi-storey building with people inside is swept away by floodwaters.
Our investigation found that several buildings were indeed swept away by the devastating floods in Nepal. Reports (here, here, and here) and visuals from the affected areas showed homes and other structures being destroyed or swept away by powerful floodwaters. However, the video going viral on social media is AI-generated and does not show a real incident.
Video 7
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a real incident in Nepal where a young child is caught in floodwaters and seen holding onto a pole.
In our investigation, we found that the viral video is AI-generated and does not depict a real incident. The Hive AI Detection tool gave the video a score of 99.9%, indicating that it is likely AI-generated.
To sum up, none of these videos shows actual visuals of the August 2026 Nepal floods; they are AI-generated.

On Tuesday (September 1, 2026) morning, the medical camp at Gollaguppa village in Yetapaka mandal of Polavaram district looked like any routine camp held across the agency areas of the undivided districts of Visakhapatnam, Srikakulam, and East and West Godavari. But a pall of gloom descended on the camp by afternoon following the death of a seven-year-old girl, Madivi Jamuna. She was not alone — 52 others had taken ill, 47 of whom are children.
Polavaram District Collector K. Dinesh Kumar said on Wednesday (September 2, 2026): “As many as 23 children have been shifted from Lakshmipuram PHC to Bhadrachalam Area Hospital for better medical treatment.”
The cause of Madivi’s death and the sudden illness of the others is attributed to the administration of Chloroquine tablets.
This tablet is a routine drug administered in malaria-prone areas — both as a cure for malaria and as a preventive measure against the endemic that has plagued these tribal hamlets for decades.
These regions are heavily dominated by Plasmodium falciparum (P. falciparum), the species responsible for cerebral malaria, which historically accounts for 70% to 80% of Andhra Pradesh’s total malaria burden.
Though fatalities have declined over the last decade thanks to preventive measures implemented by the authorities, malaria remains rampant, especially after the monsoon season.
In 2024 and 2025, Alluri Sitharama Raju district, carved out of Visakhapatnam, recorded about 3,690 and over 3,500 cases, respectively. During the same period, Parvathipuram Manyam, carved out of Srikakulam, recorded approximately 2,650 and 1,820 cases. The State’s total stood at roughly 7,800 and 7,000 cases during those years.
‘A lifesaver and also a life taker’
“Chloroquine is a drug that is a lifesaver and also a life taker if not administered properly and monitored post-intake,” says Dr. P.V. Sudhakar, former principal of Andhra Medical College.
It can be administered as a treatment for someone suffering from malaria or as a preventive (prophylactic) drug. It is a potent medication, and certain conditions must be assessed before it is prescribed. During the initial days of the COVID-19 outbreak, it was widely discussed as a potential treatment, with U.S. President Donald Trump — he was then in his first term — requesting India to supply the drug, Dr. Sudhakar noted.
The drug has a very narrow therapeutic index, meaning the margin between a safe, effective dose and a toxic or lethal one is extremely small.
Improper dosing or administering it on an empty stomach, particularly to young children, can cause severe adverse effects and lead to fatalities.
Common initial symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, headache, dizziness, and skin rashes. High doses can trigger a sudden drop in blood pressure (hypotension) or blood sugar levels (hypoglycemia).
Severe reactions can lead to seizures, vision impairment, central nervous system damage, and cardiac arrest. “This is why, before administering it, healthcare workers must verify that patients, especially children, are not on an empty stomach and do not show signs of underlying diseases, malnourishment, or dehydration. The dosage must be calculated based on these parameters and cannot simply be generalised,” Dr. Sudhakar explained.
Why have people fallen sick?
This drug has been in wide use across tribal districts throughout the State for a long time. Why, then, have so many people fallen sick all at once?
Apart from the standard risk factors, senior doctors from King George Hospital in Visakhapatnam emphasise the need to inspect the quality of the administered batch. The batch numbers, expiry dates, and storage conditions must be investigated by the authorities, as improper storage can lead to drug degradation or contamination.
The medical fraternity strongly recommended an immediate chemical analysis of this batch to determine why it affected such a large number of people.

Former lawyer sues DOJ claiming she was fired for refusing to recommend Mel Gibson get his gun rights back
Liz Oyer claims she was told to ignore her concerns because Gibson is an acquaintance of Donald Trump
The former U.S. pardon attorney has sued the Justice Department, alleging she was wrongly fired last year in the face of pressure from the Trump administration after she refused to recommend that actor Mel Gibson have his gun rights reinstated.
“This case is about much more than what happened to me,” Liz Oyer, who served as pardon attorney between 2022 and March 2025, said in a Thursday statement. “All Americans rely on nonpartisan civil servants to keep them safe and to uphold the law without fear or favor. I was fired because I refused to put politics ahead of my duty to the American people.”
Oyer’s suit alleges the Trump administration violated both her constitutional rights and federal law protecting civil servants by terminating her last March without notice or a chance to be heard.
The complaint, filed in Washington, D.C., federal court, claims that the staff of then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche asked her to add Gibson’s name to a list of individuals who would be recommended to get their gun rights restored.
Oyer says she refused, noting Gibson had not been thoroughly vetted and had previously pleaded no contest in 2011 to a charge of battering his former girlfriend.
A Blanche staffer then allegedly called Oyer, speaking in a “bullying tone and suggested to Ms. Oyer that she would be wise to make the recommendation,” according to the lawsuit. President Trump named Gibson a Hollywood ambassador in January of 2025.
In a March 7 memo to the attorney general’s office, Oyer again did not recommend that Gibson have his firearm rights restored, and she was terminated the same day.
Oyer then challenged the firing before the Merit Systems Protection Board, a panel designed to review claims from government workers, but said in her suit the petition has yet to receive “any substantive review” and is stuck in “prolonged limbo.”
Asked for comment, the Justice Department pointed to testimony this summer from Attorney General Todd Blanche’s confirmation hearings.
“I had known nothing about Mel Gibson or that letter when I fired her, nothing,” Blanche testified.
The DOJ, in a statement to The Independent, also criticized the “killers whose death sentences she recommended be commuted.”
Republican lawmakers have criticized Oyer for recommending that 40 death sentences get converted to life sentences without parole during the Biden administration.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
Since her firing, Oyer has become a vocal critic of the Trump administration.
In July, she testified against Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general, claiming he had “laid waste to the Department’s most valuable assets: its credibility and its talented workforce.”
Last year, she alleged the Trump administration was abusing the pardon power to give relief to individuals convicted of corruption.
The president is “liberally pardoning corrupt public officials who are charged with offenses that involve abusing their political offices to enrich themselves,” Oyer told PBS.

Krystle D’Souza and Rida Tharana have emerged as the winners of The Traitors Season 2. The finale saw the two contestants reach the end of the game as Traitors and successfully keep their identities hidden from the other finalists.
The Traitors Season 2 finale: Krystle D’Souza and Rida Tharana emerge as winners
The final group included Mallika Sherawat, Sahil Salathia, Dalip Tahil, Shalini Passi, Krystle D’Souza and Rida Tharana. As the game reached its final stage, trust became central to the contestants’ decisions, eventually leaving Krystle and Rida to make the final call.
The two chose to trust each other and revealed themselves as Traitors, securing the win.
Krystle D’Souza’s journey as an original Traitor
Krystle entered the palace as one of the original Traitors and managed to avoid elimination despite repeated suspicion from the other contestants. Speaking about her strategy, she said, “Being a Traitor sounds glamorous until you actually have to lie every day to people you genuinely like.”
She added, “Since I was a Traitor from the very beginning, I knew over-explaining or getting defensive would give me away. So I learnt kab bolna hai, kab chup rehna hai, and when to just smile and sit back.”
Reflecting on her ability to survive suspicion, Krystle recalled her comment to Karan Johar, saying, “I even told Karan, ‘Boo ke baad main hi yahaan ki billi hoon,’ and somehow, I kept landing on my feet.”
Rida Tharana’s unexpected turn
Rida started the competition as an Innocent and initially focused on identifying the Traitors. Her game changed after Krystle recruited her, turning her into one of the very contestants she had been trying to expose.
Rida admitted that the change was difficult, particularly because she had formed genuine bonds in the palace. “If someone had told me on Day One that I would end this game as a Traitor, I would have laughed,” she said.
She added, “As a Traitor, I had a clear roadmap to the finale, but the hardest part was dealing with the guilt of playing against people I genuinely cared about.”
Rida summed up her journey by saying, “I walked into the palace as an Innocent, became a Traitor, and walked out a winner. I couldn’t have imagined a more unexpected ending.”
Hosted by Karan Johar, The Traitors Season 2 is streaming on Prime Video.

Donald Trump has claimed his commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, erroneously stated that no Americans had been killed in the war with Iran because he was thinking about a previous US operation, in Venezuela.
The claim, at odds with the Pentagon’s count of 18 US service members dead in the US-Israel war on Iran, sparked a swift backlash as Trump struggles to end the conflict after six months.
In a post on his Truth Social platform on Thursday, the US president wrote: “Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed. 18 people were killed in Iran!”
The rebuke came a day after Lutnick appeared on CNBC’s Squawk Box and framed the Trump administration’s approach to Iran as primarily economic. Describing the strategy as an “economic choke-out”, he erroneously told the network there had not been American deaths in the conflict, adding that he was optimistic bond markets would respond well to the approach.
Lutnick this morning acknowledged the mistake, posting on X that he had misspoken and also claiming he had been thinking of the US operation in Venezuela, where US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January with minimal US casualties. The Pentagon said seven US troops were injured and none were killed in that operation, while Venezuelan officials put their overall death toll at 47, and Cuba said 32 of its military and police personnel were killed.
Trump’s post landed as Iranian authorities detailed heavy casualties from the latest US strikes. Iran’s health ministry said Tuesday night’s strikes killed 18 people and wounded 108, while the country’s Red Crescent identified that four people were killed and 67 wounded when a US strike hit a wedding ceremony near the coast of the strait of Hormuz, which also killed a child. Reuters said it was able to verify the location of the damaged building using satellite imagery.
A US Central Command spokesperson, Capt Tim Hawkins, said the US military does not target civilians and that the reports, which originated with Iranian state media, were being reviewed.
The strikes were part of a broader operation that Central Command said hit Iranian air defense systems, radar installations, maritime assets, mine-laying equipment and communications sites near the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which a large share of the world’s oil passes.
The Pentagon’s capacity to independently verify such claims has been sharply reduced. Its Civilian Protection Center of Excellence has been cut from 40 staff to nine since the start of last year, according to the Pentagon’s own inspector general, while the department has also stopped developing a database meant to track civilian harm from US operations.
The episode has exposed a wider tension in how the White House is presenting the conflict.
Officials have sought to characterize the campaign (estimated to have cost at least $37.5bn as of July) against Iran in economic terms even as it continues to produce US military deaths, mounting Iranian civilian casualties and rising oil prices.
Polling from UMass-Amherst in late August found that 54% of Americans disapprove of the war initiated by the US and Israel, and one in six Trump voters would go back and change their vote in 2024.
The current round of fighting began after the US struck rocket launchers on Larak Island that officials said were being prepared to mine the strait, prompting Iranian missile and drone attacks on US and allied positions in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq. Jordanian authorities said 13 ballistic missiles were fired at the country, of which 10 were intercepted.
Trump described Iran’s retaliation as a “love tap”, but warned that further strikes remained an option. “It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one anytime we want,” he said earlier this week.

Trump made the post on June 19, 2025 — it was not a 2026 "Labor Day message," as some people claimed.
Rumors spread in early September 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump posted a message to social media claiming that it costs America "billions of dollars" to keep businesses closed on federal holidays.
People on social media platforms and Reddit shared a screenshot of the alleged post and added comments like, "a president notorious for spending weekends at Mar-a-Lago to golf and ham it up at sycophantic dinner parties, thinks American workers get too many non-working holidays."
The screenshot circulated as the United States approached the annual Labor Day holiday on Sept. 7.
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., wrote a lengthy criticism of what she called Trump's "Labor Day message" on her X account on Sept. 2.
Trump shared the post on Truth Social, but it wasn't a Labor Day message, nor was it posted in 2026.
Trump posted the message at 7:03 p.m. on June 19, 2025. It can also be viewed on Trump's Truth, an archive of all of Trump's Truth Social posts.
The full post read:
Too many non-working holidays in America. It is costing our Country $BILLIONS OF DOLLARS to keep all of these businesses closed. The workers don't want it either! Soon we'll end up having a holiday for every once working day of the year. It must change if we are going to, MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!
A search revealed 29 Truth Social posts from Trump on June 19, 2025, including the post in question, but none of the others appeared to be related to that post.
While it was unclear what specifically Trump was posting about at the time, June 19 is recognized as Juneteenth, a holiday commemorating the end of slavery in the U.S. Juneteenth became a federally recognized holiday under then-President Joe Biden in 2021.
Given Trump's track record at criticizing Biden in speeches, online posts, debates and in interviews, it's possible this post was another attempt at diminishing his predecessor's accomplishments.
We reached out to the White House to clarify whether Trump's post from June 19, 2025, was indeed meant as commentary on Juneteenth and/or Biden and will update this article if we receive a response.

Smelling a potential victory in the midterms, House Democrats are starting to think about oversight investigations next year and how to wield the power of the purse to make the Trump administration comply. In short, Trump’s West Wing renovations and DC arch could be on the chopping block, sources tell Inner Loop.
The nature of any investigations, and where Democrats will try to wrestle back power from the executive, are still to be determined, in part because taking back the House majority is not a foregone conclusion.
But House Democrats have a slew of investigations planned if they do end up controlling the chamber come November. Congressional committee aides have already been exploring how to force recalcitrant officials and family in Trump’s orbit to answer subpoenas.
With Trump uniquely focused on personal vanity projects this term, among the ideas is to more aggressively wield the power of congressional appropriations and threaten funding for Trump’s construction projects.
If Trump tries to block an investigation or ignores Congress and renames more buildings, House Democrats might cut off funding for any of Trump’s future West Wing renovations or perhaps block money for Trump’s triumphal arch.
The top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Jamie Raskin, also suggested this week that cutting off funding could be used to rein in projects Trump has already started.
“We have the power of the purse, and we will make sure Donald Trump doesn’t destroy any other federal buildings or landmarks,” Raskin told reporters when asked what recourse Democrats have after a sharply divided Supreme Court permitted Trump to keep building his ballroom.
“Congress established the appropriation for the White House, and it's up to Congress to decide, and it's not up to the president to decide to bulldoze half of the White House because he wakes up that day thinking it's a good thing to do,” says Raskin.
Traditional enforcement of subpoenas through the courts can take years, as a case makes its way through the federal district court in Washington and then any inevitable appeals. In his first term, for instance, Trump asserted executive privilege for former White House counsel Don McGahn, who was subpoenaed but never testified while Trump was in office.
Democratic aides have also been weighing other ideas to make subpoena noncompliance unattractive, like adding cumulative monetary fines through an inherent contempt provision in the House rules, sources tell Inner Loop.
But legal experts have long believed the only way to give subpoenas teeth is for Congress to pass legislation that fast-tracks judicial review for contested subpoenas so they get resolved while the president is still in office.
The most viable idea kicked around in recent years has been a bill that sends a subpoena dispute to a federal district court panel, with an appeal that goes straight to the Supreme Court. Still, it is no panacea, given that the Justice Department prosecutes subpoena noncompliance, and it would never prosecute its own officials.
Trump might have to choose—subpoena or arch.

In Summary
- Instagram has announced a new feature for its app, called First Draft. Available only for iPhone users at the time of writing, it trims and blends selected videos, converting them into a reel within seconds.
- Although First Draft’s editing is on the basic side, it is nevertheless extremely useful for those newcomers (or even veterans) who are not comfortable with editing videos.
- Experts might find First Draft to be very basic, but its ease of use and speed make it perfect for content creators who feel held back by their lack of basic video editing ability.
Instagram has just rolled out a new feature, which it claims is going to make creating Reels easier. As its name suggests, First Draft basically gives users a quick “first draft” by turning all the video clips that they have selected into a quick Reel. The feature is an iPhone exclusive for now and only available on the main Instagram app, and not on Edits (the Reels editing app by Instagram), but an Android release is likely to follow soon.
Given all the AI hype and how much Meta is focusing on it, you might think First Draft is a new AI feature, but Instagram has confirmed that First Draft does not use Artificial Intelligence. Nevertheless, it has made people wonder if its ease of use could actually reduce the role of conventional, “manual” editing in the Reel world. Well, we have used the feature for a short while, and here is what we think.
How to use Instagram First Draft
Using First Draft is a pretty simple affair. Just follow these steps:
- Open the Instagram app on your iPhone (do remember to update it to the latest version), then tap on the “+” icon present on the top left side of the app to add new content.
- From there, swipe to Reels on the panel on the lower part of the app.
- Tap on the camera to record footage or select an existing video from your gallery, which will be displayed.
- Once you have selected all the clips you wish to add, look for the First Draft option, which will appear on the panel at the lower part of the app – it appears the moment you select a video. Tapping it will open a First Draft box, with a “Try it” button. Tap on this button.
- Hitting the button puts the selected videos into a processing phase where the app analyses the clips, identifies highlights, trims clips, and reduces the length.
- In a matter of ten seconds, the feature will present a pretty basic edited version of your videos, trimming them and cutting out awkward pauses, with preview frames beneath the result, which you can move back and forth to reorder.
- If you like the results, tap on the Next button in the bottom right corner of the app to go to the Instagram Reels posting page (you can also take your results to Edits), make more changes, if need be, and hit Publish.
How First Draft works
Instagram has stressed that the new editing feature is just a “starting point” on which creators can then build their final Reel. The social media platform says the feature can identify silences, awkward pauses, and other such moments. It then removes these moments, trims the video, and gives a first draft that highlights what it assumes are important parts of the video. It allows creators to select or record, edit, and share all without leaving Instagram.
Instagram has been ensuring that users know that all that is done by the feature is reversible, and does not come as an attempt to replace a creator’s creativity, but actually offers ‘early video trimming’ so users can move their focus from the technical part of editing to its creative part. Instead of using AI (which comes as a surprise), First Draft actually uses internal processing and audio detection to find moments of silence in selected videos. We have fiddled with the feature for a short while and can say that it actually works,serving up a very basic edit of videos (or of a single long video), even while leaving the “creative work” to the user.
Going by our first encounter with First Draft, it cannot really replace manual editing. It is not a very creative feature and only offers what can be termed as the ‘bare-bones’ of what your edited Reel might look like. We found the feature does eliminate pauses and silence, but when it trims videos, there seems to be no method to its madness, which basically means you can end up with some of the important bits removed from the video. In its current form, it might come in handy for people who create piece-to-camera video formats, but you would still need to revise and re-edit the whole thing on your own.
Also See: Instagram Edits vs CapCut: Best Video Editing App for You
First Draft: Who is it for (and who might not like it)
It is rather basic, but those who are new to creating videos and struggle with editing might find First Draft useful. It offers a very quick, hassle-free edit of videos. This can be helpful for creators who are not as skilled when it comes to editing their content, or are intimidated by the task. First Draft can be a very simple, quick-fix solution for them. But it is unlikely to appeal much to those creators who have been in the game for a while, are good at editing, and have their own style and flair in the editing field. We can already see them skipping this new feature.
But given that a large number of Instagram users do not really know much about video editing, First Draft seems to be an extremely handy tool, especially for those who do not want to get into the hassle of going through all their videos one by one and trimming out stutters and pauses. The fact that one can do so right from within Instagram, without having to open an additional app, is a huge bonus. As mentioned by the platform itself, First Draft is just a starting point and nothing more. Even in its current form (and we think it will get better in clip selection), it will help new creators start their content journey and feel more comfortable without getting knee-deep in editing hassles from the get-go.
Experts might shake their heads at how basic the feature is, but then remember how DSLR photographers shook their heads at 0.3 MP cellphone cameras? First Draft might be the first step to breaking down the editing barrier that holds back many content creators, and if it gets better (maybe with even options to automatically choose background audio or add subtitles in other languages, and so on), who knows, even experts might find it a handy tool to save them some time. But that’s in the future (and we bet AI will come into it at some stage). As for now, First Draft is mainly for Instagram newbies who want Reel creation with zero hassles. And that actually is a bigger deal than some of the pros might admit.

The MAGA Right Is Only Pretending to Be Censored
The conspiracy theory that persists even though no evidence supports it
For nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case. Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases. Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined. Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist website, then the undersecretary of state for public diplomacy—sent out a request for files on anyone who had communicated with or written about the Global Engagement Center, a now-dissolved agency that once worked to expose propaganda campaigns by Russia, China, Iran, and other countries around the world.
The request, seen last year by the MIT Technology Review, was far-reaching. Beattie was seeking information on Bill Gates; the commentator Bill Kristol; Chris Krebs, a former U.S. cybersecurity official; a German government minister; the analyst Renée DiResta, formerly at Stanford University, as well as others associated with a research project called the Election Integrity Partnership; and, as it happens, me.
This unprecedented investigation was meant to expose the Biden administration’s “censorship–industrial complex,” a shadowy network allegedly dedicated to the mass suppression of American free speech. Since 2020, internet trolls have accused Biden-administration officials, social-media companies, and university researchers of weaving a nefarious plot to censor conservatives. Since 2025, MAGA ideologues have been using this alleged plot as an excuse to dismantle government programs, stifle research, intimidate American citizens, and even distort American foreign policy.
And yet for the past year and half, neither Beattie nor anyone else has actually managed to prove that the plot ever existed. Like a soap bubble that vanishes with the touch of a hand, the “censorship–industrial complex” belongs to that mystical category of things that disappear when you examine them too closely.
The failure to produce evidence is not for lack of trying. During the Biden administration, MAGA allies and politicians filed multiple lawsuits with the goal of exposing alleged censorship. None has done so. One of them, brought by the Missouri attorney general, made it all the way to the Supreme Court before justices asked for underlying evidence that the government had censored anyone. The answer was no. Another, brought against the Stanford research project by America First Legal—Stephen Miller’s team—failed in July, when a judge found the suit had no standing, no jurisdiction, and, after a discovery process requested by the plaintiffs, no evidence. There was no proof, in other words, that the Stanford research had resulted in anyone being censored. Other cases against the Biden administration were simply settled by President Trump’s Department of Justice without finding any evidence of “censorship” either.
Now the Trump administration’s most dedicated ideologues have also failed, spectacularly, to prove the existence of a “censorship–industrial complex” inside the State Department. After months of searching, Beattie’s successor as undersecretary for public diplomacy, Sarah Rogers, recently decided to publicize the unimpressive results of the inquiry into the Global Engagement Center. But instead of writing a report admitting that the documents that surfaced contained nothing of interest, she leaked them, selectively, to an internet troll known as DataRepublican.
Here is where the story becomes especially convoluted, and I will simplify as best I can. “DataRepublican” is the X pseudonym of Jennica Pounds, who has a history of misreading data and connecting dots to describe nonexistent conspiracies. But the plan went wrong: Upon receipt of raw documents from Rogers, including screenshots without context, Pounds decided that Rogers was a “Deep State” operative and refused to release them. Subsequently, it emerged that Pounds herself has been secretly employed by the Pentagon, which presumably makes her a deep-state operative too. But that’s another story.
Because Pounds would not publish the documents, Rogers did so herself, in a long thread on X. As she must have known, they contained no evidence of conspiracy, no proof that anyone in the Biden administration censored millions or even dozens of social-media posts. Instead, Rogers, who is theoretically responsible for promoting good relations with people in foreign countries, went after a series of U.S. citizens. She found a GEC official who had about a dozen email exchanges with the Stanford project, almost all about Russian accounts. She posted a brief excerpt of the congressional testimony of Daniel Kimmage, a former State Department employee and GEC deputy coordinator, who truthfully explained that the center was set up to deal with foreign disinformation, not American media. Rogers wrote that “that was a lie,” without offering proof.
Rogers also included several misleading posts about the Stanford project, plucking a number from a table and implying that it meant the researchers had somehow targeted more than 400,000 tweets, when they in fact had merely noted their existence. More to the point, the Stanford team did so after the election, not in some kind of smoke-filled room but in an academic report that is still publicly available and that DiResta has cited repeatedly.
Rogers also criticized another very public, not remotely secret report, written jointly by the United States, Britain, Canada, Germany, Slovakia, and the European Union, investigating “gendered disinformation,” a subject that sounds very “woke” until you realize that deepfake porn videos and orchestrated misogyny are tactics regularly used against female politicians such as Annalena Baerbock, a former German foreign minister, or Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister. The Iranian regime uses them to harass female dissidents around the world. Democratic governments would be negligent if they did not try to understand them. But even if you are not bothered by the online harassment of women in politics, it’s still impossible to argue that the publication of a report (and its translation into nine languages) proves the existence of a secret censorship–industrial complex stifling Americans’ views. “Watergate it was not,” Orna Blum, a former State Department official, wrote last week.
And if the scandal wasn’t Watergate, Rogers is not Bob Woodward. She is a public servant who dumped raw data online, seemingly without asking whether anyone would be damaged or which American foreign-policy interests could be served, all in the name of proving nothing.
In the normal course of things the saga of the GEC documents would be, and should be, dismissed as a storm in a teapot. But unfortunately, the administration’s pursuit of a nonexistent censorship–industrial complex has already had real consequences for real people. In April 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that he was closing the Global Engagement Center because it had “spent millions of dollars to actively silence and censor the voices of Americans they were supposed to be serving.” This was untrue, and even at the time there was no evidence for such an extraordinary statement. On the contrary, the GEC was the only institution in the U.S. government that was publicly tracking hostile international information operations, including by exposing websites in Africa or Latin America that appeared local but were in fact run by Moscow or Beijing. Rubio’s statement maligned the people who worked on these reports. Will the secretary of state now apologize to them? Compensate them? Rehire them?
The closing of the center also means that no one is now doing that work. Thanks to Rogers, Beattie, and a handful of others, the U.S. decided to blind itself to the reality that Russia, China, and Iran, with its viral animated Lego videos, all run deceptive campaigns that reach millions of people around the world. And now Americans do nothing to halt, explain, or counter them.
But it is not only American foreign policy that has been damaged. Following a series of expensive lawsuits as well as public harassment, Stanford shut down its internet-monitoring projects too. DiResta, one of the most prominent scholars in the field, left the university and was subjected to years of online harassment, an experience she has previously described in The Atlantic. Other research projects across the country also suffered, as funders and university provosts were, paradoxically, scared away by the Trump administration’s threats to curtail their free speech in the name of halting “censorship.”
The study of foreign online campaigns and the proliferation of conspiracy theories has now become difficult and controversial, for people both inside and outside the government. That doesn’t mean that these campaigns don’t exist. It just means that Americans don’t know about them, don’t understand them, and cannot track them.
As if this same conspiracy theory had not done enough damage, Rogers and others at the State Department are also putting the nonexistent censorship–industrial complex at the center of American foreign policy toward Europe now too. At a conference at the Hudson Institute last spring, Rogers said that a “censorship class” had already “scuttled to Europe” to pursue a supposed vendetta against Americans from across the ocean. At the same event, Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri—who, in his previous role as the state’s attorney general, had brought one of the failed lawsuits against Stanford and supported legal challenges to the 2020 election—declared that “we are witnessing a deeply troubling assault on free speech” in Europe.
These views, all of which derive from the same set of false stories, are actively shaping American policy in Europe. Late last month, the State Department put forth plans to spend $4 million to support right-wing media in Europe, including a consortium of “independent journalists” who would support the Trump administration’s view of the world. In recent months, the U.S. has imposed visa restrictions on Thierry Breton, a former EU commissioner who is now a private citizen, for his role in creating the Digital Services Act, a European law designed to protect minors, provide transparency around algorithms and targeted advertising, and ensure that behavior on the internet conforms to existing legislation. The U.S. also sanctioned four European researchers who campaigned for the digital-services law or against hate speech—essentially punishing them for their free speech, in the name of promoting free speech. Two of them, the leaders of a German organization called HateAid, called the visa ban “an act of repression by a government that is increasingly disregarding the rule of law and trying to silence its critics by any means necessary.”
Belatedly, even some part of the Trump administration appears to have quietly concluded that all of this has gone too far and that maybe, in fact, it would be useful for the U.S. government to understand how hostile governments seek to manipulate the internet. In May, the State Department put out a tender for software developers who could help analyze “foreign adversarial propaganda” and thus replicate the work once done by the Global Engagement Center. In August, a State Department contractor also posted a job opening for research analysts who can, among other things, “evaluate how foreign governments, state-sponsored organizations, terrorist groups, and other malign actors use social media and digital communications to influence public opinion and targeted audiences.”
As DiResta wrote this week, “they’re hiring people to do the very job they just spent 16 months claiming was a conspiracy.” So much time, energy, and money was wasted pursuing a fiction. Now more time, energy, and money will need to be spent to clean up the damage.

The story so far: As OpenAI last week launched its Health offering in ChatGPT for U.S. users, a new lawsuit against the company began gaining traction online. Dated June 12, 2026, the U.S. lawsuit focuses on a suicide linked to an older ChatGPT model that is no longer available, but was until recently used by people all over the world: GPT-4o.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani announces ban on AI use for students until high school
What is the latest case linked to OpenAI’s GPT-4o?
The lawsuit focuses on Christian Faith Madison, 29, a late mother and working professional based in the U.S. state of Alabama. Ms. Madison began using ChatGPT (model GPT-4o) in December 2024, according to the lawsuit, with her work-related interactions shifting to praise, affection, and flattery from the chatbot.
The interactions then began to take on a dark, religious tone, with the chatbot allegedly convincing Ms. Madison that she was a religious saviour or messiah-like figure who needed to suffer and die to be resurrected. She later died by suicide on June 9, 2025. The lawsuit was filed by an administrator of her estate, on behalf of her minor son.
In particular, the legal filing highlighted the development of OpenAI’s GPT-4o, claiming that the system’s rushed development and inadequate safety performance training made existing issues even worse.
“The system’s design prioritized keeping users engaged above all else. It portrayed anthropomorphic traits, convincing some users that it was more than just a coded chatbot. It was excessively sycophantic, which fueled vulnerable users’ psychosis and delusions. And in tragic cases, the design flaws led ChatGPT-4o to push users to self-harm or suicide. Releasing ChatGPT-4o in this manner was a calculated decision – a conscious choice with enormous risks,” stated the lawsuit.
The filing observed that OpenAI’s Dr. Ilya Sutskever, a co-founder, resigned the day after GPT-4o’s launch, while researcher Jan Leike resigned days later.
What made GPT-4o different from other models?
On May 13, 2024, OpenAI introduced GPT‑4o as a “step towards much more natural human-computer interaction”.
Between February and April 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman praised the updates that were introduced to the model. However, on April 28, 2025, he noted that the “last couple” of updates made the model’s personality “too sycophant-y and annoying” and that the company was working to fix this immediately.
In a blog post dated April 29, OpenAI observed that “GPT‑4o skewed towards responses that were overly supportive but disingenuous,” adding that people would instead be using an earlier version with more balanced behaviour. For context, 16-year-old Adam Raine — a ChatGPT user — had died by suicide on April 11.
OpenAI announced in January this year that it would be retiring GPT‑4o, GPT‑4.1, GPT‑4.1 mini, and OpenAI o4-mini in ChatGPT. The transition triggered a range of negative reactions as a number of users had become emotionally attached to GPT-4o and its responsive style, catching even Mr. Altman by surprise.
Sycophancy in AI
Will the U.S. government take action against OpenAI over GPT-4o?
Multiple lawsuits against OpenAI are ongoing in the U.S., so a definitive answer has not yet emerged. These actions have been filed by separate legal teams in many cases, and cover both user suicides and injuries, as well as homicides.
For example, the U.S. legal firm Edelson PC said it had filed seven wrongful death and negligence lawsuits on behalf of families affected by the Tumbler Ridge shooting in Canada. These lawsuits alleged that OpenAI did not act to stop the shooting in spite of having knowledge of the shooter’s profile and plans. Edelson PC is also representing the family of Adam Raine, and the estate of Suzanne Adams, a woman who was murdered at 83 by her son who used ChatGPT.
Several related lawsuits, including the one for Ms. Madison’s case, echo the same points: they allege a hurried GPT-4o launch, inadequate or highly sped-up safety training, a focus on keeping users engaged for longer, high levels of sycophancy that encouraged the users’ thoughts of self-harm or suicide, and a design that evoked the feeling of intimate interactions with other human beings — even if this led to dangerous offline actions.
Is OpenAI legally in the clear with its later AI models?
Mishi Choudhary, a technology lawyer and activist who founded the Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in) organisation, told The Hindu there was not yet enough independent evidence to say whether OpenAI’s newer models were “reliably safe” for young people or those in distress.
“Some recent research suggests that newer models may be better at asking direct questions about suicide risk and may produce fewer overtly harmful responses in controlled tests. But the same studies identify continuing failures,” Ms. Choudhary explained.
“We see from research studies that models continue to miss indirect or culturally expressed warning signs, respond inconsistently across a longer conversation, and cannot be relied upon like a human therapist to pick up warnings,” she added.
From a legal perspective, Ms. Choudhary cited past pharmaceuticals and software cases, noting that a manufacturer does not ordinarily escape liability just by withdrawing or replacing a product after an alleged injury.
While OpenAI’s users and customers look forward to adopting newer and more advanced AI models, the lawsuits against GPT-4o call on tech users to remember and pay attention to the past.

A Ravenloft series is currently in development from executive producer Alfonso Cuarón, writer and executive producer John August, and Hasbro Entertainment, Deadline reports. It could bring to life one of Dungeons & Dragons’ most iconic campaign settings, which got an update earlier this year with Ravenloft: The Horrors Within.
Dungeons & Dragons is getting a ‘Ravenloft’ live-action Netflix series
The series will reportedly delve into the origins of D&D’s most famous vampire, Strahd von Zarovich.
Netflix’s Ravenloft series will reportedly center on the infamous Strahd, according to Deadline:
At its heart, the series follows the making of the vampire Darklord Strahd von Zarovich, whose story of power, love, obsession, and undead transformation charts his origins from tragic antihero to one of Dungeons & Dragons’ most notorious villains.
Unfortunately, the announcement also comes with a disappointing update for another Dungeons & Dragons adaptation. Deadline says Netflix is no longer developing its live-action Forgotten Realms series from Shawn Levy and Drew Crevello. Hopefully the Ravenloft series doesn’t meet the same fate.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".
