In Summary
- The Poco M8x is the latest phone from Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, and is targeted at the budget segment.
- The phone is the first in the Indian market to come with the new Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also boasts a massive 7900 mAh battery.
- At Rs 20,999, the Poco M8x packs a punch in everyday use. It cuts some corners in the display department, but remains a very good option for those wanting reliable performance on a budget.
Even as smartphone prices head north, a new budget contender has entered the Indian smartphone market. Xiaomi’s sub-brand Poco has launched the Poco M8x 5G. With a starting price of Rs 20,999, the smartphone is the first in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also packs in a huge 7900 mAh battery. It also packs in some good specs and some decent ones, but is that enough to help it deliver a performance that can make it stand out in a segment which is not as spec-forward as it once used to be? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Poco M8x Appearance and Design: Premium looks even at a budget price
The Poco M8x may be a budget smartphone but does not look like it. We received the Leather Green variant, and it is, without a doubt, the best-looking version of the device. There are plain-ish black and blue colors on offer too, but the combination of muted gold and that vegan leather back makes the Leather Green look very good indeed.
The back has a rectangular camera unit with rounded sides. This is slightly raised and comes with a matte gold finish and a shiny metallic gold outline around it. There are two large, dark camera lenses arranged vertically on the left side of the camera unit, while the flash is encased in a long, vertical pill-shaped island on the right. The Poco badge appears on the lower portion of the back, which is covered with textured green eco-leather goodness. This not only helps the phone stand out from the usual budget segment crowd but also keeps scratches and smudges at one arm’s distance. We are guilty of packing multiple gadgets in the same bag compartment, which often roughs them up, but the Poco M8x still looks brand new in spite of many such crowded trips.
The front of the phone is more regular-looking. It is all about a tall display, surrounded by bezels which can be termed “thick” now, for those who notice them. There is a punch-hole notch in the middle of the top of the display, which is home to the front camera. The sides of the phone also come in the same gold shade as the camera unit and house ports and buttons. The left side of the frame is completely plain, while the right side carries the volume rocker and the power/lock button, which doubles up as a physical fingerprint scanner as well. While it has been written off in almost every other smartphone segment, you do get to see the mighty 3.5 mm audio jack in the budget segment. The Poco M8x comes with one right on top of the phone, although the trademark IR blaster has been skipped. The base holds the hybrid SIM card tray, along with a USB Type-C port and a speaker grille.
The Poco M8x is a big phone, and this is immediately noticeable – it is 170 mm tall and 78.4 mm wide. It is relatively slim at 8.8 mm, but at 232 grams, it makes its presence felt both in hand and in pocket. While the phone feels very good in hand, one needs both hands to use. It is a pretty sturdy customer too – it comes with an IP64 rating which provides some dust and water resistance, while the screen has Corning Gorilla Glass 7i protection.
Poco M8x Spec sheet: Fit for its segment
Its design may look more premium than its price, but the Poco M8x’s spec sheet slots very well in the budget segment, or rather the new budget segment that has been defined by increasing component prices. It is the first smartphone in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor. This is paired with 4 GB and 6 GB RAM and 128 GB storage, which can be expanded up to 2 TB using a microSD card.
The display on the phone is big – a 6.9-inch HD+ LCD display (yep, those have made a comeback) with a 120 Hz refresh rate. There are two cameras on the back of the phone, one being the main 50-megapixel sensor and the other an “auxiliary” one, while the one on the front for selfies and video calls is an 8-megapixel sensor.
One of the major spec USPs of the Poco M8x is its battery. The phone comes with a large 7900 mAh battery, with support for 45 W fast wired charging and 22.5 W reverse wired charging as well. The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 out of the box with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3 on top of it, with a promise of 4 years of OS and 6 years of security updates. In the sound department, it features stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack as well. Since it has an LCD display, the fingerprint scanner is on the side. All in all, these are good specs for the price the Poco M8x charges.
Poco M8x Performance: A consistent daily driver
The Poco M8x delivers the performance its spec sheet promises. The processor and RAM combination is budget-level, and the phone manages to get through everyday smartphone tasks with ease. Jumping from one app to another, social media scrolls, messaging, emails, photography, and calls are all handled without strain. Casual games like Tetris and Subway Surfers run with ease too. The phone is not designed to handle high-end games – we tried Genshin Impact, and not surprisingly, the experience was laggy even with tweaked settings.
The display is big, and the 120 Hz refresh rate does make the process of scrolling on social media a pretty smooth one. However, it is an LCD display with HD+ resolution, which makes the content feel a little less sharp, even though the colors do seem quite vibrant. This, combined with stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack, makes the Poco M8x a good device for those who like to watch content on their smartphones.
We had said waaay back in 2020 that the real home of a fingerprint scanner is on the side of the phone, so the fingerprint scanner placed on the side of the Poco M8x is something we actually liked. It worked smoothly and was easy to access. There is the option of using face unlock as well, which turned out to be impressively accurate and speedy, although it is supposed to be less secure than the fingerprint scanner. Call quality was good, and we did not face any abrupt call drop issues. In short, the Poco M8x is a terrific daily driver, handling everyday life and delivering entertainment with ease.
Poco M8x Cameras: Good main and selfie camera for the price
The Poco M8x comes with a 50-megapixel main sensor on the back paired with an auxiliary lens. The daylight performance of the main camera is pretty good. It captures basic shots well, with a decent amount of detail. The colors look a little muted as compared to the natural settings, but still turn out good enough for a quick social media post. You get a 2x digital zoom, which basically crops an image. The details do get compromised here, but it comes in handy when you need a closer look. The camera, however, struggles a bit if you push it out of its comfort zone.
It struggles to capture macro photos – you have to keep your hand very (very) steady to get a decent photo, and the portrait mode on the phone did not really add a lot of visible difference – the bokeh added was very light and almost negligible, which was disappointing. The low light performance of the phone is nothing too special either. As the light dims, details take a hit, and the colors remain muted here as well. There is a night mode which makes results a bit better, but low-light pictures in general take a second to process, and it is very important you keep your hands very steady for that second (there’s no OIS, remember). The phone comes with a number of modes like Document, Dual video, and Pro, that give users more shooting options and utility.
The front camera also performs surprisingly well for a modest-sounding 8-megapixel shooter, in terms of both color and detail. With beauty mode off, it can capture skin texture well, and colors seem good too. The portrait mode on the selfie camera actually delivers deeper bokeh than what we got from the primary camera. It does not catch edges very well (blurred out my ear once), but the photos are good enough for social media posts. There are a number of beauty filters, all of which do their job well. However, it follows the path of the primary camera and struggles with details and color in low light. The primary camera is capable of capturing full HD videos at 30 fps. Videos also turn out well in daylight but get noisy in low light. All said and done, we were actually surprised by the cameras on the Poco M8x, which performed well beyond our expectations (we still don’t know what difference the auxiliary camera makes, though).
Poco M8x Battery: Where the phone is BOSS
This is one department where the Poco M8x shines most brightly, and how. The phone comes with a massive 7900 mAh battery, and it is safe to say it just keeps going on and on. The combination of a low-resolution display, an efficient everyday processor, and a big battery is a terrific one. The Poco M8x comfortably lasted for two days of hectic usage, with hours of Instagram scrolls, YouTube, and some Modern Family episodes here and there, emails, messaging, WhatsApp, calls, sessions of Tetris, and some photography. The phone handled it all like a champ.
With a bit of careful usage, we even got it to last the third day. It is safe to say this is perhaps the best battery performance we have experienced in this segment. The phone comes with 45 W fast charging support and a 45 W adapter in the box, which took about one hour 15 minutes to go from 20 percent to full. But so big is the battery that even a 30-minute charge session can easily give you a full day’s battery. And as it comes with a 22.5 W reverse charging feature as well, it can double as a power bank for your other devices, including smartphones and wearables. This is pretty much the battery boss of the segment.
Poco M8x UI and software: A mixed bag of functionality and third-party apps
The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 with Hyper OS 3, and on budget devices, Hyper OS is a bit of a mixed bag. The first thing that hits you when you fire up the phone is the large number of third-party apps. It is a little overwhelming – there are even multiple casual games of the same type. Although there are also popular apps like Instagram, YouTube, YouTube Music, and LinkedIn, the interface can seem very crowded. Thankfully, these can be uninstalled, and we recommend doing so.
Now on to the good bits. HyperOS is otherwise quite functional and customizable. There are a number of personalization options – from icons to fonts, to themes and wallpapers; you can personalize them all to your liking. There are also features like interconnectivity that allow you to connect your device to other Xiaomi products and carry out functions over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and you can also link your device to a Chromebook.
There are some basic AI features on the phone as well – Google Gemini for writing and other assistance, and features like Circle to Search. Of course, given its specs, we do not recommend pushing the phone too hard in the AI zone. Finally, the phone has an array of accessibility features (divided into general, vision, physical, and hearing), which aim to make the experience smooth for all users. Get rid of the bloatware, and the Poco M8x’s UI experience can be a pleasant one.
Poco M8x Price: In line with the new budget zone
The Poco M8x comes with a starting price of Rs. 20,999 for its 4 GB/ 128 GB version, while the 6 GB/ 128 GB version is priced at Rs. 22,999. Keeping in mind the rising prices of smartphones, the Poco M8x is quite fairly priced for the specs it offers. It does face competition, though.
One of its most notable competitors is the Samsung Galaxy M17, which starts at Rs 17,999 and comes with triple cameras on its back (50 MP+ 5 MP+ 2 MP), a 13-megapixel front camera, and most notably, a Super AMOLED Full HD+ display with a 90 Hz refresh rate. That said, its display and battery (with no charger in the box) and its Exynos 1330 processor are a step behind the Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 on the Poco M8x. There is also the Moto G37 Power 5G, which starts at Rs 19,999 and is powered by MediaTek Dimensity 6400, and has RAM that goes up to 8 GB, but comes with a smaller display and battery and also starts with a 4 GB/ 64 GB version.
Poco M8x Review Verdict: The big battery boss of the budget segment
For its starting price of Rs. 20,999, the Poco M8x is a pretty budget smartphone. It mainly shines in two areas: design (Green Leather variant) and battery. It also does well in other departments, and we can see many people liking its large display, good speakers, and main and selfie cameras (in good light conditions). It also delivers very consistent everyday performance and comes with a very functional OS as well. All of which make it a great option for those who are looking for a good-looking but reliable device with days of battery life.
- Leather Green design stands out
- Good main and selfie cameras
- Great battery life
- Handles everyday tasks well
- Big display and screen combo make it great for consuming content
- Relatively low-resolution HD+ display
- LCD display, rather than an AMOLED one
- Portrait shots from the main camera are disappointing
- Bloatware in the UI

The conclusion of the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history has left a country in turmoil, and a grieving family still searching for answers.
At 7.30pm on Wednesday, gasps and cheers echoed around hall 22 of the courts of justice in Valletta, as a jury pronounced a businessman accused of ordering the murder of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia not guilty.
Yorgen Fenech, 44, had been facing a life sentence if convicted. Now, after nearly seven years in and out of custody, he is free to return to a gilded life as the heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes.
In her reporting, Caruana Galizia had taken aim at many powerful figures, including Fenech and the politicians he was close to. Her revelations, and the fallout from her violent death in a car bombing in October 2017, had ultimately led to the resignation of the prime minister, Joseph Muscat, and several members of his government.
Within weeks, three hitmen accused of planting the bomb were arrested. Two were sentenced to life in prison after pleading guilty to murder, while the third was given a reduced 15-year sentence in exchange for evidence against his accomplices.
After Wednesday’s decision, the long search for whoever was responsible for hiring them must begin again.
The opposition leader, Alex Borg, has demanded the recall of parliament from its summer recess, and called for the government to act to strengthen press protection and anti-corruption measures. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” he told the Guardian, describing the failure to find the culprits as a black mark against the Labour government. The party has been in power since 2013.
Caruana Galizia’s family described the verdict as “justice denied”.
The attorney general is considering whether to appeal for a retrial. The chances of success may be slim: both charges brought against Fenech were dismissed by an 8-1 majority.
It had taken nine years, a relentless family campaign and a determined judge to bring Fenech before a jury. In the end, they took him at his word. During his evidence, he was adamant: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.”
While the identity of the mastermind remains a mystery, what the trial did reveal was the full extent of the challenges faced by those leading the search for Daphne’s killers.
Witness after witness spoke of attempts to block and sabotage the murder investigation. As detectives worked to identify all of those involved, from the bomb makers to the hitmen to their ultimate client, they heard evidence that the most sensitive details were being leaked. Most disturbingly of all, the jury was told much of the information was coming from the prime minister’s right-hand man.
“Don’t worry about me, nobody can touch me,” Fenech was heard saying in secret recordings that formed a cornerstone of the case against him, and played to the jury.
The man who had made those recordings was a taxi driver, Melvin Theuma, who testified to acting as the middleman between Fenech and the bombers. He was the key prosecution witness, having secured a pardon two years after the murder in return for giving evidence.
In July 2020, he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Overcome with remorse, he had attempted suicide while staying at a safe house, and it took intensive support to get him back in the stand.
What follows is the story of the search for those responsible, based on pre-trial hearings, the trial itself, and related court cases.
Consumed by an investigation that would kill her
In the last summer of her life, Caruana Galizia was deeply isolated.
As a younger woman, she had not only been brilliant, but strikingly beautiful, with big statement earrings and shining black hair. She had co-founded a national newspaper, was a lifestyle magazine publisher, and had become one of Malta’s most-read columnists, all while raising three sons.
In later life, it was the investigative work that consumed her.
Her blog Running Commentary was among the most-read news sites in Malta, but its popularity, and her often scathing satires of public figures, made her a target.
She had as many detractors as fans, and on social media she was vilified as a “witch”. There were arson attacks, and the family dogs were killed.
“I was worried about her,” her middle son, Andrew, told the trial. “The atmosphere around her was horrible. People would stare at her in Valletta. She wouldn’t leave the house.”
Caruana Galizia knew she was at risk and had already started varying her routine. For added security, she drove a rental car.
It was in that car that she died on 16 October 2017, aged 53, metres from her house. A bomb placed under the driver’s seat ripped through the vehicle, scattering burning remains across the road and into a field.
Barricaded inside their home, sheltering from the media storm, Daphne’s sons and her widow, Peter, wondered who they could trust. They felt sure her work would hold clues, but also that they could not hand sensitive source material to the police. Her eldest son, Matthew, a software engineer who had been part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers, a giant leak of offshore company data, suggested contacting journalists outside Malta.
“I didn’t have the resources to do the investigation on my own,” he told the jury at Fenech’s trial.
He reached out to the Guardian, which joined Reuters, the non-profit Forbidden Stories and others to form the Daphne Project.
Before her death, Caruana Galizia had published a series of stories that plunged the Maltese government into scandal. She had found evidence in the Panama Papers that the energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, a businessman turned political fixer called Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies held via anonymous trusts. Posts she published, read out during the trial, suggested she thought they were planning to use these to receive kickbacks.
Those allegations are now the subject of a criminal case, in which Fenech, Schembri, Mizzi and others are pleading not guilty to corruption, trading in influence and criminal association.
At the time she died, Caruana Galizia was receiving a leak of information about a large government contract – a concession to build a €500m gas power plant that would supply electricity for the national grid. The leak came from the servers of the company building the plant, Electrogas. One of its shareholders was Fenech, and the email traffic suggested he was a driving force, handling communications with the government, and the refinancing of a crucial bank loan.
The jury heard how, in her blog, Caruana Galizia had described the venture as a “magic new corruption power station”.
The prosecution had claimed, in its closing submissions, that Fenech’s motive for ordering her murder was to prevent any further revelations.
The Electrogas data was shared with the Daphne Project. As reporters combed the files, following the money trails, Keith Arnaud, a homicide detective, searched for the killers. At first he made rapid progress, thanks to the FBI. The agency’s cellphone analysis team had been in Europe when the bomb went off, and they diverted to Malta, landing there within hours.
The hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio, and their accomplice Vincent Muscat, had used burner phones but they had been careless, often carrying them alongside their usual mobiles. The FBI made the link, tracing a text message sent by George to detonate the bomb. In December 2017, the trio were arrested.
In April 2018, Vincent Muscat told police he was ready to turn on his accomplices, in exchange for a shorter sentence. While the hitmen had never known the identity of their ultimate client, Muscat had the name of the middleman: Melvin Theuma.
The mosquito and the lion
For Theuma, a fatherless teenager, the Malta Racing Club was a home from home. He started as a groom, tending to the ponies that pull small carts around the bare-earth track. Before long he was working as a scout for a bookmaker. The old betting shop still stands across the street from the Fenech family stables.
Theuma and Fenech became friends, but it was not a relationship of equals. As the taxi driver said in court: “I was hanging out with a lion, and I’m a mosquito.”
Police said in court they had identified Fenech as a suspect by September 2018. But it would take until February 2019 for a warrant to be authorised to intercept his calls.
The person signing the warrants was the prime minister, Joseph Muscat. From the beginning, Muscat had been receiving updates about the investigation directly from Arnaud and his colleagues. That decision was controversial because, along with his ministers, he had been one of the main subjects of Caruana Galizia’s reporting.
Muscat has indicated it was customary for the prime minister to sign warrants in cases of national importance. He has previously said he fulfilled his duties “without fear, prejudice or favour”. In a statement on Thursday, he said that from the beginning, and while he was still in office, “no one was protected from or immune to justice”.
Schembri was allowed to attend the police briefings and told the trial he was kept informed throughout.
The two men were close – Schembri had started out as Muscat’s campaign manager – but Schembri had another good friend: Fenech. They had played football together as children, and when Fenech, a few years younger, stepped up to run his family business, Schembri had mentored him. They would often holiday together and gather for family events.
Schembri is accused of repeatedly leaking sensitive details about the homicide investigation to Fenech. He denies the allegations, and is being prosecuted over the matter in a separate criminal case.
During his trial, Fenech sought to paint Schembri as the ultimate mastermind, describing himself as a go-between, passing messages to Theuma. Fenech’s lawyers depicted the taxi driver as a blackmailer and a liar, and accused the police of framing Fenech because they had failed to properly follow other leads. They said the searches at Schembri’s home and his office had been bungled. His phone, active 28 minutes before the raid, was never found.
“All roads lead to Keith and all bridges leading to Keith were burnt,” Fenech’s lawyer said. “And so a bridge had to be built to Yorgen Fenech.”
Schembri denies any involvement in the murder. In their evidence, police said he was never a murder suspect.
Under questioning, Fenech admitted paying €400,000, via Theuma, to the hitmen to cover their legal bills. He said this was to keep Theuma calm, and that the cab driver had “drained” him of money. He also admitted giving Theuma money before the murder, but said he warned that it should not go ahead, telling the taxi driver to “stop it here”.
He admitted passing information about the police investigation from Schembri to Theuma, starting soon after the assassination.
“Keith Schembri was continuously informed and in a way you can say real time,” Fenech told a court in 2019, in a constitutional case regarding his right to a fair trial. “The information was passed to me by Keith Schembri but it came from Mr Arnaud, and he used to tell me that it came from Mr Arnaud.”
Recordings, messages and testimony from Fenech himself indicate that in the first months after the murder he had passed on to Theuma the identity of who had made the bomb and the date on which the police were planning to arrest the hitmen. When the police raided their shed by the docks, they had already thrown their mobile phones into the water, and one of them had written his wife’s number on his wrist.
In April 2018, Fenech also shared that Vincent Muscat was offering to become a witness for the prosecution. The news sent Theuma into a spin and he started to record his exchanges with Fenech, using a spare phone switched to airplane mode so it would not ring.
It was around this time that Arnaud’s investigation seemed to lose momentum. Eventually, details of what had been uncovered began to leak. By May 2019, reporters had Theuma’s name.
Europol, which had been supporting Arnaud and his team, threatened over the summer of 2019 to withdraw unless arrests were made. The family were also losing patience. “We had known what was being alleged about Melvin Theuma for months,” Matthew Caruana Galizia has said. “And it reached a point where I just wanted to go into the street and spraypaint his name on a wall. I wanted the world to know that he was the middleman, to just push the police into action.”
While the walls around the prime minister and his friends looked strong from the outside, when the police finally went for Theuma, Joseph Muscat’s administration crumbled.
Theuma had been warned of his planned arrest date but police swooped two days early, on 14 November 2019. Fenech had urged him in messages beforehand to dispose of the evidence. The jury saw one message in which he said: “Be 100% sure everywhere is clean.”
But Theuma held on to his recordings. On 19 November, the prime minister signed a memorandum guaranteeing Theuma immunity from prosecution in exchange for testimony. Within hours, Fenech was making preparations to flee, messages seen by the jury suggest. “Go while you’re still in time,” his uncle texted. He planned to sail to Sicily, and then head for France. However, the police had been tipped off. His yacht was intercepted a mile off the coast, and he was arrested. The interrogation tapes, played at his trial, showed he offered to implicate Schembri in return for a pardon.
As Fenech talked, heads rolled. Schembri was arrested in relation to the suspected leaks, and resigned. The economy minister, a frequent subject of Caruana Galizia’s blog, suspended himself and Mizzi, by now reassigned from energy to tourism minister, quit, citing “political, extraordinary and general circumstances in the country”.
Public outrage brought hundreds on to the streets, filling the grand plaza outside the prime minister’s office, chanting: “Mafia, mafia.”
Fenech’s pardon request was rejected and on 30 November, he was charged. Two days later, Joseph Muscat resigned. Defiant to the end, he insisted: “This case cannot define everything that our country is.”
The saga is once again drawing attention from outside Malta. Shami Chakrabarti, the British Labour peer, has been appointed rapporteur of a Council of Europe investigation into the Maltese government’s response to the murder. Caruana Galizia’s family members intend to give evidence at the first hearing next week.
“The failure to ensure individual accountability for the murder risks perpetuating a culture of impunity,” Chakrabarti said on Thursday. “A culture where … those who try to shine a light in the darkness pay the ultimate price.”

How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of women
- Published
Gloria Steinem was a powerful icon of America's feminist movement and her career spanned numerous roles that changed the lives of generations of women.
With her iconic aviator sunglasses and long, blonde-streaked hair - which she considered rebellious in the 1970s - Steinem was an internationally recognised activist in the fight for women's equality.
She spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage, and equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.
Her activism was not without a backlash - from both men and women - and harassment that could be as vulgar as it was intimidating.
The early years
Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, Gloria Steinem did not have an easy childhood.
Her father Leo Steinem was a travelling salesman and, together with her mother Ruth and older sister Susanne, they lived in a caravan, crisscrossing the country.
Leo abandoned the family and moved to California when Steinem was 10 years old, leaving her to care for Ruth who had long suffered with mental illness and had terrifying hallucinations.
As a result, Steinem did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.
She would later remark that she had never wanted children because she had already had one - her mother.
In the late 1950s she went to India on a research scholarship, and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.
Steinem left India and moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. It was a time when male-dominated newsrooms made it difficult for women to get hard-hitting stories.
Breakthrough article
Her big break came in 1963, when Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny cocktail waitress and wrote A Bunny's Tale, an exposé for Show magazine detailing the seedy and sexist reality of Hugh Hefner's empire.
As soon as she arrived for the interview, a security guard called out, "Here bunny, bunny, bunny."
Using the fake name Marie, she lied about her age - telling Playboy she was 24 years old when she was actually four years older.
Steinem lifted the lid on the underpaid life of a Bunny, and the physical pain of wearing the high-heels and tight corsets for hours.
Despite the fame - and infamy - that followed, she still found herself struggling to be taken seriously by editors.
Though the Playboy exposé helped land her assignments for the New York Times and New York Magazine, often they were about ladies' stockings and the latest hairstyles.
"To this day when people don't like me they introduce me as a former Bunny, as a put-down," she told the New York Times in 2016. "On the other hand, I did improve the working conditions for those women."
All-female journalism
Undaunted, by 1968 Steinem was a columnist for New York Magazine, focusing on progressive social issues and women's rights.
Her article, After Black Power, Women's Liberation, external brought her national fame, making her the face of the US feminist movement in the 1970s.
"I was the only woman, and after I wrote an abortion article, my [male] friends there said to me: 'Don't get involved with these crazy women. You've worked hard to be taken seriously,'" she told Rachel Cooke for The Guardian in 2011.
So she took matters into her own hands.
In 1972, she launched Ms. magazine with a group of feminist activists. It was the first all-female founded and operated periodical, designed to be an alternative to other women's magazines that typically focused on housekeeping and fashion.
Critics - mainly men - were quick to write it off. News presenter Harry Reasoner said he gave it six months "before they run out of things to say".
The first issue sold out within a week and generated 26,000 subscribers. The magazine is still going today.
In 1978, Steinem wrote one of Ms. magazine's most infamous and widely read essays - If Men Could Menstruate.
Her satirical reflection on how different power, political and economic structures might be if men had menstrual cycles is still referred to in discussions about gender roles.
By the end of her career, Steinem had become a prolific and award-winning writer, penning numerous books including her own memoirs, a biography on Marilyn Monroe and a collection of her own famous quotes in the wryly titled, The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off.
Abortion rights campaigner
Though still considered one of the world's best-known feminist activists, Steinem came to advocacy rather late in life - in her thirties.
At an abortion awareness rally in 1969 where women were sharing their experiences of having abortions, Steinem was encouraged to share her own story about terminating a pregnancy. It had taken place years earlier in London when she was 22 years old, just before going to India.
Abortion was illegal in the UK at the time, unless the woman's mental or physical health was in danger. The doctor took a great risk for Steinem, telling her: "You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."
Nearly 60 years later, Steinem broke one of those promises, when she dedicated her memoir, My Life On The Road, to Dr John Sharpe.
She described that abortion speak-out event as a "light bulb moment" - when she realised the US needed a bigger women's rights movement.
Almost overnight, Steinem became a crusader for abortion rights, calling it "reproductive freedom". The phrase she coined is credited with making the subject more approachable for political discussion and continues to be used in abortion debates.
Steinem organised marches and quickly became a draw at demonstrations, although she admitted later that she found talking to the huge crowds "utterly terrifying".
After Congress failed to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1970 - legislation granting women equal rights to men - Steinem co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus with fellow feminist leaders and more than 300 women across the US. The group worked to include women in all aspects of political and public life.
The same year, she testified at Senate hearings for the ERA, telling the predominantly male audience: "I have been refused service in public restaurants, ordered out of public gathering places and turned away from apartment rentals all for the clearly stated, sole reason that I am a woman."
Second-wave feminism continued to gain momentum and Steinem was one of its most famous figureheads.
She was also supportive of same-sex marriage, but was criticised for an essay she wrote in 1977 on transgender people. She clarified her position in 2013, saying the words in her "old essay" had been taken "out of time and context".
"I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned," she wrote in an opinion piece, external.
Steinem was also criticised for a 1998 essay in the New York Times, where she showed support for then-President Bill Clinton after news broke of his scandalous affair with intern Monica Lewinsky - who was 22 years old at the time.
"The truth is that even if the allegations are true, the president is not guilty of sexual harassment," Steinem wrote. "He is accused of having made a gross, dumb and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life."
In 2017, she said she "wouldn't write the same thing now".
Too glamorous?
Critics came from the left as well as right, targeting Steinem for everything from her looks to her motives. Some claimed she was too glamorous to be a true feminist, while others said she was successful only because of her appearance.
Betty Friedan, author of The Feminine Mystique, the book credited with launching second-wave feminism, was annoyed that Steinem became the face of the movement, accusing her of "ripping off the movement for private profit" when she launched Ms.
The media were trying "to make her a celebrity," fumed Friedan, "but no one should mistake her for a leader."
US President Richard Nixon was recorded during a secret conversation furiously ranting about Steinem, to which she responded: "There is some opinion that Richard Nixon is the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon".
Al Goldstein, the notorious pornographer and publisher of Screw magazine, launched a campaign of attacks that included publishing her phone number next to fake advertisements for oral sex.
He also printed a graphic centrefold image of a Steinem look-alike, and hung it open on display at the newsstand outside Ms. magazine's office building. She had to look at it every day.
As she got older, harassment to this degree became less common. However, given she was a recognisable figure in New York City, it was not uncommon for Steinem to be stopped on the street by strangers wanting to debate - sometimes with an edge of hostility.
But she welcomed the continued debate. In 2020, she was among a cross-section of public figures who signed an open letter denouncing cancel culture, saying it weakens open debate by shutting people down.
"If you care about having the conversation, surely you want to try in a humane way to convince the other person, not do away with them," she told the New York Times.
'I can't mate in captivity'
Gloria Steinem once quipped: "I can't mate in captivity" - a reference to her disinterest in marriage. But she publicly enjoyed a healthy dating life with a number of rich and famous bachelors, giving critics more ammunition to use against her.
They included Frank Thomas who was head of the Ford Foundation; film director Mike Nichols and Olympic decathlete Rafer Johnson (who helped tackle the man who assassinated Robert F Kennedy in 1968).
"I was the one always accused of using men, of being too sexual. Someone once sent me a cartoon of a tombstone that said 'at last she sleeps alone'," she wrote.
But in 2000, aged 66, she wed David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist, and father of actor Christian Bale.
At the time, the union drew gasps of surprise and even disappointment from some feminists, who had spent years following Steinem's heated debates surrounding marriage laws.
But she said those laws had finally changed. "If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That's not true anymore. It's possible to make an equal marriage," she explained years later.
Steinem also confessed to it being a "green card marriage" because Bale's US visa was running out - but said that they loved each other and were going to be together regardless.
Bale died three years later from brain lymphoma.
Steinem had her own health scare with breast cancer in 1986, and underwent a lumpectomy.
'So much to do'
Gloria Steinem once said she wanted to live to 100 because "there's so much to do".
In her near-century of life, she even became a talented tap dancer.
She was given America's highest civilian honour - the Presidential Medal of Freedom - in 2013 by President Barack Obama, who credited her work with giving more women "the respect and opportunities that they deserve".
In 2024, she reached the age of 90. She lived alone in New York, content in the knowledge that Ms. Magazine was still publishing.
Steinem seized the occasion to tell the BBC that she hoped her legacy "might help individual people... to become more the unique, valuable, loved and lovable person that they want to be."
She will be remembered for amplifying the voices of women in a way that mainstream media at the time either could not, or would not.
And, in so doing, she altered the landscape and language of women's rights in America.

A video (here & here) claiming to show the bodies of victims who died in the Nepal flash floods on 26 August 2026, is circulating widely on social media. Let’s examine the veracity of this claim.
Claim: Video showing the deceased victims during the flash floods that struck Nepal on 26 August 2026.
Fact: This video is unrelated to the Nepal floods. It is a staged video shot for entertainment purpose by an Instagram creator. The Nepal floods occurred on 26 August 2026, but this video was uploaded on 03 August 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is misleading.
A reverse image search of the keyframes from the viral video revealed that the same video (archive) was uploaded to Instagram on 03 August 2026 by a content creator named Simran SK. This confirms that the video has no connection to the Nepal floods, as it was uploaded well before the actual disaster took place.
A closer review of Simran SK’s Instagram account indicates a pattern of uploading comedy and scripted videos. We also found other scripted videos (archive) on the account featuring individuals pretending to be dead. Furthermore, during the Assam floods in July 2026, another scripted video from this very account was falsely circulated as a real incident. Our previous fact-check article regarding that instance can be read here.
To sum it up, a scripted video is being falsely shared as genuine footage of deceased victims from the 2026 Nepal floods.

The deadliest ever Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now claimed the lives of more than 3,000 people, according to the latest official toll released on Wednesday.
The epidemic, which has hit the conflict-hit east and northeast of the country, has caused 3,007 deaths and infected 6,186 people, the Congolese National Institute of Public Health said.
The fatality rate is 48.6%. A total of 1,409 people have been reported to have recovered, it added.
Ebola, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and causes haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa in the last 50 years.
The worst outbreak previously recorded in DR Congo left nearly 2,300 people dead from 3,500 reported cases between 2018 and 2020.
The current outbreak originated in the remote northeastern province of Ituri and is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is currently no approved vaccine or treatment.
The virus has spread to six provinces and is ravaging areas where the presence of the Congolese state is weak and insecurity is widespread due to the presence of armed groups.
The health response lacks sufficient resources and has been overwhelmed by the surge in cases, while there has been widespread mistrust in parts of the community.
Several treatments and vaccines are being tested against the Bundibugyo strain. Approved vaccines are only effective against the Zaire strain, which is responsible for the largest-known Ebola outbreak to date.
The World Health Organization has in the meantime recommended the implementation of a phase three clinical trial using the Ervebo vaccine deployed against the Zaire strain.
WHO experts are still unclear as to whether Ervebo protects humans against Bundigbugyo but initial data suggests that it could offer a degree of protection.
A batch of 16,250 doses for use by frontline medical personnel arrived in DR Congo at the end of last month and vaccination began shortly afterwards in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province in the northeast.

A video showing a woman being attacked by a group of men, while policemen are seen protecting her, is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that a “female Hindu teacher was attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh.” Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing a Hindu teacher being attacked by Muslims in Bangladesh.
Fact: The woman seen in the viral video is Zakia Sultana, a woman entrepreneur who runs a clothing business called ‘Astha Poshak Shilpa’ at Kaderia Market in Rajbari. The incident reportedly stemmed from a business dispute between Zakia and her former employee, Shahana Parveen Brishti. Uttam Kumar Ghosh, Officer-in-Charge of Rajbari Sadar Police Station, confirmed that there was no religious angle to the incident. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several Bangladeshi media reports covering the incident and featuring the same visuals (here, here, here, here). Based on these reports, we learned that the woman seen in the viral video is Zakia Sultana, a woman entrepreneur who runs a clothing business called ‘Astha Poshak Shilpa’ at Kaderia Market in Rajbari. The incident reportedly stemmed from a business dispute between Zakia and her former employee, Shahana Parveen Brishti.
According to Zakia, Brishti left her shop without settling the accounts and later started her own business. Zakia alleged that Brishti, along with several others, went to her shop and threatened her. She further claimed that she was assaulted while she was at the market seeking a resolution to the dispute. However, reports quoting traders and other local sources said that the dispute arose after Brishti left Zakia’s shop and started her own business in the same market.
Rajbari Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Uttam Kumar Ghosh said the incident was related to a business dispute. He said police reached the spot after receiving information, rescued Zakia from the situation, and took her to the police station for her safety. The viral video shows her being attacked by several men while police officers are present.
We also contacted Uttam Kumar Ghosh, Officer-in-Charge of Rajbari Sadar Police Station, over a WhatsApp call. He confirmed that there was no religious angle to the incident. According to Ghosh, the victim, Zakia Sultana, is Muslim, and three individuals accused in connection with the incident are all Muslims and have been arrested.
To sum up, this video does not show a Hindu teacher being beaten up by Muslims in Bangladesh.

In late August 2026, people shared a video allegedly showing a kindergarten teacher saying she was fired for helping students discover their gender identity.
The video trended (archived) on X with the caption "Kindergarten Teacher's Gender Lesson Video Prompts Firing Debate." Under the trend, a popular post (archived) from Aug. 28 featured an earlier clip as well as the video in question.
The earlier clip (archived), captioned "Helping My Students Discover Their Genders," shows the alleged teacher saying she asked her students, "Who wishes that they were born a different gender?" She says half her class raised their hands, leading her to tell the other children to sit in a corner. The post's caption includes the words, "Might be parody."
The second video (archived), featured on top in the post below, has the same caption as the first clip with the addition of "Update (I Was Fired)." In the second video, the purported teacher says, while appearing to cry, "I got fired. This is like the worst day of my life. I lost my teaching license, so now these children will never be able to discover their true selves."
Other users shared the purported firing video on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived) and YouTube (archived).
Snopes readers searched this website to investigate its legitimacy, leading us to first perform reverse image searches of both videos. Those searches led us to determine the clips' source was TikTok account named phoebe! (@bhoepe), whose bio — "do i appear to be joking?" — hinted the user shared satire and parody.
In sum, the video originated as satire.
The user in both videos, who told us in an email we could reference her simply as Phoebe, originally posted the first video (archived) on Aug. 21 with a caption containing the hashtags #skit and #satire. The caption jokingly features the words, "next step is reassignment surgery in the nurse's office."
The second video (archived) from Aug. 28, which received more than 15 million views, also had the #skit and #satire hashtags, as well as comments from users appearing to believe the story was real. Some of those comments received hundreds of thousands of likes.
Phoebe confirmed to Snopes her videos are skits. She also told us she's not a teacher and has "never worked in a school in any capacity." Other videos on her TikTok account show her saying she's a kindergarten teacher and keeps cat litter boxes in her classroom (a reference to a debunked conspiracy theory), lost her job as a school nurse and fought a funeral procession — all jokes.
"None of my skits are based on real events and are exaggerated for comedic purposes," she said. "Humor has always been a huge aspect of my personality, and even as a kid I wanted to be a comedian." She continued:
I made the video as sort of an experiment; I intentionally told a bizarre story. I made the whole thing up. I also put "skit" and "satire" in the caption of the video. I wanted to see if the majority of viewers would go through the trouble of reading the caption or looking at the other satire/skit videos on my account, and, astoundingly, most people seemed to just take everything I said at face value.
There were also quite a few larger creators who clipped my video and covered it and intentionally hid the "satire" disclaimer, presumably to get more engagement. I think context matters, but even with context some people still believe it! It's as if I could tell them to their face that it was a joke and it wouldn't change their mind.
So, the overall reaction to my video is honestly very concerning, especially with AI advancing and the internet being full of widespread misinformation. I feel I did my due diligence by labeling it as satire, and I think ultimately anything can be clipped and taken out of context by people with ulterior motives, particularly if it fits their agenda.

A 50-year-old man allegedly killed his 45-year-old wife with a machete before slitting his own throat with the same weapon after an argument in Assam’s Biswanath district early Thursday, police said. Both died in the incident.
The incident took place in the Balighat area. “Their blood-stained bodies were recovered from their house and they were declared dead at a local government hospital. Both had suffered severe injuries to their throats and died due to excessive blood loss,” an investigating officer said.

The deceased man was a daily-wage labourer, and the couple had two children.
“We are investigating the matter and statements of family members and neighbours are being recorded. We are also waiting for the postmortem reports to gather more information,” officials said.

The Trump administration still aims to make state citizenship lists ahead of midterms
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR.
The Trump administration is taking steps to advance a mysterious and unprecedented project to compile state-by-state lists of people it has decided are eligible citizens over the age of 18 who can vote in the upcoming midterm election. But it will no longer meet its own deadline to publish that information on a portal on Friday, which is 60 days before Election Day.
Department of Justice attorneys told opposing counsel in two separate lawsuits that instead of meeting the Sept. 4 deadline, they would give 48-hours notice to plaintiffs' counsel before the state citizenship portal was launched, according to recent court filings.
The U.S. has never attempted to create a comprehensive list of American citizens before this administration. Maintaining voter lists is the responsibility of states, not the federal government, as the Constitution dictates that states control elections. But President Trump has repeatedly taken steps to try to exert executive control over elections.
The basis for the federal government creating state citizenship lists is an executive order Trump signed on March 31. A lower court had blocked implementation of key parts of that executive order in 23 states and Washington, D.C., but the Supreme Court stayed that injunction late last month, opening the door for the plan to be implemented after all.
The March 31 executive order directs U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Social Security Administration to create "State Citizenship Lists" of individuals the agencies believe are citizens in each state, and send those lists to state officials "no fewer than 60 days before each regularly scheduled Federal election."
The next section of the executive order says the U.S. attorney general will prioritize investigating and prosecuting state and local officials who issue federal ballots to anyone not eligible to vote.
"States here have a strong incentive to actually use these lists to try to avoid federal investigation," said Jules Torti, counsel at the nonprofit Protect Democracy, in an interview with NPR. "But we know that these lists are going to be based on really inaccurate data. So the risk of disenfranchisement here is really, really palpable."
The privacy group Electronic Privacy Information Center, along with individual voters, filed a motion Thursday asking a federal judge in Maryland to block the administration from creating the citizenship lists and publishing them on a portal. Specifically, they seek to block a June 8 implementation memo authored by USCIS director Joseph Edlow that outlines the plan.
The motion, which was brought by Protect Democracy, along with another nonprofit legal group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, argues the administration's plans to share Americans' personal data between agencies and then disseminate the data to states violates multiple federal laws, including the Privacy Act, the Social Security Act and the Administrative Procedures Act. Under the Privacy Act, federal agencies must give the public 30 days notice and the opportunity to comment before they collect and disseminate Americans' personal data for a new purpose.
The EPIC lawsuit also argues the government does not have access to accurate, up-to-date information on American citizens, especially those who move frequently, have changed their names, or are foreign-born. For example, Social Security's citizenship data often isn't updated when people naturalize, and the SAVE data system, operated by USCIS, frequently doesn't include records for people who became citizens as minors when their parents naturalized.
Torti said it is "deeply concerning" that the administration is still planning to go ahead with the creation of citizenship lists but is no longer going to meet the deadline, since that means the lists will be completed even closer to Election Day.
"It means additional chaos, additional confusion for the state election officials and just for voters," Torti said. "And I think that's the point. The point here is to create chaos in advance of the election."
Neither the Department of Justice, nor the Department of Homeland Security, which is tasked with compiling the citizenship lists, responded to NPR's request for comment.
The June 8 implementation memo stated that the portal for state election officials would be available around June 30 and a second portal where citizens could check their information would be available at a later date – but that deadline passed without further updates.
The federal government has secured a domain for the state citizenship lists portal. While the portal is not currently online, it was briefly live in recent days with a landing page that said "Coming Soon," according to court filings.
Lawyers representing Democratic party groups that had challenged the March 31 executive order in a separate lawsuit filed in April, accused the administration in a recent filing of failing to notify the court or the parties about its plans to move forward with the state citizenship portal. They asked the judge to require the federal government to give immediate updates about their plans to implement the executive order.
This latest legal battle over the administration's plans to compile state citizenship lists comes as the Department of Homeland Security is ramping up its efforts to analyze state voter rolls with the goal of identifying potential noncitizens who are registered to vote. Previous audits have found instances of noncitizens casting ballots to be incredibly rare.
Additionally, last week, ICE published a request for information on a federal procurement site seeking vendors who can compile public voter rolls and voter history files from all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and U.S. territories, "to support Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) fraud detection and data segmentation activities."
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang contributed reporting to this story.

Four arrested over boxing champion's murder in South Africa
- Published
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.
Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.
One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.
Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.
The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.
Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.
The motive behind the attack is unclear.
Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."
Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".
Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.
He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.
Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.
He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.
After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.
Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.
According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.
