Hong Kong poised to top New York, London in finance-hub ranking: GFCI creator
‘It’s going to happen,’ creator of Global Financial Centres Index says, as long as city maintains openness and predictability
An Asian city will eventually overtake London and New York as the world’s leading financial centre, with Hong Kong well placed to compete for the top spot given its legal predictability and low tax burden, according to the creator of a closely watched ranking of financial hubs.
“It’s going to happen because it’s so tight,” said Michael Mainelli, chairman of London-based think tank Z/Yen Group, in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Tuesday, referring to the narrowing gap between Hong Kong and the traditional leaders.
In the March edition of the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI) – compiled twice a year by Z/Yen and Shenzhen’s China Development Institute – Hong Kong placed third, trailing London by a single point and New York by two. The next edition is set for release later this month.
Mainelli attributed the tightening race to a broader structural shift towards Asia, which now accounts for roughly 40 per cent of global finance.
“At some point, there will be an event,” he said, meaning a change at the top of the rankings.
Recent macroeconomic volatility, including geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, had weighed on the ratings of some major hubs, but Hong Kong’s underlying framework was unusually resilient, Mainelli said.

A group of saffron-clad men painted the walls of the Anandabazar Patrika (ABP) office in Kolkata saffron on September 1, days after West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari had demanded an apology from the daily for describing the recent violence at Jadavpur University as “gerua gundami” — or “saffron hooliganism”.
Videos show two men painting two pillars at the main entrance of the office while several police personnel stand by. Some of the police officials can also be seen recording the incident on their cellphones.
Several other saffron-clad men had gathered at the spot, raising slogans including “Bhagwa ka apmaan nahi sahega” (“We will not tolerate the insult of Bhagwa”) and “Anandabazar Patrika haye haye”. An ABP editor told Alt News that the demonstration began around 1:30 pm on Tuesday and continued for nearly an hour.
In another video, the group can be seen addressing a motley crowd and saying, “This land belongs to Shyama Prasad Mukherjee. This land belongs to Swami Vivekananda. This land is Saffron”.
Alt News procured more footage from the incident where the saffron-clad men could be seen sloganeering near the main gate in Hindi and Bengali before being escorted away by the police.
Anandabazar had carried the headline “Saffron Hooliganism: Logo broken during raid on JU campus” on its front page on August 21. Following this, Adhikari launched a sharp attack on the media outlet while maintaining that his demand for an apology did not amount to a threat to the media.
Meanwhile, Kolkata Police lodged an FIR at Bowbazar police station against editor Ishani Dutta Roy, chief reporter Soma Mukherjee and “others from its editorial team” following a complaint by Sanjay Shastri Maharaj. He alleged that the headline that Anandabazar Patrika had used implied an intention to “hurt Hindu sentiments and disturb public peace”. He stated that the phrasing was “highly objectionable, derogatory, misleading and offensive”.
“It is necessary to ascertain through investigation who proposed the expression, who approved it, who was involved in editing the report and determining the headline…” the complaint said.
“…An apology will have to be made. Otherwise thousands of sadhus in saffron robes are getting ready. They only want my consent…”, Adhikari declared during his rally in Jadavpur on August 28.
Anandabazar, however, did not issue apologise or retract its reports. In fact, they carried a follow-up story containing the chief minister’s statements.
Alt News spoke to a senior editor at Anandabazar Patrika, who said additional security had been deployed at the newspaper’s office near Chandni Chowk since Saturday, following Adhikari’s statements.
“We had a hunch something like this might happen. We were told not to go to office today. Police officials had come with them and left with them as well,” the editor said. Asked whether the men were affiliated with any organisation, the editor said, “They were not carrying any banners. But I do know that most of them were non-Bengalis.”
Alt News contacted Bowbazar police station, which said that no FIR had been lodged yet. Police also confirmed that the officials present at the scene were from Bowbazar PS, before ending the call.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.
Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.
The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.
Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.
Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.
Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.
Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.
One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings.
“Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.”
In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.
In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.
“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.
Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.
“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.
On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”

Wrexham complete signings of Ekomie and Kabore
- Published
Wrexham have completed the signings of Issa Kabore from Manchester City and Jacques Ekomie from Angers.
Burkina Faso international Kabore featured 32 times across all competitions during a loan spell with Wrexham in 2025-26 and has now signed a three-year deal with the club.
"I'm very happy to be back. It feels good to be here again," said right wing-back Kabore.
"Everybody knows our ambition is to get to the Premier League, and I'm here to fight for that promotion."
The deal for Kabore is worth up to £4.75m - with City having a 20% sell-on clause and matching rights.
Left-back Ekomie was in the final year of his deal with Angers and reportedly attracted interest from Wrexham's Championship rivals West Ham United and German side Hamburg.
On signing for Wrexham, Ekomie - who has put pen to paper on a four-year contract - said: "I'm excited to be here. It is a very big and interesting project for me - I'm here to progress, and I'm very happy to be here.
"I want to achieve great things at Wrexham. I think it's an ambitious project and I want to bring all my experience to help the team achieve our goals."
The Red Dragons recruited Liberato Cacace from Italian side Empoli during the 2025 summer transfer window, but the New Zealand international has been plagued by injuries since moving to north Wales.
Ekomie - signed for an undisclosed fee - will bolster Phil Parkinson's left-sided options, with the Gabon international joining right wing-backs Kabore and Danny Imray, goalkeeper Anthony Patterson and midfielder Ben Whiteman in moving to the Racecourse Ground this summer.
Kabore made a dream start to life with Wrexham last season as he registered a pair of assists on his debut to help the Welsh side earn a 3-2 win over Norwich City at Carrow Road.
His eight assists in the Championship were more than any other Wrexham player.
He was a mainstay under Parkinson before sustaining a hamstring injury while on international duty during the November break.
Kabore made his long-awaited return to action for Burkina Faso in the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations before again featuring prominently for Wrexham in the second half of the season.
The 55-cap international moved to Man City from Mechelen in 2020 before immediately returning to the Belgian club on loan.
He went on to have loan stints with Troyes, Marseille, Luton Town, Benfica and Werder Bremen prior to joining Wrexham on transfer deadline day in September last year.
He leaves Man City having failed to make a senior appearance for the club.
On Kabore's return, manager Parkinson said: "We're delighted to welcome Issa back to the football club.
"He had a successful loan spell with us last year, and we're looking forward to working with him again and watching him really develop as a player this coming season."

Ekomie started his professional career with Bordeaux but secured a switch to top-flight side Angers in the summer of 2024.
He made 21 appearances across all competitions in his debut season for the club, and his impact increased last term.
The 23-year-old featured in all but two of his side's Ligue 1 matches in 2025-26 - with 25 of his 32 league appearances being starts.
On Ekomie's signing, manager Parkinson said: "We're very pleased to sign Jacques. It's a transfer we worked very hard on.
"Jacques is a good young player and we're looking forward to integrating him into the group."
Ahead of his side's 1-1 draw with Watford, Wrexham manager Parkinson stated deals for various players to join the Red Dragons had fallen through in what had been a "difficult window".
But speaking in his post-match press conference after the Championship contest with the Hornets, the boss said there were "no guarantees" that Wrexham would further bolster their squad prior to the 23:00 BST transfer deadline on 1 September.
Midfielder George Thomason has operated as a makeshift wing-back in the absence of Cacace - who started just eight of Wrexham's 46 league games last season.
Cacace has missed all three of the Red Dragons' matches across all competitions so far this season and still has two years left to run on his contract at the Racecourse Ground.
Wrexham could yet add to their midfield and forward options in the final stages of the summer window.
Parkinson's men return to action against Birmingham City at the Racecourse Ground on Friday night (20:00 BST).

The younger brother of Dominic Perrottet has denied asking his brother to appoint a cabinet minister to achieve outcomes for a property developer, a corruption inquiry has heard.
Charles Perrottet told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that claims made in an intercepted phone call featuring developer Jean Nassif days before his brother became the NSW premier – in which Nassif described Dominic Perrottet as “my boy” – did not reflect promises allegedly made to Nassif.
Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating the allegation that conservative factional figures Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis received prohibited donations totalling $2m from Nassif or his company Toplace between 2020 and 2023 in exchange for political outcomes.
Those outcomes allegedly included damage to the career of David Elliott, a former NSW Liberal minister, who had opposed Nassif’s developments and the removal of the former building commissioner David Chandler, who was scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.
On Friday, the commission heard a phone call featuring Nassif, lawfully intercepted by police, made on 2 October 2021. Three days later, Dominic Perrottet was chosen as premier by Liberal MPs, defeating Rob Stokes, under a deal Charles Perrottet helped broker between conservative and moderate factions.
In the call, Nassif allegedly told a relative: “This week is going to be the worst week of my life … because we’re reshuffling the government.”
“We thought we [had] done it, then this wanker the police minister he did it, and he had a caucus, and he convinced Rob Stokes to challenge my boy,” Nassif continued, saying he supported Perrottet’s campaign. “They’re my people, they’re the right wing”.
Nassif told the relative he had been promised that then police minister Elliott and the then fair trading minister Kevin Anderson would be removed.
“I put my lady in in his position [sic], the consumer affairs minister … then I’m gonna … have to step on fucking David Chandler and get rid of him.”
The former NSW fair trading minister Eleni Petinos has previously told the inquiry she may have been used by fellow Liberals, including Chris Spence and Charles Perrotet, to get rid of Chandler, including attempts to persuade her Chandler was “dodgy”. She is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
On Friday, Charles Perrottet told counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, that following his brother’s accession as premier, he did not discuss the makeup of his cabinet with him. He later said he did recall “a conversation about the balance of women in the cabinet”, which he said he did not include names.
He said he did not discuss Petinos, or put her forward for the fair trading portfolio. “Dom would have made his own decisions,” he said. He said he did not recall having a conversation with Nassif about Petinos.
In another intercepted phone call to an unnamed person in January 2022, after Elliott had been moved to transport in a reshuffle the previous month, Nassif claimed he had “stripped him from his police ministry”.
“I’m gonna fuck everyone. The commissioner, [in] a couple of weeks he’ll be gone.”
Charles Perrottet, acknowledging that “commissioner” probably referred to Chandler, said: “You can’t take this seriously.”
Chandler resigned in July 2022 citing concerns with Petinos, who was sacked in that month amid bullying allegations which she denied at the time. Chandler, who was later persuaded to reverse his resignation, is not a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
The inquiry has previously heard that following a meeting between him and Nassif at the fine-dining Nobu restaurant in Melbourne in May 2021, Charles Perrottet wrote he had told Nassif “the best way to get the building commissioner off his back is to take the fight to Elliott and dismantle his infrastructure”. In another message he asked for payments in relation to Toplace developments.
Charles Perrottet, asked if Nassif’s claims were consistent with promises made at the dinner, said on Friday: “I wouldn’t put it that way”.
He has repeatedly denied taking payments from Nassif for political outcomes, saying he would regularly lie to the developer, adding a “political flavour” to advice in order to chase payments for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, a firm controlled by Greenwood and Ellis.
Nassif, who fled Australia for rural Lebanon in 2022, withdrew from an expected appearance by video link on Friday after providing a medical certificate. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Greenwood will appear before the commission again next week.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

The EPA classified trifludimoxazin as having "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential," which essentially means that while there is evidence the chemical could potentially be one that causes cancer, there isn't enough data to say for sure. Additionally, the EPA does not consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS, though the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development does.
In late summer 2026, some people on social media claimed that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration approved the use of a potentially carcinogenic pesticide that's a "forever chemical," also known as PFAS. PFAS, an abbreviation for perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are long-lasting chemicals that persistently remain in the environment, capable of accumulating in things like rivers, plants, animals and people's bodies, that often have harmful health effects on people, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed that the EPA "just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin," to be used on crops including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples and tree nuts such as almonds. According to the post, environmental groups consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS pesticide and "forever chemical." 
The U.S. EPA just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin for agricultural use on a wide range of crops, including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples, and tree nuts such as almonds.
Trifludimoxazin is also considered by many environmental groups to be a PFAS pesticide because it contains highly fluorinated chemical structures and can break down into persistent fluorinated compounds - i.e. nature can't break it down properly as it's synthetic. Environmental organizations have described it as a "forever chemical" and have filed lawsuits challenging the EPA's approval.
Environmental groups have also pointed out that the company's own studies showed evidence suggesting cancer concerns and that the EPA downplayed those findings whe not was approved. The EPA claims the product is safe and that people shouldn't be concerned. Not a good look for MAHA.
Similar Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same claims, which were also spread on X (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent us emails asking if the rumor is true.
The Trump administration's EPA proposed approving trifludimoxazin in June 2025 and went through with the approval in June 2026. Researchers have found some evidence suggesting the chemical may be carcinogenic, but it's not a "known carcinogen" like some posts claim. Trifludimoxazin is a PFAS as defined by the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, although not as defined by the more narrow EPA definition.
Trifludimoxazin is a pesticide, specifically an herbicide, that kills certain broad-leafed plants and grass weed species at agricultural sites farming "row crops (e.g., cereal grains, legumes, soybean) and tree orchards and groves (citrus, pome fruits, and tree nuts)," according to the EPA (PDF Page 6).
This wasn't the first time the EPA has tried to approve trifludimoxazin. In 2021, while Joe Biden was president, the EPA approved pesticide products containing trifludimoxazin, however; this approval was halted by lawsuits filed by environmental groups. The EPA then changed rules to require further EPA assessments before approving a new pesticide, and, ultimately, the makers of trifludimoxazin dropped their request for approval at the time.
The same environmental groups are attempting to halt the new approval for trifludimoxazin through lawsuits, as they did previously.
Potential carcinogen
The EPA did find evidence suggesting trifludimoxazin could possibly be carcinogenic, although it did not do enough research to confirm with certainty whether the chemical is carcinogenic.
In one study of rat carcinogenicity through chronic dietary exposure (PDF Page 8), the EPA found "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential." According to the EPA, such a classification means that the data raises a concern that the chemical has "potential carcinogenic effects in humans," but the EPA has determined the data is "not sufficient for a stronger conclusion."
Trifludimoxazin's entry on the pesticides properties database maintained by the U.K.-based University of Hertfordshire says that the chemical is "known not to cause a problem" as a carcinogen. The entry does report that trifludimoxazin is a potential liver toxicant, though. The database also notes "no serious health implications have been identified" with trifludimoxazin.
So while trifludimoxazin could potentially be a carcinogen, there currently isn't enough evidence to say with certainty that the chemical causes cancer.
Forever chemical
There are at least three definitions of PFAS, according to a 2022 paper in the peer-reviewed journal Digital Discovery: a broader definition from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development that is widely used internationally, a narrower definition used by the EPA and a definition that is a compromise between the two other definitions.
The University of Hertfordshire's database also classifies trifludimoxazin as a PFAS.
Where else has it been approved?
According to the University of Hertfordshire's database, trifludimoxazin has not been approved for use in the United Kingdom or the European Union as a whole. However, each individual state within the European Union has approved the pesticide for use in their individual countries. It has also been approved for use in Canada.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked claims about potentially toxic chemicals, including a claim about the use of paraquat by the parent company of the pomegranate juice brand Pom Wonderful.

India has been named the host of the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy, ICC announced on Wednesday.
The Brabourne Stadium in Mumbai and the Vadodara International Cricket Stadium will host the T20 tournament, from February 14 to 28.
Missing from the host roster is the D.Y. Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai, a popular women’s cricket venue in the country, and even one that the players of the national side have deemed the spiritual home of the women’s game in India.
The D.Y. Patil, a privately-owned venue within the D.Y. Patil University campus, was also the venue of India’s famous triumph in the Women’s ODI World Cup in 2025, where India beat South Africa in a high-octane and well-attended final. It is also a popular host in the Women’s Premier League, India’s top flight women’s franchise tournament.
ALSO READ | From Motibaug to Kotambi: Vadodara’s cricket passion finds a new home
D.Y. Patil earns NGT ire
During the conduct of the Indian Premier League’s 2026 edition, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) issued notices to six mainstream cricket stadiums and their respective associations raising concerns about sustainable use of water to maintain grounds and facilities.
The NGT bench comprised of chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and expert members A Senthil Vel and Afroz Ahmad who passed the order on April 16, directing cricket associations to regular groundwater extraction and put in place rainwater harvesting for maintaining pitches. Even installations of sewage treatment plants were taken into consideration at venues where rainwater harvesting might not entirely be feasible for operations as a primary way.
The six stadiums in the firing line were Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi, Sawai Mansingh Stadium in Jaipur, Shaheed Veer Narayan Singh International Stadium in Raipur, Dr. DY Patil stadium in Navi Mumbai, Bharat Ratna Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee Ekana Cricket Stadium in Lucknow, Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium in Hyderabad and Barabati Stadium in Cuttack.
“In such a background, the submission of counsel for the applicant is that all the activities in these six stadiums should be completely stopped and they should not be allowed to carry out any sports activity therein,” the NGT noted in its order.
The tribunal had also questioned why sporting activities shouldn’t be stopped for failing to furnish disclosures to the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA).
Sources suggest that this is why the venue has dropped off the radar for the prestigious Champions Trophy and will need to receive clearance for further sporting activity to happen at the premises.
Neither the ICC nor the BCCI has addressed reporters explaining the choice of venues or why D.Y. Patil Stadium has failed to make the cut.
The BCCI’s rotation policy for venues, which seeks to give more venues a chance to host marquee games, might have worked in favour of the Brabourne Stadium in Churchgate. This is also frequently used to stage WPL games across its four editions. CCI president Madhumati Lele Shrivastava was a member or the WPL Governing Council as well.
The Vadodara International Cricket Stadium, inaugurated in December 2024, has also found favour as a venue for women’s cricket fixtures in India from bilaterals to the WPL. Indian Olympic Association CEO Raghuram Iyer had even hinted at the city, 100km away from 2030 Commonwealth Games host city Ahmedabad, being considered to stage the cricket events of that edition.

Beyerdynamic's new Aventho Y headphones last up to 90 hours per charge
This is especially noteworthy, as the cans cost just $150.
Beyerdynamic just announced another pair of headphones in its Aventho line. The Aventho Y headphones have one standout feature, and it's a doozy. The battery lasts up to 90 hours per charge, so long as the ANC is turned off.
This drops to 60 hours with ANC turned on, which is still a mighty fine metric. There's a quick-charge feature that'll provide six hours of use with five minutes at the outlet. This is also a highly repairable set of headphones, which is always much-appreciated. The battery and ear cushions can both be replaced by the user. The sliders and hinges have been designed to "make it easy to replace high-wear components instead of the entire headphone."
The company is selling a handful of accessories for these headphones, including a boom mic and a USB-C dongle for connecting to Wi-Fi. This dongle can actually be stored underneath one of the ear cups, which is handy.
The Aventho Y headphones integrate with Bluetooth 6.0 multipoint connectivity, so folks should easily be able to swap between different audio sources. They ship with a lengthy USB-C cable that can be used to charge the device or for wired listening. There's a proprietary app for EQ, which includes genre-based sound presets. This is also where the firmware gets updated.
The specs look mighty solid on this one, and the price is too. The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y headphones cost $150. They are available in four colorways.
This isn't the only pair of Beyerdynamic headphones that include a user-replaceable battery. The flagship MMX 230 cans also boast this feature. I'm getting some FOMO here, as my current pair of over-ear headphones lack a user-replaceable battery and last for around, sigh, 30 minutes. Lithium battery degradation is no joke.

Bank of Canada unveils new vertical $20 bill featuring King Charles
The bill will enter circulation in 2027
It's official — Canada has a new $20 bill.
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem unveiled the new, vertical bill featuring a portrait of King Charles on Thursday in Ottawa. It's the first Canadian paper currency to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.
In a press conference, Macklem called the unveiling "historic," and added the new bill is both "visually stunning and more secure than ever."
The new note is polymer, predominantly green and vertical in orientation. The Canadian National Vimy Memorial remains on the back. Charles is centred on the front.
The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.
The Bank of Canada has previously noted that the $20 bill is its most-circulated currency.
This is also the second bank note in the bank's vertical series. The first, the $10 note, features civil rights pioneer and businesswoman Viola Desmond. That bill won won the coveted Bank Note of the Year Award for 2018, beating out top designs from places like Switzerland, Norway, Russia and the Solomon Islands.
- King Charles won't be featured on $20 bills until 2027, Bank of Canada says
- Donald Trump mistakes Bank of Canada for retail bank
The government announced that King Charles would replace his mother on Canada's currency during his coronation celebration in 2023. The first Canadian coins bearing the image of the King began circulating that December.
The reigning monarch has been featured on Canadian bills since 1935.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Trump’s Antitrust Gambit May Backfire
What the Live Nation Case Says About the Fate of Monopolies Now.
In March, one of the most important antitrust cases in recent memory went to trial. The Department of Justice and 39 states plus the District of Columbia had sued the ticketing-and-entertainment giant Live Nation, alleging that its 2010 merger with Ticketmaster had created an effective monopoly on live shows. According to the suit, Live Nation controls 70 percent of what the government defined as “major concert venues” in the United States, and Ticketmaster handles 86 percent of concert ticketing at those venues. The DOJ accused the company of exploiting this monopoly by compelling venues to use Ticketmaster as their exclusive seller, jacking up prices, and saddling concertgoers with unavoidable junk fees. This certainly looked like an archetypal case of a company’s size leaving consumers worse off—precisely what our antitrust laws are designed to prevent.
This is what made it so disappointing when, a week after the trial began, DOJ announced that it had reached a settlement with Live Nation. Although the agreement mandated changes to some of the company’s practices, including granting access to other booking agents at some venues and limiting fees, the deal fell well short of the more aggressive remedies that many people had hoped for, including—most obvious—breaking up the company.
This odd turn of events makes sense only because we know now that the decision to settle was made not by anyone in DOJ’s Antitrust Division but by the president himself, according to a recent report in The Wall Street Journal. Just before the trial was set to begin, Donald Trump met with the CEO of Live Nation in the White House a couple of times and allegedly told a senior DOJ official, “Settle it.” In other words, the federal government abandoned one of its strongest antitrust lawsuits in years because Trump wanted it to.
This may then seem like yet another story about how Trump has wrecked norms and corrupted the rule of law. But in this case, there’s a twist. After the Department of Justice announced in March that it was settling with Live Nation, many observers expected that the states involved would drop the suit and sign on to the deal, as typically occurs when federal regulators reach a settlement. But in this case, 32 states—including Republican-led Florida, Tennessee, Texas, and Utah—and D.C. refused to settle. In April, they won their case: A jury found that Live Nation had illegally monopolized the live-events business and overcharged consumers. The judge is still determining the remedy, but it will almost certainly be tougher than the deal Live Nation got from DOJ.
This will not be a one-off. A peculiarity of federal antitrust law is that state attorneys general can bring lawsuits on behalf of their citizens for violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act, and many states also have their own antitrust laws on the books. This gives them a great deal of leeway to act on their own. And because of the Trump administration’s attitude toward antitrust laws, what we saw in the Live Nation case—states refusing to defer to the feds, and instead pursuing litigation—will become more common.
This is because Trump, despite having campaigned as a populist who would fight to lower prices, has presided over an administration that’s been almost completely deferential to the interests of businesses looking to get bigger. Since his return to office, the Department of Justice has filed exactly one lawsuit to block a merger—the $14 billion acquisition of Juniper Networks by the Hewlett Packard Enterprise Company—only to quickly reach a settlement. Stanley Woodward, a top DOJ official who oversees antitrust enforcement, appears to be an active opponent of antitrust litigation. Bloomberg reports that he’s wondered aloud in meetings why DOJ can’t simply stop reviewing deals. That’s not exactly the guy you want in charge of preventing monopolies.
As the Live Nation case shows, even when a lawsuit does move forward, CEOs can simply go to Trump to get his support. After describing the settlement as “shocking” to lawmakers on Capitol Hill in May, Roger Alford, a Notre Dame law professor and former Antitrust Division senior official in Trump’s first term, observed that Trump’s interference in the case both undermined norms and set a new precedent for behind-the-scenes advocacy: “The rule of law quickly becomes the rule of lobbyists.”
Presidents historically avoided interfering directly with antitrust cases. The exceptions were few and notoriously corrupt (such as Richard Nixon’s meddling in an antitrust lawsuit against the International Telephone & Telegraph Corporation in exchange for a financial donation to the Republican National Convention). But Trump views the entire executive branch as an extension of his will, and he has turned regulatory agencies and DOJ into tools he can use to dole out favors, reward friends, and punish enemies. The only companies that have to worry about a federal antitrust prosecution at this point are those that Trump fiercely dislikes.
But as the Live Nation case demonstrates, any sighs of relief among leaders of America’s oversize businesses would be premature. In an ideal world, antitrust regulations wouldn’t be fragmented and enforced by a panoply of states. But when the president effectively turns national antitrust laws into dead letters, the virtues of federalism become apparent: States will do what DOJ fails to do. This arrangement also makes it harder for companies to simply lobby their way to good deals across multiple states.
The paradox is that by trying to hand out sweetheart arrangements to companies that are either trying to merge or flexing their monopoly power, Trump has made it more likely that those companies will have to navigate a gantlet of state lawsuits. And in asserting total control over the federal government, Trump has ended up making state governments much more aggressive and influential than they were before.

Revenue officer found dead days after he goes missing in Maharashtra
The deceased had gone missing since the morning of August 28, when he left home around 8.45 am, stating he was attending a post-funeral ritual.
Four days after a revenue officer posted in Thane went missing, his body was found in Shahapur in the district on Thursday morning, police said.
The deceased, identified as Arun Shelar, 56, served as a Mandal Officer and headed the vigilance team in the sand mining branch at the district collectorate.
The victim was found hanging inside a metal corrugated shed located near his residence.

‘Point of grievance’: Philippines urged to rethink school safety approach
A new bill aims to establish a comprehensive safety framework, but experts say measures must target mitigating violence much earlier
A bill pushed by lawmaker Bam Aquino will require schools to establish a comprehensive safety framework, including localised safety plans with guidelines on prevention, emergency response and recovery.
The bill also includes establishing common standards for safety infrastructure, such as the use of surveillance cameras, mandatory screening and visitor management.
Aquino, who chairs the Senate Committee on Basic Education, urged immediate approval of the bill as he invoked the names of students who died in the recent school attacks, warning that no more names must be added to the list.
“We cannot accept that this will be part of a normal school life. We cannot wait for the next incident to happen before we act,” Aquino said on August 26.

Last September, Steve Ballmer insisted in an ESPN interview that the Clippers weren’t involved in a shady-looking $28 million endorsement deal for his star player, Kawhi Leonard, that involved no actual endorsing. Now, the former Microsoft CEO has been suspended by the NBA for a year, while the league says his team will forfeit five future draft picks and pay a $30 million fine, among other penalties.
Steve Ballmer got suspended by the NBA because of a podcast and a jumbotron corruption scandal
Pablo Torre found out, and now the results of the NBA’s investigation are hammering the LA Clippers.
A year later, an NBA-commissioned 35-page report by Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is basically calling him a liar, saying those claims were “inaccurate (at best) with respect to Mr. Ballmer” and “clearly false” when it came to Clippers president of business operations Gillian Zucker, who is also suspended for a year. Leonard has accepted the punishment of a $700,000 fine and a ban for his business manager.
Now the Clippers are writing angry letters to the NBA, claiming a biased investigation spurred by “a podcaster’s baseless claims” has cost Ballmer $50 million for lawyers, cost more for his reputation, and upset partners like Daktronics, the company that built a massive 4K scoreboard for the team’s new arena, with its many, many bathrooms.
That unnamed podcast, of course, is Pablo Torre Finds Out, which is cited at the beginning of the document for kicking this whole thing off one year ago today.
The episode made largely unknown fintech startup / green bank / massive fraud Aspiration a household name, and launched a series by the former ESPN reporter and his team. Now the league’s report is filling out the role partners like Daktronics played in getting Leonard money above and beyond the NBA’s mandated salary cap and how it was tied to that massive scoreboard.
In the spring of 2020, and in response to a request-for-proposal process initiated by the Clippers, Daktronics began to compete to obtain a lucrative contract to supply digital scoreboard and signage technology at the Intuit Dome. In May 2020, the Clippers informed Daktronics that it was the team’s preferred provider for this project, but that the team wanted to agree on a “spend back” arrangement whereby Daktronics would provide some amount of business back to the Clippers—which Daktronics told investigators is not uncommon in its industry. Ms. Zucker thereafter suggested to a Daktronics senior executive that this “spend back” could be accomplished through an endorsement agreement between Daktronics and Mr. Leonard.
The report says that an unnamed Clippers executive told Daktronics exactly how much to pay Leonard ($3 million for two years), and eventually told the company in 2021 “that, because the team had decided to increase the amount it would spend on the scoreboard, Daktronics should correspondingly increase the amount it would pay to Mr. Leonard.”
As we mentioned at the time, costs for the eventual Intuit Dome had reportedly ballooned to over $2 billion, including the Daktronics-built “Halo Board,” a double-sided 44,000-square-foot wraparound 4K screen with a price said to be over $100 million. Said the now-suspended executive Zucker when it was announced, “We are excited to partner with Daktronics, an innovator in video displays, to develop a Halo Board that will create one of the most intense live experiences in sports.”
Daktronics, according to the investigators, along with now-incarcerated Aspiration cofounder Joe Sanberg and what remains of the company in bankruptcy proceedings, cooperated with the investigation. However, there are two other Clippers-affiliated companies apparently involved in paying Leonard an extra $18 million, including Lockton Insurance, which refused to cooperate, and Boingo Wireless, which should probably add an anti-snitching policy to its terms of service. According to investigators, Boingo “purported initially to cooperate, but then supplied information that was inconsistent or not credible to investigators and ultimately refused to cooperate further.”
Aspiration, which kicked the whole thing off and had advertised itself as “Wall Street greed’s worst nightmare,” turned into just that for investors including Ballmer, as reported sham endorsement deals by cofounder Joe Sanberg were part of a scheme to create fake revenue. He would eventually be sentenced to 14 years in prison for costing investors $248 million.
While the league’s punishment for Ballmer and the Clippers largely ignores the details of Aspiration’s deal and Ballmer’s $50 million investment, the report now includes a note that at the time, Sanberg explained the curious arrangement to other executives differently, emailing an employee to say that “[the Forum is] going to purchase $7mm of reforestation capacity each year from Aspiration to make the ticket experience carbon neutral and potentially carbon negative. To be clear, the $7mm figure per year is set so what’s variable is how they choose to use it.” That figure matched Leonard’s endorsement payments.
Other explanations were even more clear about the connection to Kawhi Leonard:
When these concerns were conveyed to Mr. Sanberg, he told the Aspiration executives that “the Clippers are asking us to do this with Kawhi Leonard” and that the team would provide additional business back to Aspiration to help offset the financial impact on Aspiration. In an email exchange among Aspiration’s CEO, CFO, and general counsel, one wrote, “[Mr. Sanberg said] that the Clippers are promising to increase the amount they pay us per quarter in line with what we pay this guy [i.e., Mr. Leonard].” Another responded: “Thanks for verifying. . . . We should be fine if it’s cashflow neutral.”
One Clippers executive called its stadium deals with Aspiration “super shady” and full of red flags in text messages to the team’s CFO, and the investigation revealed that while Ballmer and Zucker claimed the $7 million annual arrangement was the result of a study done by a team consultant, the consultant disagreed.
No Clippers witness could provide a credible alternative explanation for the initial appearance of the $7 million annual payment from the team to Aspiration in the Forum Agreement. Mr. Ballmer and Ms. Zucker both claimed that it was based on a study done by a team consultant who had determined that the Forum needed $28 million to offset its carbon emissions and that the team would pay Aspiration for these offsets over four years. But investigators spoke directly with this consultant, who said that the Clippers had given him a $28 million budget with which to address the Forum’s emissions—not the other way around.
After untold hours of podcasts (including Torre’s triumphant two-hour live reaction to the report), repeated blanket Clippers denials, and at least one fraud conviction, the investigation still isn’t over. The investigators are looking into a claim that “the consulting agreement one company signed with the Clippers was in fact a ruse, designed and intended to be a vehicle for the team to provide the company with funds to be paid to Mr. Leonard.”
Ballmer’s lawyers say they are “exploring every legal remedy to address this gross injustice,” but if I were on the investigation I’d just want to know which one is a bigger regret — giving up 10 draft picks and the rights to a future two-time MVP in the Shai Gilgeous-Alexander trade or launching Windows Vista?

Tamil Nadu will launch the ‘Chief Minister’s Elderly Health Insurance Scheme’, covering nearly 38 lakh senior citizens aged 70 and above. The scheme will provide free medical treatment, including cancer care packages, advanced cardiac surgeries, organ transplants, and high-end diagnostic services, at empanelled government and private hospitals, with no ceiling on income, Health Minister K.G. Arunraj announced in the Assembly on Monday (August 17, 2026).
The Minister made 115 announcements for the Health Department at a total estimated outlay of ₹2,997 crore. It covered areas including policy reforms, universal free health services, new posts creation, infrastructure projects, equipment and procurement, direct beneficiary programmes and digital health initiatives.
The 87-year-old Tamil Nadu Public Health Act, 1939, will be replaced with a modern, comprehensive Act to address contemporary and future health challenges. Dr. Arunraj said a new provision would make unsupervised home births outside hospitals a punishable offence. Noting that Tamil Nadu was known as the country’s health capital, he said that ‘TN Medicity’, a world class integrated medical hub comprising clinical services, research, medical tourism, and AYUSH, would be established. The government will allocate ₹10 crore for the preparation of a Detailed Project Report in the first phase.
‘Nalam 360-Annual Free Health Check-up for All’ scheme will be rolled out. Under this, everyone aged 30 and above will receive 14 basic tests annually, free of cost, across 1,257 government health facilities in the State.
This will include blood pressure, ECG, haemoglobin, complete haemogram, random blood sugar, urea, creatinine, total cholesterol, serum bilirubin, urine albumin, and VIA screening. For the first time in the State, the Health Department will introduce Home Based Diagnostic Services — sample collection and testing services — in metropolitan areas on a public-private partnership model, he said.
Policy reforms
The department will come up with a ‘Positive Health Policy’ to promote holistic health and wellbeing at the community, family, and individual levels, accompanied by the “Nalam 360” mobile application. A new legislation ‘TN Institutions of State Importance in Health Care Act’ will come up to create institutions of State importance to provide world-class medical services.
Addressing a long-standing demand, Dr. Arunraj said 2,500 permanent posts of staff nurses would be created. Existing contract nurses on consolidated pay will be absorbed into regular time-scale pay. A total of 1,695 nursing posts on consolidated pay will be created at a cost of ₹42.72 crore.
A total of 3,594 medical staff across 24 categories, including pharmacists, nursing assistants, village health nurses, and ophthalmic assistants, will be recruited through the Medical Services Recruitment Board. Additionally, the department will create 284 temporary super speciality posts across 25 specialities such as neurology, cardiology and nephrology on time-scale pay to take advanced medical care to the district-level.
These posts will be created to accommodate doctors who complete their post-graduation every year and are posted in government hospitals on bond conditions. A number of announcements for infrastructural development such as new hospital buildings and medical equipment were also made.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday (August 28, 2026) submitted in the Supreme Court a proposal to provide information relating to added sugar, fat and salt in pictorial form on the front-of-pack (FOP) of food products, in line with international regulations.
“The proposal is intended to provide a simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning to consumers regarding food products which are high in specified nutrients of concern,” an FSSAI affidavit filed in the Supreme Court said.
The affidavit proposes an FOP warning label in red hexagonal shape for food products which are high in any two or more “nutrients of concern” such as added saturated fat, added sugar and salt, based on thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024.
The warning label would read ‘High Fat’, ‘High Sugar’, ‘High Salt’ or ‘Highly Sweetened Beverage’ and be displayed in a font one point larger than that used in the nutrition information table on the back of the pack to help customers readily identify at-risk foods.
The FSSAI said single-ingredient food products and those which are “inherently rich in fat, sugar or salt, like ghee, edible oil, jaggery, honey” are proposed to be exempted from FOP warning requirement.
Phased implementation
The affidavit said the FOP labelling mechanism is intended to be implemented in phases to “facilitate consumer acceptability and provide industry adequate time for reformulation”.
Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients and specified sweetened beverages. Phase II would extend the warning mechanism to products high in any one of these nutrients.
The affidavit in the Supreme Court came in a petition filed by NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi. Mr. Dvivedi said the NGO would file a comprehensive rejoinder to the FSSAI’s compliance affidavit in the apex court after inviting public comments.
The compliance affidavit by the food regulator follows scathing comments on August 13 from a Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala on the state’s obligations to protect public health. The court had observed that not only developed but even developing countries were adopting international standards of packaging food products.
Bringing awareness
“A positive step in that direction would further accelerate our country’s endeavour to be fully developed, by bringing awareness to the public in general of the ill-effects, emanating even from indigenous foods, despite our conviction that indigenous foods coming from diverse cultures in this country were never intended to be packaged,” the court had recorded in its August 13 order.
The court had noted that the Economic Survey has already suggested FOP labelling, and the Union government would not have any impediments in implementing the changes.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind,” Justice Pardiwala had addressed the government on August 13.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to work on his Washington, D.C., beautification projects, thus making those workers unavailable for immediate rescue efforts in the aftermath of the Aug. 29, 2026, Grand Canyon National Park flash floods, is unproven.
- The rumor stemmed in part from users sharing a Sept. 1 article from the online publication The Lever, which reported, "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
- The Lever cited a CNN article published days before the flooding reporting hundreds of NPS first responders were reassigned without saying exactly when the staffing shifts occurred. The CNN story cited its own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources.
- Snopes has not been able to review the same internal CNN documentation, nor have we located information confirming or debunking the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hampered flood rescue efforts.
- An Interior Department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers hampered the flood response, "That is 100% false." We reached out to numerous other relevant parties and will update this article if we receive further details.
A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to Washington, D.C., to work on his administration's beautification projects circulated online in early September 2026. People sharing the claim suggested they would have proved key in rescue efforts, possibly saving lives, had they been available immediately following the Aug. 29 flash floods inside Arizona's Grand Canyon National Park. We have not yet found evidence that would confirm or debunk this rumor.
The National Park Service, an agency under the Interior Department, announced closures to bridges, the Colorado River, lodging and trails, as well as confirming two deaths, one person missing and around 80 people rescued or evacuated.
An NPS news release said the two people who died, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, both of Granbury, Texas, were hiking in Bright Angel Canyon and were a part of the same group as the missing person. A key water pipeline sustained severe damage, as well.
In one example of the rumor, on Sept. 1, an X user posted (archived) a message appearing to place blame for the deaths on Trump.
(@factpostnews accessed via X)
Other posts featured the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).
Some posts directly cited the online publication The Lever, which published an article on Sept. 1 with the headline "Before Deadly Floods, Trump Diverted Emergency Responders To Beautify D.C." The story's subheading reads: "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
The Lever's article cited a CNN story published prior to the floods on Aug. 25, telling of Trump's administration sending 300 NPS incident management team workers — a division responding to wildfires and other incidents — to work on what CNN dubbed Trump's Washington, D.C., "pet projects," such as the past renovations for the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the future overhaul of the East Potomac Park golf course. The CNN article does not say exactly when the purported staffing shifts occurred.
The CNN reporters cited their own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources regarding other information.
Neither the Lever's article nor users' posts explicitly said the Trump administration's reported diversion of 300 workers hampered rescue efforts surrounding the flash floods. Either way, users inferred it, some believing Trump very recently diverted the workers, with one Snopes reader emailing, "Did tRump divert 300 specialized emergency first responders from American national parks to work on his Reflecting Pool, in the midst of needing them for Grand Canyon rescues?"
Snopes has not been able to review the same internal documentation CNN cited, nor have we located information that might allow us to conclusively rule on the veracity of the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hindered Grand Canyon flood rescue efforts. This claim is therefore unproven and we have left it unrated.
Via email, the White House referred us to the Interior Department, where a department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers to Washington harmed the flood response, "That is 100% false."
We requested documentation, information and/or comment from the Arizona Department of Public Safety, CNN, Coconino County Emergency Response, Grand Canyon National Park, The Lever and NPS, and will update this article if we receive further information.
A brief timeline of rescue efforts
Within three hours of the flooding on Aug. 29, NPS Grand Canyon shared details about officials evacuating 50 people by air. By the next morning, the division reported 62 total evacuations out of the roughly 80 rescues to date, and said it had gotten assistance from the Arizona Public Safety Department.
A Sept. 1 notice from NPS Grand Canyon announced the continuation of search-and-rescue operations, as well as that the "NPS Western Type 3 Incident Management Team" — the same as the incident management teams CNN and The Lever reported about — would be taking over command as of that morning. The Arizona Daily Sun published a photo reportedly showing a member of that same team observing an Aug. 31 news conference, two days following the flooding.
For further reading about Trump's beautification efforts in the nation's capital, we previously reported about an allegation that his administration chopped down dozens of beloved cherry trees to renovate a golf course, as well as that his motorcade ride inside the reflecting pool caused damage he later blamed on others.

HIV is no longer a word that frightens young people. For a generation that has grown up seeing HIV transformed from a feared death sentence into a manageable chronic condition, the virus no longer carries the deterrent power it once did.
But the fading fear of HIV is confronting Keralam with a new public-health challenge. Changing sexual behaviour, gaps in information and awareness, and growing substance use are increasingly putting young people at risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
The numbers seeking care at the 23 District STI/RTI Centres (DSRCs) under the Kerala State AIDS Control Society (KSACS) have been rising steadily. However, these figures do not capture the full picture, as Keralam does not have routine STI surveillance across public and private hospitals. STIs also rarely figure in formal public health conversations.
World Sexual Health Day
On World Sexual Health Day (September 4), experts say Keralam needs more open conversations with young people about sexual health, safe sexual practices, consent and healthy relationships. Equally important is ensuring that youngsters know where they can seek confidential testing, advice and treatment without fear of judgement.
KSACS data compiled up to December 2025 show that attendance at DSRCs rose from 41,417 in 2023-24 to 63,129 in 2024-25. Another 51,243 people visited the clinics during April-November 2025 alone.
The proportion of DSRC clients undergoing RPR screening for syphilis also increased—from 55% in 2023-24 to 70% in 2024-25 and 79% during April-November 2025. The increase in screening means more infections are being detected, and the figures cannot by themselves be taken as evidence of a corresponding rise in prevalence.
Of particular concern is the increase among younger clients. Among those aged up to 19, clinic attendance rose from 1,547 in 2023-24 to 2,255 in 2024-25; another 1,910 had been recorded during April-November 2025. The proportion of newly detected HIV infections among those aged 15-24 also rose from 10% in 2022-23 to 15% during April-October 2025.
Change in societal attitudes
“There is a change in societal attitudes towards casual sex and today, the earlier message of abstinence that we used to give youngsters no longer works. Many youngsters are sexually active today and our only message to them is to remain safe, because their health is at stake,” a senior Health Department official said.
Being safe goes beyond HIV prevention. Condoms significantly reduce the risk of many STIs, including HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia, but do not eliminate the risk of infections such as syphilis, HPV and genital herpes, which can spread through skin-to-skin contact. HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, regular testing, timely treatment and reducing exposure to multiple or unknown partners are also important.
Consent and communication also need to be part of sexual-health messaging. Being safe means being able to say no, respecting a partner’s decision and discussing protection before sex.
Substance use among young people is another concern for sexual-health professionals, who say intoxication can increase risky sexual behaviour and impair the ability to make informed decisions.
Testing is crucial
“One of the most important messages we can give youth today is that testing matters, even without symptoms. Many STIs cause no symptoms, so someone can have and transmit an infection without knowing it. Testing becomes particularly important after a potential exposure or when starting a new sexual relationship,” said V. Sam Prasad, who heads AHF India Cares, an NGO working in HIV.
Keralam’s STI clinics are seeing a range of infections, with syphilis emerging as a particular concern. Doctors also report a resurgence of gonorrhoea, which they say is increasingly being encountered in clinical practice.
KSACS data show that clients found reactive for syphilis on screening increased from 1,206 in 2023-24 to 1,455 in 2024-25, with another 1,121 recorded during the first seven months of 2025-26.
Complicated infections
“We are quite concerned that some STIs are now presenting differently and with serious complications. We have had reports of neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and cardiovascular syphilis, which are complicated and require long and intensive treatment,” a Health official said.
At STI clinics, young people diagnosed with an infection are encouraged to bring their partners for testing to prevent reinfection. They are also advised to complete treatment and undergo HIV testing, given the close relationship between HIV and other STIs.
Self-assessment tool
To encourage confidential testing, KSACS has launched a digital self-assessment tool through which users can privately assess their sexual-health risk. By scanning a QR code and answering questions about lifestyle and behavioural practices, users receive guidance on whether testing may be advisable, along with information on the next steps and the nearest STI clinic.

US President Donald Trump has rejected claims that the United States is running short of ammunition amid its military operation in Iran, calling reports about dwindling supplies “100% wrong” and accusing those spreading them of being “treasonous.”
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said critics and media outlets were suggesting that the US lacked sufficient ammunition because they wanted to see the country lose the war.
“For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition,” Trump wrote.
Trump claimed the US has far more ammunition than it could use in the current conflict or in any other potential war.
He also said the United States is producing munitions at “levels never seen before” and is building up stockpiles to prepare for possible future contingencies.
According to Trump, the US has temporarily prioritised keeping its ammunition for domestic military needs rather than selling it abroad. He said weapons sales to US allies would resume “soon.”
Trump also turned his criticism toward the previous Biden administration, claiming it provided substantially more ammunition to Ukraine than the US has used in Iran.
He alleged that the Biden administration gave “hundreds of billions of dollars” in assistance to Ukraine and NATO without requiring European allies to pay for it.
Trump said the US would seek repayment for that support, although he did not provide details on how or when such payments would be pursued.
The President's comments came as he sought to push back against reports and criticism questioning US military stockpiles during the Iran operation.
Trump accused media outlets and others of undermining the US war effort by highlighting ammunition concerns.
He maintained that the US military has sufficient supplies and that American weapons production is continuing at historically high levels.
The US military has used up much of its global stockpile of highly accurate, long-range missiles during its five-month war with Iran, raising concerns about the Pentagon’s readiness for future conflicts, Reuters reported on August 4.
According to three people familiar with the data cited by the news outlet, the US Army has used “virtually all” of two key surface-to-surface missile systems — the Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) and the newer Precision Strike Missile (PrSM).
The sources did not disclose how many missiles remain in US stockpiles.
The long-range missiles, which cost more than $1 million each, allow US forces to strike targets accurately from relatively safe distances.
ATACMS has also played an important role in the Ukraine war, where US-supplied missiles have been used by Ukrainian forces to strike targets inside Russia.
The newer PrSM is designed to replace ATACMS and offers greater range and capabilities. Reuters reported that PrSM supplies were already relatively limited because it is a newer weapon, although the Army has placed large orders for the missile for 2027.
The Army has said ATACMS is being phased out as production shifts toward PrSM.
The depletion of precision missiles has raised concerns among US officials about the country's ability to respond to future threats from major adversaries such as Russia and China, Reuters reported.
Military leaders have also warned President Donald Trump in recent weeks that supplies of defensive weapons, including Patriot missile interceptors, were falling.
Patriot systems are particularly important for defending against ballistic missile attacks.
Several media reports last week suggested Trump had decided against another major offensive inside Iran partly because military advisers had warned about declining US weapons stockpiles.
However, a US official disputed that explanation, saying Trump chose not to proceed with another attack because of pressure from Gulf states.
Despite concerns over depleted precision weapons, one person familiar with the situation told Reuters that the US military remains capable of replenishing its supplies.
US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, has been able to draw from US military stockpiles located around the world, the person said.
