Quick Answer
Instagram uses icons for likes, comments, reposts, saves, messages, Reels, Stories, calls, profile tools, notifications, active status, and more. This guide explains what every major Instagram symbol means and what happens when you tap it.
Instagram is the most popular app with billions of users around the world. The platform has lately been getting plenty of new features and fixes.
Instagram is also one of the few platforms that are known for experimentation. Meta often changes their layout very often, which can sometimes confuse users. If you are new to Instagram, or even an existing user, the new features and some icons you never use can be confusing.
Some of the features on Instagram don’t have an undo option, so it is better to know what they do before pressing them. In this guide, you will learn everything about Instagram icons, their meanings, and what they are used for. To make it easy for you, we have included each and every icon on every page of Instagram and explained what it does.
Table of Contents
What Do Instagram Symbols and Icons Mean?
Instagram Post Symbols Meaning
Instagram posts are what we see and interact with most on a daily basis while using the app.
They come with several engaging elements. Most of them are easy to understand, but if you are confused, here is what they mean:
- Like: Wherever you see this heart symbol on Instagram, it represents a like for posts, comments, and all
- Comment: This represents a comment on the post. Tapping on it reveals all the comments, and you can also add a comment.
- Repost: Instagram has recently introduced the ability to repost. The reposted post also appears on your feed.
- Save: The save feature lets you save posts; in other words, it works like a bookmark.
Instagram Home Screen and Bottom Navigation Bar Icons Meaning
Now let’s look at what the icons mean on the home screen and on the bottom navigation bar.
You won’t find many icons on the home screen, except for the ability to create a new post and to view all your notifications.
If there is one area that Instagram constantly experiments with, it is the bottom navigation. Meta keeps changing the positions of the icons and also changes their designs frequently.
Here is what they mean:
- Notifications: The heart symbol here represents notifications. Here, you can see all the notifications you receive inside the Instagram app.
- Create: The plus symbol here represents “create,” which you can use to create a post or a story and more.
- Home: Tapping on the home icon takes you to the home screen. It is part of the main bottom navigation. Tapping on it also takes you to the latest posts.
- Reels: Instagram has added a dedicated Reels tab, where you can tap on it to go to the Reels section.
- Messages: Tapping on this icon takes you to the Instagram Messages screen, previously known as DMs.
- Search: Tapping on the search icon takes you to the Explore page.
- Profile: This is a profile icon, which takes you to your profile page.
Instagram Reels Tab Icons Meaning
Instagram offers a dedicated Reels tab where you can see all the latest Instagram Reels. It also comes with several interactive elements, some of which are already used for posts.
Here is what each and every icon means in the Instagram Reels tab:
- Create: You can also add new posts directly from the Reels page. You can tap on the Plus icon.
- Like: It lets you like the Reel you are watching. You can like it, and tapping on it removes your like.
- Comments: Lets you add a comment and see comments for the Reel you are currently watching.
- Repost: It lets you repost the Reel you are currently watching.
- Share: It lets you share the Reel with your friends. You can also copy the Reel link using this option.
- Save: You can save or bookmark the Reel using this icon.
- More options: Gives more options for Reels, including Playback controls, Meta AI, and much more.
- Audio: It represents the audio used for the Reel. Tapping on it reveals more details.
Instagram DM Page Icons Meaning
Instagram DMs are among the most feature-packed, yet Instagram somehow manages to keep them minimal. However, they do come with several icons. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram message space:
- New message: It lets you create a new message. After tapping, you can select the user and send a message.
- Notifications off: It appears if you turned off notifications for Instagram.
We missed highlighting the Instagram Instant feature that the company introduced very recently. It lets you share a random photo with other users without complex editing.
It is turned on by default, and tapping on it shares whatever your phone camera sees, so be careful before pressing it. There is also an option to turn it off completely
Instagram Profile Page Icons Meaning
Instagram profile page also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what they mean:
- Create: Lets you create a new post, Reel, or Story from your profile page too
- Menu: Lets you access main and global Instagram app settings
- Threads: Lets you open the Threads app by Instagram.
- Discover people: The icon lets you discover new friends. It appears when you have a lower following count.
- Posts: Represents the Posts tab
- Reels: It represents the Reels tab
- Tagged posts: It represents the tagged posts where you can see all the posts you were tagged in by your friends.
- Pinned post: It means the user has pinned the post. Instagram lets the user pin up to three posts.
Instagram DM Message Icons Meaning
The chat interface also comes with plenty of icons, which can be confusing for a beginner. Here is what each icon means inside Instagram chats:
- Instagram Blend Feature: This is an Instagram Blend feature where you can invite the user to the Blend, where you can see each other’s suggested Reels, new Reel suggestions based on the chat, and much more.
- Voice call: Lets you make a voice call to the user
- Video call: Lets you make a video call to the user
- Voice message: Lets you send a voice message in the chat
- Photo library: Lets you select the local photos on your phone and send them to the chat
- Stickers: Lets you access the stickers
- More options: Gives you more options, including the ability to send location, draw, and access Meta AI and much more
- Camera: Lets you access the camera, where you can quickly take a photo and share it with the user.
Instagram Share Screen Icons Meaning
The share screen on Instagram is very simple. It is very similar to the other share screens, but it comes with one unique icon that lets you create groups. Here is what that icon means:
- Create group: This is the share screen that appears when you tap on the share button under the post or the Reel. The user icon means you can create a new group.
Instagram Call Screen Icons Meaning
Instagram calling screen also comes with several icons during the call, and here is what each of them means:
- Camera off: During the video call, it lets you control the camera. If you see a cross line, it means your camera is turned off
- Mute microphone: Lets you mute or unmute your camera
- Speaker off: Lets you turn on or off sound from the other user
- End call: End the video or voice call using this button.
Instagram Story Editor Icons Meaning
If you are adding a story for the first time, it can be confusing because Instagram Stories are feature-packed and let you customize everything you upload. Here is what each icon means on the Instagram Stories screen:
- Add text: While adding an Instagram Story, tapping on this icon lets you add text
- Stickers: It lets you add stickers to an Instagram Story
- Music: Lets you add and select music.
- Effects: Lets you add effects
- More tools: More creator tools. Tapping on it lets you access more tools
- Next: Once added, you can move to the next screen while adding a Story
Instagram Profile Bio Options Icons Meaning
Instagram profile bio also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what each icon means and what it does:
- Notifications: Lets you turn on or off notifications for this account.
- More options: Gives you more options about the Instagram profile you are viewing
- Profile link: Instagram lets users add links in their bio. The link icon represents the link the creator added to their Instagram bio. It is also available for regular users.
More Instagram Profile Icons Meaning
Here are more icons that you see when you visit any Instagram profile, including icons in the top right corner of the post and the verified blue checkmark right next to the profile. Here is what they mean:
- Verified badge: Instagram has verified the account, which means it represents the official account. Also, Instagram allows users to pay for the verified badge.
- Video or Reel: If you see this on top of the post, it means the post contains a video or Reel.
- Carousel post: If you see this with a number, it means it is a carousel post.
Instagram Reels Controls Icons Meaning
In the Reels tab, when you pause the Reel, Instagram displays more icons. Here is what they mean, including the recent Friends tab icons:
- Create: The plus icon lets you create a new post or Reel
- Trending audio: If you see an arrow next to the audio file name, it means that audio is trending
- Sound: Lets you turn off sound or turn on sound for the video. It appears when you tap on the video
- Play: It appears when you pause the video. Lets you play the video again
- More options: Again, tapping on this option gives you more Reel options
- Reposted by a friend: If you see a purple arrow icon, it means the Reel is reposted by your friend. If you see the like, it means the Reel is liked by your friends.
More Instagram Messages Icons Meaning
Here is what the different icons mean in the Instagram DM space. If you have multiple accounts and unread messages, Instagram will notify you with different color badges. Here is what they mean:
- Pinned chat: It appears when you pin the chat for any user in your Instagram DMs.
- Muted chat: It means you muted the chat. You won’t receive any notifications for their messages.
- Unread message: It shows the unread messages inside the chat. If it appears, it means you have unread messages.
- Account switcher: Lets you switch between accounts, and if you see the red icon, it means you have unread notifications from the other account
More Instagram Post Icons Meaning
Instagram recently launched collaborations, which allow users to collaborate with each other and publish posts. It joins with older tags, the ability to add music, and much more. Here is what each icon means:
- Collaborative post: Instagram lets you add collaborative posts. If you see multiple profile pictures, it means it is a collaborative post from those accounts.
- More options: It lets you access more options for the posts
- Explicit audio: If you see an E icon right next to the sound or audio, it means the song contains explicit content
- Tagged people: It lets you view all tagged users for the post. Tapping on the user takes you to their profile
- Sound: It lets you mute or unmute the sound for the post.
Paid Instagram Post Icon Meaning
You don’t need a special introduction for the ads on Instagram. If you see a post and you are confused about whether it’s a regular post or not, you can find a little “Ad” label under the profile.
- Ad: If you see Ad, it means it is a sponsored post or ad inside the Instagram feed.
Instagram Story Viewer Icons Meaning
Fortunately, Instagram has kept stories minimal. They also come with several interactive elements. One is the ability to like them and also share the story with others.
- More options: Gives you more options for the Instagram Story you are viewing, which includes options like the ability to report it and more
- Like Story: Like means you can like your friend’s Story
- Share Story: You can also share the Story with others. Tapping on it lets you share the Story with your contacts.
Instagram Close Friends Story Icons Meaning
If you see a green icon in the stories, it means that the user has added you to their close friends list. It comes with an extra “Close Friends” tag, and while the rest of the elements look the same, it doesn’t come with a share option.
Here is what each icon means in the Instagram Close Friends Story screen:
- Close Friends: If you see this green star, it means they have added you to their Close Friends list and shared a Story with you
- More options: Lets you access more Story options
- Like Story: Lets you like your Close Friend’s Story.
Instagram Reels Comments Symbols Meaning
Finally, ending this guide with the post or Reels comments, it also comes with several elements which can be confusing for the beginner. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram post or Reels comments section.
- Sound: You can turn the Reel sound on or off using the icon
- Like comment: You can like any comment made by users. The number below shows how many people liked it.
- Photo: Instagram recently announced the ability to add a photo as a comment.
- GIF: You can also add a GIF in the comments.
- Gift: Send a gift in the comments. You can tap on it and buy points with real money and help the creator to make money.
Instagram Active Status Symbol Meaning
- Green dot: If you see a green dot, it means the user is active on Instagram. If you hide your active status, it won’t appear for you even if others are online.
Story Rings Meaning
- Grey colored ring: If you see a grey-colored ring, it means you have already viewed their story.
- Colorful gradient ring: It means they added a new story or a story you have not watched yet
- Green ring: If you see a green ring, it means a story for a close friend that the user added. In simple words, the user added you to their close friends list and shared a story with close friends.
Still Confused About an Instagram Icon?
Those are the icons and symbols and their meanings on Instagram. Instagram constantly tests new icons and new features, and also changes existing features. As I said before, the platform has undergone several fresh layouts over the years.
To stay updated with the latest, we also update this post regularly when Instagram changes the layout and announces a new feature. We update this post regularly to keep the same layout and make it less confusing compared to what you currently see on your Instagram app.
Fortunately, Instagram also uses the same icons for its desktop version and for the Instagram app on other platforms as well. If you still find any icon confusing on Instagram, you can comment below, and I am happy to guide you.

China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.
The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.
China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February.
How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.
The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.
This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.
In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.
Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”
Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.
In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.
Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.
“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

A year after crash of an iconic Lisbon streetcar, a memorial but no promises for restored service
Lisbon’s iconic funicular streetcars remain halted, with safety questions still unanswered a year after a tragic derailment killed 16 people
LISBON, Portugal -- Lisbon inaugurated a memorial Thursday to the 16 people killed in a funicular derailment a year ago, as questions persist about the safety of the city's iconic hillside streetcars, which remain at a standstill.
Near the crash site, a 150-year-old olive tree stood at the center of a ring of limestone blocks laid into the ground featuring the names of the victims. Foreign ambassadors laid wreaths and the Patriarch of Lisbon, a senior Catholic church official, offered a blessing.
The accident was one of the Portuguese capital’s worst tragedies in recent memory and cast a shadow over the city’s ongoing tourism boom.
The picturesque yellow streetcar, called a funicular because it travels up and down a steep hill in tandem with a second car, is a popular tourist attraction. Authorities said that 11 of those killed were foreigners, likely tourists who stand in long lines to board it.
Lisbon attracted about 10 million tourists last year, and they are one of the city’s economic mainstays. Portugal receives around 30 million visitors each year.
Service on the Gloria funicular remains halted while the official investigation proceeds. Two other city funiculars also remain out of service during inspections. The regular streetcars that rumble through the city's streets are running as usual.
The anniversary brought renewed attention to delays in identifying the causes of the crash, which also injured 24 people, and attributing any blame.
Carris, the Portuguese company that runs the city’s road transport, said Wednesday it plans to open an international tender in the first quarter of next year for the affected funicular to be modernized, with the goal of it returning to service by 2029.
Portugal's public prosecutor's office said it hoped to publish a final report by March regarding the accident’s causes and whether there is any criminal liability.
Families of the victims complained in a letter obtained by public broadcaster RTP about “a year of silence” from authorities. They had been kept in the dark about the investigation, receiving no contact from officials, they said, according to RTP.
A preliminary report into the accident published last year said that the failure of a steel safety cable and maintenance flaws contributed to the crash. The streetcar hurtled down the hill before coming off the rails on a bend and smashing into a building, leaving the wooden cabin a crumpled wreck.

New Delhi, Sep 3 (PTI) The Supreme Court on Thursday flagged the issue of encroachment and stationary vehicles on highways and asked the National Highways Authority of India why it cannot install a camera surveillance system and monitoring rooms across toll plazas to deal with it.
A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta, which was hearing a suo motu case related to an accident in Rajasthan's Phalodi area that claimed 15 lives, said that encroachment and stationary vehicles on highways were the two major issues.
The counsel appearing for the NHAI said they have issued circulars for regular inspection and patrolling to check unauthorised parking on the highways.
"Why can't you think of having a camera surveillance system? You can have monitoring rooms at all toll plazas," the bench said.
Senior advocate ANS Nadkarni, who is assisting the top court as an amicus curiae in the matter, said one of the major issues was illegal parking of vehicles on highways, which leads to road accidents.
The bench noted that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Tamil Nadu government have not yet filed their compliance affidavits in the matter.
It granted two weeks to both the ministries to file their affidavits.
The bench posted the matter for October 6 and directed the Tamil Nadu government to file an affidavit before the next date of hearing.
In November last year, the top court took suo motu cognisance of the November 2 road accident in Phalodi in which a tempo traveller rammed into a stationary trailer truck.
The incident occurred near Matoda village on the Bharat Mala Highway when the tempo traveller was going from Bikaner's Kolayat temple to Jodhpur.
On April 13, the top court issued a slew of interim directions, including that no heavy or commercial vehicle shall park or stop on any national highway carriageway or paved shoulder except at a designated bay, lay-bye or wayside amenity.
It had also prohibited construction/operation of any new 'dhaba', eatery, or commercial structure within the right of way of any national highway.
The top court directed the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways/NHAI to identify accident blackspots and critical areas and publish a comprehensive list of accident blackspots on national highways.
"It is seen that national highways constitute approximately 2 per cent of India's total road length but account for nearly 30 per cent of all road fatalities. A road, particularly a high-speed expressway, must not become a corridor of peril due to administrative lethargy or infrastructural gaps," it had said.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Google hasn’t released a frontier-level Gemini Pro AI model since early 2026, but it sure loves rolling out new Gemini Flash variants. Today, Google is announcing its third Flash model release in just six weeks, making it more likely that we’ll never see the promised Gemini 3.5 Pro. But no matter, says Google, because Gemini 3.8 Flash is its best reasoning and coding model yet.
Gemini 3.8 Flash comes in two variations. There’s the standard Flash, which Google describes as a “workhorse” model that’s good for anything from agentic tasks to software development. Then we have Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, which runs on the same foundations but has been tuned for vulnerability detection and mitigation.
For developers, Google has the same pitch as it did for the 3.7 Flash release just a couple of weeks ago. API access to the model is available at an “introductory rate” through the end of the year: $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens. The regular price will be $1.50 / $7.50, but it’s likely there will be new models available long before the price changes. Google probably sees the lower prices as a necessity given that other AI labs have recently dropped token pricing to keep increasingly wary businesses engaged with AI tools.
Google has offered its usual raft of benchmark numbers, which appear to show Gemini 3.8 Flash competing with (or even beating) larger and more expensive models. The numbers show a marginal improvement over Gemini 3.7 Flash in most tests, but the gains are larger in coding evaluations.

How the Early Dreams of the Internet Changed
Technology was once seen as countercultural. What happened?
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.
During the 1984 Super Bowl, an advertisement launched a technological revolution. If you were alive, you probably know the one. Directed by Ridley Scott, the minute-long spot showed men in gray uniforms, heads shaved, eyes blank, marching in unison toward a lifeless auditorium. A Big Brother figure speaks from a giant screen, droning on about “the first glorious anniversary of the Information Purification Directives.” All the while, a woman in red shorts and a white tank top is running to the auditorium. She looks like she’s just come from an aerobics class, but she has a sledgehammer, and authorities are in pursuit. Entering the room, she hurls the sledgehammer into Big Brother’s face. There’s a flash of light, and a wind blows over the stunned, awakened audience. A different voice—a comforting one—announces, “On January 24th, Apple Computer will introduce Macintosh. And you’ll see why 1984 won’t be like 1984.”
Although the ad did not show an actual Macintosh computer, it worked. Apple went on to sell 250,000 of its user-friendly, mouse-driven little machines in that year alone. The ad also asserted what was to be a defining idea of the emerging digital age: that personal computers, far from massive instruments of centralized control, were vessels of individual freedom. The coming of the internet, with its invitation to universally accessible knowledge and the free exchange of ideas, seemed to affirm the promise: Our machines wouldn’t enslave us; they would liberate us.
The dystopia depicted in the ad came by way of George Orwell’s imagination, but the fears underlying it had deep American roots. As mass consumer culture expanded in the early 20th century, American artists, intellectuals, and critics worried over the problem of “conformity” and the loss of individualism that came with it. Most didn’t see the dark totalitarianism of 1984; instead, they saw a world of ready-made desires, a soulless existence brought to you by corporations, advertisers, media, and politicians. As The Atlantic’s review of Sinclair Lewis’s Babbitt put it in 1922, “the ‘standardized American’” was becoming “as much a national product as the Ford car”—a person like Babbitt himself, whose entire life and very personality were shaped by forces beyond him. Such criticism formed a fault line that ran from the cultural commentary of the ’20s to the outbursts of Beats, folkies, and academics in the ’50s.
The earthquake, of course, would come in the counterculture of the 1960s. No longer would people need to be stuffed into “Little Boxes,” as the folk singer Malvina Reynolds worried early in the decade. The counterculture promised liberation from such confinement. Visiting San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district for The Atlantic in 1967, the novelist Mark Harris wondered whether he was seeing Babbitt’s descendants finally rebelling against conformity in ways that Babbitt himself could not. The counterculture’s sensibilities migrated into the mainstream, where popular culture and advertising absorbed its language of liberation and transgression, so that admen could pitch 7 Up using hippie iconography or Virginia Slims cigarettes by way of the women’s-liberation movement.
Digital culture would prove especially receptive to these countercultural ideals. Northern California, after all, was the center of both the counterculture and the tech industry, and the cross-pollination between the two was considerable, as the historian Fred Turner has shown. By the 1990s, as the internet was becoming a mass medium, some of its first boosters (many of whom had roots in the counterculture) were presenting it as the realization of countercultural ideals. John Perry Barlow, a poet and sometimes Grateful Dead lyricist, wrote his 1996 “Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace” in response to an early effort to regulate the internet. It reads like a Port Huron Statement for digital culture, describing a realm of individual freedom and free-flowing ideas that would break from existing forms of cultural and institutional authority. According to Barlow, a new “civilization of the Mind” was coming.
In the dot-com and digital revolutions that followed, many of the people who sold the hardware, coded the software, and built the platforms were seen as iconoclasts themselves. Digital entrepreneurship became a form of transgression, not just in the casual dress and informal culture of the Silicon Valley office but also in what it promised to users. Tech visionaries pledged to create a world that would make possible precisely the kind of self-expression, open exchange, and communal connection that the counterculture had promised. It was no coincidence that by the late 1990s, Apple’s advertising—again with almost no reference to the machines themselves—simply pictured groundbreaking figures such as Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., Bob Dylan, and John Lennon, alongside the slogan “Think Different.”
In many ways, those promises were fulfilled. The internet did splinter 20th-century mass culture, and the effects have been every bit as revolutionary as promised. We don’t all watch the same networks anymore; we don’t see the same movies; we don’t get our news from the same places or read the same books (mostly, we just don’t read); we “do our own research.”
Even as the conditions of mass culture and conformity that shaped the counterculture and the early dreams of the internet have faded, we continue to live in their shadow. In the fractured age of social media and the unknowable algorithm, our devices give us the feeling of freedom, even as they serve the interests of corporate forces that track our movements, catalog our interests, and profile our wants. The oppressive monoculture has been replaced by countless minicultures, each with their own devoted acolytes; we still inhabit little boxes, partially of our own making.
The transgressive ethos, meanwhile, continues to thrive. Subversion is perhaps the dominant language of digital culture, spoken across the political spectrum by podcasters “just asking questions,” wellness gurus swilling at-home health hacks, manosphere kingpins lashing out against wokeness, and lefty influencers denouncing the billionaire class. Everyone, it seems, is hurling a sledgehammer at something.

After U.S. President Donald Trump announced in August 2026 that he would rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," social media users spread a screenshot appearing to show a Truth Social post from the president that announced the construction of the "Melania Canal" that would 
The screenshot circulated across Facebook (screenshot) and Threads. Here's what Trump allegedly said:
The FAKE NEWS is saying we need the Canadian canals that connect to LAKE AMERICA. Total lie! We don't need their small, low-energy Welland Canal! America built the Panama Canal, we built the Suez Canal — incredible, beautiful, high-IQ canals! I have officially instructed the Army Corps of Engineers to build a much BIGGER, DEEPER, WIDER, and far more powerful canal bypass connecting straight into Lake America! It is going to be magnificent! And we are naming it after my stunning, beautiful wife: THE MELANIA CANAL. Every American will be able to EASILY enter the Melania Canal from BOTH the front end and the back side for a very minimal fee! Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Some users seemed to interpret the rumor as true, and Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
A closer look at the screenshot indicated that this post was labeled as satire, both under the usual spot for "Likes" on a Truth Social post and as a watermark across the image.
According to the watermark, this post originated with a Facebook account called Mrs. Putin, which identifies itself as "Satire/Parody" in its description. Mrs. Putin first shared the post (screenshot) on Aug. 29.
As Mrs. Putin pointed out in a Facebook message conversation with Snopes in 2025, the account's posts often include several indicators that they are satire, including misspelled names. In this case, aside from the "satire" label, other indicators that the post is fake include that Mrs. Putin changed "Likes" to "disLikes" and misspelled Trump's social media tag, "@realDonaldTrump," as "@realDotardTurmp" and his last name as Turmp.
(Mrs. Putin)
A search of Trump's social media accounts using the databases Trump's Truth and Factbase also determined that, as of this writing, the president has not declared the construction of a "Melania Canal." He did, however, float renaming the Strait of Hormuz to "Trump Strait" in a Sept. 2 Truth Social post.
For more on Lake Ontario and its renaming, Snopes previously debunked a claim that Canadian officials were refusing passage to ships with "Lake America" in their documentation and confirmed that Lake Ontario was not named after the Canadian province.
Snopes also has previously written about numerous satirical Mrs. Putin posts.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Two trapped tunnel workers rescued in Nepal
The men were named as Sanjay Shah, 30, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, 45, a mechanical supervisor.
KATHMANDU: Two hydropower workers were pulled from a tunnel buried by debris in Nepal on Friday (Sep 4), more than a week after catastrophic flooding swept through the area, government ministers said.
Rescuers cheered as one man was pulled from a muddy opening, video released by the energy ministry showed. He was helped to his feet by rescuers.
A photograph showed the second man caked in mud, his hands pressed together in prayer, as rescuers carried him away on an orange stretcher.
The men were named as Sanjay Shah, 30, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, 45, a mechanical supervisor, by Home Minister Sudan Gurung.
"I am so happy, my heart is lighter," Amir Maharjan, the brother of rescued worker Kabir Maharjan, told AFP.
The two are among hundreds of hydropower workers missing since a wall of mud and debris swept through the region on August 26.
Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha confirmed that one person had been safely rescued from the Trishuli 3A tunnel, followed shortly afterwards by a second.
"We have just received news that another person ... has also been rescued," Gurung said in a statement.
The government had initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive inside multiple tunnels. Searches were continuing at Trishuli 3A and other sites.
"BACK IN MIRACLE COUNTRY"
Rescue teams in Nepal have recovered more than 1,250 bodies, and more than 5,000 are missing, after the gigantic wave triggered by a rock and ice avalanche roared down the China-Nepal border.
Australian rescue expert Arnold Dix, who has advised on multiple tunnel-collapse rescues, has been supporting the operation remotely and is travelling to Nepal to support teams on the ground.
Earlier on Friday, Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, said teams at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project believed they had heard a faint response from inside the tunnel.
He said rescuers had called into the tunnel: "Don't worry, we are rescuing you."
"They believe they received a faint response from inside saying, 'hunchha', yes or OK," Dix told AFP, adding that he was en route to Nepal to join the rescue effort.
"Right now, I'm 'glass three-quarters full' ... After a week of 24/7 heartache, we might, just, be back in miracle country," he said.
Dix said teams had dug through debris blocking the tunnel for 50m to 60m and had been hoping for a breakthrough at any moment.
Less than an hour later, rescuers pulled the two men to safety.

Doctors from a private health facility in West Bengal have successfully treated a seven- year-old boy suffering from thalassaemia using an advanced Haplo Cord transplant process.
The parents of the 7-year-old child diagnosed with HbE Beta thalassemia, who needs monthly blood transfusions, were counseled to register under the “Save the Sibling” programme. They underwent IVF (in vitro fertilization) and pre-implantation genetic testing to produce a matched thalassemia-free sibling with compatible HLA (human leukocyte antigen), which is critical for bone marrow transplantation.
A haplo-cord transplant was performed using the cord blood from the patient’s sibling and some stem cells from his father. The transplant was conducted by Narayana Health. During the transplant period, the child developed complications such as infections, mucositis, liver derangement, and persistent low blood counts, which were effectively managed. The patient has recovered well and is now transfusion-free, the doctors said.
In another feat, the team treated a 62-year-old male patient from Myanmar with brain cancer after a successful CAR T-cell therapy (an advanced type of immunotherapy). The patient was initially found to be having gait disturbance (an unusual change in the way a person walks). He was then diagnosed to have primary CNS lymphoma, a rare, aggressive type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma where cancer cells form in the brain, spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, or eyes.
After receiving four cycles of high-dose chemotherapy yielding unsatisfactory results, the doctors decided to have him undergo CAR T-cell therapy. He underwent lymphocyte collection, bridging with radiation and other medications, before receiving a dual CAR targeting CD19 and CD22 on the cancer cells.
Speaking about these two rare recoveries, Joydeep Chakrabartty, Senior Consultant, Hemato Oncology & Clinical Lead - BMT Programme (East), Narayana Health, said that the recoveries are landmark achievements with both facing potential fatalities.
“Using the Haplo-cord technology for the child and the CAR T-cell therapy for the aged patient, the expert team of doctors attending them have been able to turn their lives around for the better. Narayana Health has always been at the forefront in breaking new grounds in medical science, and these two cases clearly reflect that,” Dr. Chakrabartty said.
Also read: Evidence of CAR T-cell therapy against cancers presented at US conference
Prasanta Chowdhury, Laboratory Director, Cord Life Sciences India Pvt. Limited, said that cord blood banking is a complex issue involving medical, financial, ethical, and scientific debates. “The core dilemma centres on choosing between private storage for family use and public donation for general use, weighed against high costs and low statistical odds of personal use. In these two cases, we have successfully addressed every single concern with absolute compassion and clarity,” Dr. Chowdhury said.

Israel’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, with the intention of sending them abroad.
Speaking in the run-up to close-fought Israeli elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of its population of roughly 2 million over the next six years.
“It’s realistic,” Ben-Gvir said, claiming there were countries that were “ready” to take in Palestinians from Gaza, without naming which ones.
While the forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, Israeli political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for Gaza, rebuffing efforts by the US president, Donald Trump, to advance a half-baked and largely moribund ceasefire deal that has been marked by continuing Israeli attacks.
Ben-Gvir said the far-right Jewish Power party would demand “a ministry in charge of emigration” during the formation of the next government, adding that his plan was “the result of a year and a half of work and … is concrete”.
The proposal is contained in a 20-page document with the euphemistic title of “National Work Plan for Voluntary Emigration from the Gaza Strip”.
Despite the use of the word “voluntary”, the plan will be seen as coercive by the international community because of the dire conditions imposed on Gaza’s population by Israel and because of Ben-Gvir’s explicit intention: to remove Gaza’s Palestinian population.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
Ben-Gvir’s comments follow hard on the heels of comments by Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the approval of the Trump administration to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he claimed was still under discussion after being “frozen” by Trump.
Katz, at a conference hosted by the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion.
Trump himself provoked international outrage at the beginning of his second term with a suggestion that all 2 million Palestinians leave Gaza and that the US redevelop the territory, a proposal he later walked back.
With elections in Israel in October, Ben-Gvir has made a series of inflammatory interventions aimed at his far-right base, including sharing footage from a site where Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks by Israeli military courts – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – are to be executed. In another video, he revelled in the mistreatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli custody.
Polling suggests that Jewish Power, the party led by Ben-Gvir – who has convictions for incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organisation, and who has been put under sanctions by various countries – would gain about seven seats.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part staged a visit to a military outpost in Gaza on Wednesday to insist that Israel would not withdraw from the areas of Gaza that it occupies.
“We are not withdrawing. We are staying on this line. We control 60% of the strip. And there is still more to come, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us – we do this day in and day out,” he said.
According to Israel’s deputy chief of general staff, Maj Gen Tamir Yadai, the country now controls 65% of Gaza. This is far beyond the 53% agreed under the ceasefire brokered last year by Trump.
As well as pushing for the expulsion of Gaza’s population, Ben-Gvir has called for the deportation of two MPs and others “who are disloyal to the state of Israel” – including Jews – saying he would promote such a policy if he is included in the next government.

US-based fintech company PayPal has handed the pink slip to about 220 of its employees based out of India as part of its global layoff exercise. Nearly 4% of its India workforce has been impacted by the exercise, a company spokesperson confirmed to Inc42. “The recent staffing changes are part of our previously announced multi-year transformation to simplify our global operations, strengthen execution, and position the company for long-term growth,” the spokesperson said. The layoffs likely impacted roles in tech, engineering, operations, payments and finance across the company’s offices in Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. Moneycontrol, which reported the development first, said around 600 employees across PayPal’s India operations were impacted. Reported earlier this year, PayPal is said to be eyeing trimming its global workforce by about 20%, about 4,760 jobs, over multiple years. The overhaul is also intended to generate at least $1.5 Bn in savings. An impacted employee told the publication that employees were asked to join a call on August 31, where they were informed about the layoffs. Their access to company systems was revoked shortly after. The job cuts in India come as PayPal undertakes a broader organisational overhaul to simplify operations, lower costs and focus investment on areas it believes can deliver stronger long-term growth. The exercise is being rolled out in phases, beginning in the Asia-Pacific region, including India, before moving to the US, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, according to media reports. "We are simplifying our organisation and reducing our cost structure to increase investment for long-term growth. Over time, we will shift from stabilisation to targeted growth investment and accelerate our momentum with next-generation innovations," CEO Enrique Lores said earlier while disclosing PayPal's Q2 performance. Layoffs Becomes A Recurring Theme In The Tech Sector PayPal’s layoffs come amid a broader wave of job cuts across the technology and startup ecosystem. Multiple reports of mass layoffs undertaken by tech giants have surfaced within this week itself. While it was reported that tech giant Oracle could cut about 3,000 jobs in India earlier this week, Uber is axing 200-250 Indian jobs as part of a broader global restructuring that would see it cut 3,300 roles. The developments are not an isolated event within this week. Multiple mass firings have happened within this year. Earlier this year, Amazon announced 16,000 job cuts globally, while Meta downsized its metaverse division by around 1,500 employees as it shifted its focus towards AI. Atlassian, the parent company of Jira, also announced 1,600 job cuts, with India-based employees accounting for around 16% of the impacted workforce. In India, ecommerce enabler GoKwik laid off around 100-120 employees as part of a restructuring exercise, while Livspace cut around 1,000 jobs as part of an AI push. AI-focused healthcare technology company Innovaccer also reportedly reduced its workforce by around 350 employees, while IPO-bound Acko trimmed approximately 5% of its workforce as part of an AI-led restructuring.

Kenyan President William Ruto on Thursday said that his government had directed Tata Chemicals to halt its operations in the country, citing that the Indian company’s presence had not delivered sufficient value to Kenya, according to Reuters. Ruto said two new companies would be brought in to take over the operations currently handled by Tata Chemicals. The development follows a decision in late July, when Tata said the Kenyan government had instructed its subsidiary, Tata Chemical Limited, to suspend activities at the Magadi Soda factory and stop exporting soda ash. While during a visit to the region in Southern Kenya, Ruto stated, “That TATA company ... had that contract for 100 years. They have not built anything in Kajiado, they have not built any factory in Kajiado.” “We have said we will bring a new company and... they should put a big glass company here in Kajiado. And another company to make chemicals here in Kajiado. Are we slaves to other people?” he asked. The company was not immediately available for comment on President Ruto’s move, Reuters said. Kenya’s mining ministry had asked Tata Chemicals Magadi Ltd. to halt operations about five weeks earlier, citing unpaid royalties and non-compliance with regulatory requirements. Kajiado Governor Joseph Ole Lenku also said the company’s mining rights had lapsed in 2023. Kenya has been extracting soda ash for more than a century, with Tata acquiring the operation from Brunner Mond Ltd. in 2005. At a public rally in Kajiado, he stated any company granted future rights to extract soda ash would be expected to establish large-scale processing facilities locally, including plants for manufacturing glass and chemicals. “Those who we will license to extract the resource must build a huge processing facility here to produce glass. They should build a big factory to produce chemicals here," Bloomberg quoted him as saying. “Come what may, because they have been unable able to do what is required, I have told them to pack and go,” Ruto added. In July, Tata Chemicals maintained that it remains in line with applicable regulations and is engaging with government authorities and relevant agencies to address the issue and ensure continued adherence to regulatory requirements. Tata Chemicals stated in a statement that it is “fully compliant with all requisite regulations and continues to work with all authorities and agencies to uphold the highest standards of compliance.” Kenya is the world’s fourth-largest producer of natural soda ash, contributing about 1% of global output, according to the US Geological Survey. Trump asks Supreme Court to lift block on USPS plan to restrict mail voting
The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to lift a block on the U.S. Postal Service plan for President Trump's attempt to restrict mail-in voting for the midterm election.
For now, key parts of that plan are blocked by a temporary restraining order from a federal judge in Boston.
As the legal fight over Trump's mail-in voting order continues, here's what to know about the state of voting by mail for the midterms:
Has the USPS plan directly changed mail-in voting for the midterms?
No, key parts of the plan, including requirements for states, are currently blocked by a court order. Voting by mail is still available to all voters who are eligible for it in their states, and USPS is expected to deliver mail-in ballots for the midterm election as usual.
How could the USPS plan change mail-in voting?
State election officials would be required to turn over lists of mail-in voters' names and addresses to USPS and have certain barcodes on their mail ballot envelopes, according to a revised rule for federal ballot mail the Postal Service issued in August. USPS says it would not deliver ballots to voters for election officials that don't meet those requirements.
When does mail-in voting start for the midterms?
North Carolina has to start mailing out its absentee ballots on Friday, which officially kicks off the voting season for this year's midterms. Many other states are set to begin sending out their mail-in ballots later this month.
Is it possible for the USPS plan to be carried out for the midterms?
Many election experts say it is too late for USPS to carry out this plan without causing major disruptions. A whistleblower report claims USPS has not properly tested the online portal system that would collect mail-in voters' information. The report also alleges the agency has set up a policy for verifying ballot envelopes that could result in many voters not getting their ballots in time for the midterm election or at all.
What are the legal arguments for and against the USPS plan?
USPS came up with this plan in response to a March executive order by President Trump, who said he issued the directives to USPS to stop illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens. Many studies and audits show, however, that problem is incredibly rare. While USPS claims its revised rule is an effort to regulate mail, challengers of the USPS plan argue it is illegal because the mailing agency has no authority to control voting by mail.
Hasn't the Supreme Court already ruled on Trump's mail-in voting order?
Yes, the Supreme Court ruled in August on a procedural question about one of the lawsuits. But so far, the justices have not ruled on the legality of the order or the USPS plan.

Fintech unicorn turned small finance bank (SFB) slice is set to raise around $100 Mn in fresh funding at a valuation of $450 Mn-$465 Mn, marking a sharp decline from the startup’s last valuation of around $1.25 Bn, sources told Inc42. The round is expected to be backed by Peak XV-backed wealth management platform Neo Group, Japan-based Kado Global and existing investor Moore Strategic Ventures, according to people familiar with the development. The round could also include a secondary component, with the exact split between primary and secondary capital yet to be discerned. Moneycontrol reported the development first. The investment deal could potentially value the startup at roughly one-third of its last known valuation of $1.25 Bn. The startup entered the unicorn club in 2021 when it raised $220 Mn in its Series B round led by Tiger Global and Insight Partners. However, the valuation dip comes amid slice's bid to establish itself as a digital bank following its merger with North East Small Finance Bank (NESFB). The transaction gave the Bengaluru-based startup a small finance bank licence and marked a fundamental shift from its earlier lendingtech model. From Fintech To SFB slice’s original business was built around credit and prepaid-card products, but regulatory changes in 2022 disrupted that model. It subsequently acquired NESFB and completed the merger in October 2024. Since then, slice has expanded its offerings across deposits, lending, UPI-linked credit and payments, while building out MSME and merchant lending businesses. The transition also changes the metrics investors use to assess the company. Rather than being valued primarily as a consumer fintech business, slice is now positioning itself as an SFB. This means that banking-related metrics — deposits, lending growth, profitability and cost of funds — have gained importance. An investor note by 8i Ventures founding partner Vikram Chachra, reviewed by Inc42, compared slice's valuation with other banks on a price-to-book basis. The note puts slice at around 4.5X book value. The valuation reset comes despite improving financial performance. slice Swings To The Black The SFB swung to the black in Q1 FY27, reporting a net profit of ₹50.9 Cr in the June quarter against a net loss of ₹10.1 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its profit for the quarter under review also surpassed the ₹48.4 Cr PAT it reported for the entire FY26. slice’s total income rose 38.6% to ₹413.8 Cr during the quarter from ₹298.6 Cr in Q1 FY26. r. Meanwhile, its gross loan book grew about 55% to ₹5,098 Cr from ₹3,284 Cr a year earlier. Its deposits nearly doubled to ₹5,765 Cr from ₹3,038 Cr during the same period, slice said in a statement. Current account savings account (CASA) ratio stood at 43.9%, with CASA and retail term deposits together accounting for 94.7% of its total deposits. The bank’s total assets increased 54% YoY to ₹7,444 Cr, while its net worth rose 16.5% to ₹896 Cr. Its outstanding debt declined 23.2% to ₹507.3 Cr from ₹660.4 Cr a year earlier.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani introduced a one-year ban on AI in schools, which he said could affect 600,000 public school students. And the tech world has a lot to say.
On Wednesday, Mamdani proposed a moratorium that would ban the use of AI in schools for children from 2-K — school for two-year-olds — to eighth grade. High school students will get "twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules." The ban also includes screen time restrictions adjusted for the students' grade level.
The same day, Los Angeles Unified School District, the second-largest school district in the US, introduced its own moratorium on AI for the rest of the school year. It would apply to all students, including those in high school, but only on district-owned devices and student accounts.
Many in the tech world have taken to social media to criticize Mamdani's AI ban, calling it counterproductive to restrict a technology that could be as transformational as the internet or computers.
Mamdani's plan does not require city council approval. Chancellor Kamar Samuels has already issued the moratorium as official NYC Public Schools guidance, stating that student-facing generative AI software "is not permitted" in grades K-8 during the 2026-27 school year.
However, some executives have called the moratorium a measured response to a technology with still-unclear ramifications for young, developing minds.
Here's what smart people are saying about the AI bans for school students.
Sriram Krishnan, a former senior White House policy advisor on AI
Sriram Krishnan, a tech executive and former senior White House policy advisor on AI under the second Trump administration, said AI's impact on development is unknown and that it makes sense not to "automate cognitive skills" before kids can acquire them.
"Kids need to struggle with all the reading writing math research and reasoning to develop these skills," Krishnan said on X on Thursday, "AI will just remove the friction."
"This is the age when foundational skills are formed, adults know this skill so automating with ai can be ok vs a 10 year old who never learns may not," Krishnan added.
Zach Tratar, engineering leader at Notion AI and angel Investor
Zach Tratar, an engineering lead at Notion AI, wrote on X that AI's effects on children should remain experimental until we learn more.
"I'm a pro-AI techno-optimist at heart," Tratar said on Thursday.
"But I also remember when we all thought simply connecting people on the internet would make communities healthier," Tratar added. "And when we didn't know if Tiktok would damage our brains."
Noah Fichter, CEO of Scout
Noah Fichter, the CEO of Scout, an AI startup in the 2025 Y-combinator cohort, wrote on X on Thursday that the tech world's reaction to the AI ban in schools makes him feel "frustrated."
"Schools have no literally idea what to do about AI," Fichter said. "Especially when many of the school-specific chatbots we're putting in front of kids are actively decreasing scores!"
"Seems pretty obvious to me that Mandani & co spent time in schools, realized the chaos these tools are causing, and decided that we need to take a second to breathe to actually figure it out," Fichter added.
Sarah Shirazyan, lecturer at Stanford Law School
Sarah Shirazyan, a lecturer in law at Stanford Law School and a research fellow at the Hoover Institution, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Thursday that she expects AI in classrooms to be a big topic for public debate and an issue in elections.
"The truth is nobody knows what's the right approach, everyone is experimenting and the moratorium reads to me as let's take time to understand the evidence--aka prove AI works for learning," Shirazyan said.
"Having said that, I tell my own Stanford Law students all the time: 'Use your brain first,'" Shirazyan added.
Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth and Investment Management
Ross Gerber, CEO of financial advisory firm Gerber Kawasaki Wealth and Investment Management, said in a post on X on Thursday that he did the opposite of banning his own children from using AI.
"All the kids use AI already. What a goof," Gerber said. "I remember when they told me I couldn't use the computer- go use the typewriter they said."
Dylan Itzikowitz, tech investor and partner at South Park Commons
Dylan Itzikowit, a tech investor, posted on X on Thursday that AI could have been the "great equalizer" of education.
"Wealthy kids won't be affected by this. Private schools will teach them the latest technology," Itzikowit said. "Another DSA policy that will hurt middle and lower income families the most."
Brendan Falk, founder and CEO of Hercules
Brendan Falk, founder and CEO of Hercules, an AI app builder, called the AI ban "unfortunate" on Thursday.
"This is like banning computers in the 90s or the internet in the 2000s," Falk wrote in a post on X.
Gabriel Petersson, cofounder and CEO of Energy
Gabriel Petersson, the CEO of an AI-powered productivity app and a former OpenAI researcher, said that banning AI is to him, similar to "banning all computers then giving someone a corporate job."
"These kids will be doing their work with assistance of ai if they choose white collar jobs," Petersson said. "Like there is a clear difference in skill in people who grew up with computer versus those that started in high school."
Will Hobick, head of design engineering at Rocket
Will Hobick, head of design engineering at Rocket, a mortgage platform, called banning AI in schools "completely backwards."
"The question isn't whether middle schoolers are going to grow up using AI. They are," said Hobick in a post on X. "The question is whether we teach them how to use it well."
"Blocking the technology is easy," Hobick added. "Teaching kids how to use it responsibly is the actual work that the administration has decided they can't do."

Anthony Joshua's driver attempted overtake before fatal crash, trial hears
- Published
The driver of a car carrying Anthony Joshua was attempting to overtake another vehicle when it crashed, killing two of the boxer's friends, a court in Nigeria has heard.
Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, 46, faces charges including causing death by dangerous driving and driving without a valid national driver's licence. He denies the charges.
The court was told that the group - who had been travelling to visit Joshua's father in Ogun State, near Lagos in Nigeria, last December - were asleep when Kayode lost control of his Lexus SUV while he overtook a moving truck and collided with a parked lorry.
Joshua's personal trainer, Latif Ayodele, and strength coach, Sina Ghami, died in the crash.

A second defendant Abubakar Adamu, 35, the driver of the stationary lorry the car collided with, denies a charge against him of obstructing the free flow of traffic.
Inspector Christopher Ajayi Taiwo of the Ogun State Motor Traffic Division told the court that by the time he arrived at the scene, both the damaged Lexus and the stationary lorry had been removed.
But debris from the crash and soya beans scattered on the road from the lorry's load were found by officers, he added.
The only items recovered from the Lexus were a logbook, painkillers and an energy drink, which were found near the driver's side, Ajayi said.

Dozens missing, 5 dead after migrant boat is found drifting near Spanish islands
At least five people have died after a boat carrying West African migrants ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean
BARCELONA, Spain -- At least five people died and dozens more were feared dead after a boat carrying West African migrants ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean. Forty-four people were brought to safety in the Canary Islands.
Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said Thursday that one of its planes had spotted a “precarious” boat drifting some 120 km (74 miles) south of the island of Gran Canaria on Wednesday afternoon.
Three survivors were immediately evacuated by helicopter to a hospital on the island. The remaining 41 migrants were brought to safety by boat and disembarked early Thursday in the port of Arguineguín, where they were cared for by the Red Cross. All survivors were men, some underage, and came from Mali or Senegal, said José Antonio Rodríguez Verona, a spokesperson for the Red Cross in the Canaries.
In a phone interview with The Associated Press, Rodríguez Verona said survivors were disoriented and dehydrated, with many collapsing or vomiting upon reaching land. While it was difficult to get precise information given their fragile state of health, migrants reported leaving Gambia and being stranded at sea for “many, many days.” Some estimated they had been at sea for nearly a month. Running out of provisions, they fell ill from drinking seawater.
Survivors also told the Red Cross that more than 100 people were originally on board, including women and a baby. As people died on the journey, their bodies were tossed in the ocean until they had no more strength to do so.
In an emailed statement, Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said that it was not able to retrieve the remains of the five dead found inside the boat due to strong winds and waves that were 2.5 metres (8 feet) high.
Separately, Helena Maleno, founder of the migrant rights group Walking Borders, which monitors deaths and disappearances on migration routes to Spain, reported that 83 people had died on the voyage, including three women and a baby. In a post on X, Maleno said the boat had departed Gambia 27 days ago.
Maleno and her NGO are frequently contacted by relatives of missing migrants and often relay calls for help and rescue to Spanish authorities. The AP reached out to Maleno and Walking Borders seeking further details but has not yet received a response.
The West African Atlantic route to Spain’s Canary Islands is one of the deadliest crossings to Europe. While arrivals to the Spanish archipelago have fallen significantly in the past year, tens of thousands of people have died or gone missing in recent years, with several migrant boats getting lost and drifting all the way across the Atlantic to the Americas.

Kathmandu, Sep 04: Around 600 children remain unaccounted for in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts after the devastating flash floods, as the death toll rose to 1,282 on Friday with more than 4,700 missing.
The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, leaving a trail of destruction.
So far, 359 bodies have been recovered in Chitwan, 218 in Nawalparasi East, 208 in Nawalparasi West, 185 in Nuwakot, 72 in Gorkha, 60 in Dhading, 140 in Rasuwa and 38 in Tanahu, according to Nepal Police.
With two people dying while undergoing treatment in two hospitals in Kathmandu, the death toll has reached 1,282.
The joint command of security forces is searching for 4,798 people missing from different areas.
An estimated 280 children are missing in Rasuwa, and between 300 and 350 others remain unaccounted for in the neighbouring Nuwakot in central Nepal, the Kathmandu Post newspaper reported, citing figures compiled by local Education Development and Coordination Units (EDCUs), local governments, and educational institutions.
Surya Bahadur Khatri, head of the Nuwakot Education Development and Coordination Unit, said, “We are actively liaising with headmasters to collect verified data on missing students, though school heads are struggling to provide exact figures due to broken communications.”
“Although a few missing students have been located, new reports of unaccounted-for children continue to arrive from various schools. We estimate that at least 300 pupils are missing in our district.”
In Bidur Municipality of Nuwakot alone, roughly 250 children are missing since the floods hit, according to Navaraj Sapkota, school inspector of the municipality's education unit.
“The situation on the ground is deeply distressing. In some cases, we have located surviving parents who cannot find their children, while in other instances, surviving students are searching for missing parents,” said Sapkota.
Bidur houses 170 educational institutions—142 community schools and 28 private schools.
In Rasuwa, Durga Prasad Silwal, chief of the local education unit, said that official verification is ongoing but preliminary records indicate that 280 students are currently missing across the district.
The disaster has also taken a toll on teachers and school staff. Education units confirmed that 22 teachers and school staff members remain missing across both districts.
Additionally, several teachers from Dhading and Gorkha who had travelled to Rasuwa for pilgrimage were caught in the deluge and remain missing.
Rasuwa reported 16 missing teachers—15 from community schools and one from a private institution—while Nuwakot confirmed six missing teachers, according to Kathmandu Post.
Although several bodies of victims have been recovered in downstream districts, authorities have yet to verify the exact number of identified students or teachers.
According to the Ministry of Education data, the floods affected 22 schools across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, with 12 institutions completely destroyed, the report said.

The Madras High Court has directed the Tamil Nadu Director General of Police to clarify whether the CCTV footage of cameras installed inside police stations is being retained for a period of 18 months, and asked why the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (V&AC) office in Coimbatore retains the footage only for 15 days.
Justice V. Lakshminarayanan wanted the DGP to submit a report in this regard by September 10, 2026, and underlined that retaining the footage even for a minute less than 18 months would amount to a breach of the orders passed by the Supreme Court as well as a Division Bench of the High Court.
The direction was issued after senior counsel R. Shunmugasundaram, assisted by advocate Shakeena Abdul Gafoor, brought to the notice of the court that an Additional Superintendent of Police, V&AC, Coimbatore, had admitted on affidavit that a digital video recorder (DVR) in the office retains footage only for 15 days.
The senior counsel relied upon orders passed by the Supreme Court in Paramvir Singh Saini versus Baljit Singh in 2021 and also a 2024 order of a Division Bench of the High Court to contend that the then DGPs had assured both courts to preserve CCTV footage of police stations for 18 months.
What is the case about?
The submissions were made during the hearing of a petition filed by A. Saravanakumar, Sub Inspector of Police, Civil Supplies-CID, Salem, who had been accused of demanding a bribe from a person booked for smuggling 1,250 kg of rice, meant for the Public Distribution System (PDS), in a private van.
The petitioner had sought a direction to secure and preserve the CCTV footage from inside the V&AC office in Coimbatore from September 15, 2025, to October 15, 2025, to prove that a false complaint of corruption had been lodged against him and to disprove the prosecution’s charges.
However, the V&AC reported to the court that it would not be possible to secure and provide data for the period mentioned by the petitioner as the DVR in the Coimbatore office could retain the CCTV footage only for a period of 15 days.
