It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Electric vehicle sales in Australia exceeded petrol cars for the first time last month as a transformation driven by high fuel prices and government policy encouraging clean car uptake accelerated.
More than 27,000 EVs were sold in August, a new record for a single month and representing 24.9% of new cars sold. The climate-friendly technology surpassed both petrol vehicles (nearly 26,000 sold) and diesel cars (23,600).
If plug-in hybrids were added, the proportion of new cars with a plug jumped to 36% of sales.
The rise in EVs has been helped by two factors – the war in Iran pushing up oil prices and making running a petrol car significantly more expensive, and the introduction last year of a federal vehicle emissions standard that required auto companies to cut average tailpipe emissions year-on-year. The latter has triggered a big increase in the number of models of low and zero-emission cars available at a range of prices.
Australia had previously trailed most OECD countries in EV take-up, and the technology has been the focus of political scare campaigns, including former prime minister Scott Morrison claiming in 2019 that introducing a vehicle emissions standard would “end the weekend”. They made up less than 2% of sales just four years ago and about 8% last year.
The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, said EV sales surpassing petrol cars was a “landmark moment”.
“Australians have seen through the scare campaigns and are voting with their wallets for cars that are cheaper to run, cleaner and reduce their exposure to international petrol price shocks,” he said.
Toyota was Australians’ most popular car brand in August, followed by Chinese EV manufacturer BYD and trillionaire Elon Musk’s Tesla. Five of the top 10 brands were Chinese: BYD, GWM, MG, Geely and Cheery. The Tesla Model Y was the most popular new model, with more than 6,400 sold.
The Electric Vehicle Council said there had been a “structural shift in the way Australians choose their cars”, with both economic and environmental benefits driving the change.
The council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio, said there were now nearly 200 EV models on offer. “The priority now is to make the benefits of going electric accessible to more Australians, including people in regional communities, apartment residents and the 30% of Australians who rent their home,” she said.
The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries CEO, Tony Weber, said consumer choice and competition were rapidly reshaping the new-vehicle market and infrastructure settings needed to keep pace.
“Accessible and dependable charging will remain critical to consumer confidence, particularly on highways, in rural and regional areas and for motorists without access to charging at home,” he said.

After turning profitable in the fiscal year FY25, furniture rental startup Furlenco saw its net profit for the fiscal year FY26 skyrocket to ₹59.5 Cr. This is a near 20X jump from the ₹3.1 Cr profit it recorded in FY25. The Bengaluru-based startup’s operating revenue surged 61.9% YoY to ₹370.4 Cr in FY26 from ₹228.7 Cr in the previous year. To note, its top line has now grown around 2.6X in the previous two fiscals, from ₹140 Cr in FY24. Including other income of ₹5 Cr, the Sheela Foam-backed startup’s total income rose 56.4% to ₹375.4 Cr in the year under review. Renting of furniture and office equipment remained the key revenue driver of the startup, accounting for 92% or ₹341.1 Cr of its total operating revenue. While rental income jumped 64% YoY, revenue from furniture sales rose 38% YoY to ₹29.4 Cr. EBITDA nearly doubled to ₹129.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹66.4 Cr in FY25, while its EBITDA margin expanded to 35.01% from around 29% a year earlier. Founded in 2012, Furlenco runs a subscription-driven furniture and appliance rental platform that offers more than 300 SKUs across 28 cities, including Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Chennai, and Kolkata. The startup also sells new furniture. During the fiscal, the startup had raised ₹125 Cr to strengthen its presence in existing markets and enter new markets in the country, invest in product innovation, technology and customer experience. Overall, it has raised a total funding of more than $ 290 Mn to date, including the latest funding round, from investors like Lightbox Ventures, Crescent Ventures, Sheela Foam, Whiteoak and Madhu Kela, among others. Furlenco’s FY26 Expenses Total expenditure increased 45.1% YoY to ₹343.9 Cr in FY26, from ₹236.9 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Other expenses, which include investments in power and fuel, rent, insurance, transportation costs, accounted for 52.7% of total expenditure. Here’s a brief breakdown of Furlenco’s top spends for the year: Employee Benefit Expenses: Including employees’ salaries, wages, gratuity, provident fund and others, costs under this head rose 17.7% to ₹36.2 Cr, from ₹30.7 in the previous year. Depreciation & Amortisation Expenses: Spending under this head stood at ₹70.3 Cr, up 57.5% compared to ₹44.6 Cr in FY25. Finance Costs: The company spent ₹32.7 Cr in the year under review towards finance costs, marking a 75.5% increase from ₹18.6 Cr in the previous year.

Ethiopia submits official bid to host Afcon 2028
- Published
Ethiopia has submitted an official bid to host the 2028 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
The country's football federation (EFF) says its government-backed proposal affirms "the nation's full readiness to host Africa's biggest footballing event".
Ethiopia has staged Afcon three times, in 1962, 1968 and 1976, but its footballing infrastructure lags well behind others on the continent.
The nation had just one stadium approved for use by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) last season but is in the process of inaugurating a new international stadium and sports complex in Addis Ababa.
That venue in the capital could provide one location for the tournament, but whether Ethiopia has enough compliant venues to host a 24-team Afcon across multiple locations remains a major question.
A number of existing regional facilities are understood not to meet Fifa or Caf standards in terms of infrastructure, facilities and overall match-day requirements.
Ethiopia played its home qualifiers for the 2026 Fifa World Cup at neutral venues in Morocco and Rwanda but did host matches in Dire Dawa earlier this year.
Last month, Caf president Patrice Motsepe said his organisation had received "exciting bids" for the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Afcons - with the tournament set to move to a four-year cycle after 2028.
Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe announced a joint Southern African bid for the 2028 finals earlier this year.
Despite reports that Morocco - hosts of the 2025 edition - could stage the tournament again in two years' time, BBC Sport Africa understands the kingdom is not in the running and instead is focusing on preparations to co-host the 2030 Fifa World Cup.
Meanwhile, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger - three countries led by military governments - have expressed interest in co-hosting in 2032.
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to take place in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year, with the competition returning to East Africa for the first time since it was held in Ethiopia in 1976.
Ethiopia won the Afcon title on home soil in 1962 but the Walia Ibex, ranked 143rd in the world and 43rd in Africa, have only qualified for the tournament three times since they last hosted.
Their most recent appearance came at the 2021 edition, when they finished bottom without a win in a group containing Cameroon, Burkina Faso and Cape Verde.
Ethiopia beat Sao Tome and Principe in the preliminary round of qualifiers for next year's Afcon and have been drawn alongside Senegal, Mozambique and Sudan in Group J.
- Is holding Afcon every four years 'totally wrong' or 'good call'? 
  - Published22 January
Infrastructure and security concerns
Analysis by Kaleb Moges, BBC Africa
The EFF's announcement that it wants to host Afcon has generated mixed reactions, with critics questioning whether the country is truly prepared to host a tournament of this scale.
Ethiopia was one of just three nations to play at the first Afcon in 1957, but the 52,000-seat Bahir Dar Stadium in the north of the country is currently the only facility it posseses which is approved by Caf.
Meanwhile, the 62,000-capacity Adey Abeba International Stadium in Addis Ababa is expected to be completed next year.
Three other proposed stadiums are at much earlier stages of development and would need significant work to meet Caf's requirements in time for 2028.
However, hosting Afcon would require more than upgrading or constructing stadiums. The country would also need adequate training facilities, gyms, accommodation and entertainment venues, as well as reliable urban transport and security infrastructure.
Security is a major concern for Ethiopia's bid. Although the capital city is comparatively safe, several parts of the country continue to experience armed conflict, political unrest and other security challenges.
Addressing these concerns, alongside the infrastructure requirements, would be critical if Ethiopia is to successfully host Afcon 2028.

Tears and tricolours - inside Irish icon Taylor's final fight week
- Published
Katie Taylor smiles as she sits down for her fight-week media commitments, but her eyes give her away.
On Saturday, she faces unbeaten Frenchwoman Flora Pili at Croke Park, bringing down the curtain on a career that has gone from disguising herself as a boy in a sport that barred women, to Olympic gold and undisputed titles.
The weight of a lifetime in the ring is catching up with an Irish icon preparing to step away.
"I thought I was handling all the emotions until today," the 40-year-old tells BBC Sport.
Taylor's usual defensive armour is slipping as the reality of a Croke Park farewell sets in. There is no next opponent waiting in the shadows, only 80,000 roaring voices, a sea of green, white and orange tricolours and the final chapter of a transcendent career.
"This is the stuff of dreams and I'm pinching myself that it's happening," Taylor adds.
"I look back at my career and think how remarkable it has been. The highs, the lows, the failures, the disappointments and the successes."
Tears and laughter as Taylor shows a new side
Taylor has never hidden her disdain for the circus of fight-week theatre, preferring the sanctuary of the gym.
But this week she has welled up under the glare of the cameras and stayed a fraction longer during face-offs to absorb the magnitude of the moment.
"Every fighter in the world wishes they were in this position," she says.
"I'm just blown away from the support from this country. I don't think there are many other countries where 80,000 show up for a female athlete.
"The crowd - hearing 'ole ole ole' one last time - feeling the atmosphere, seeing the tricolours all over the place..."
The emotion has rippled through her inner circle. Eddie Hearn choked up mid-sentence during the final news conference when it dawned on him this was the last time he would experience a Taylor fight week.
"When it's all said and done you will look at your belts, you might look at your bank balance. But you will sit there, close your eyes and recall all those incredible moments in your life that made you cry," he later told BBC Sport.
"I will cry on the ring walk. I will cry in the [post-fight] interview."
Taylor is softly spoken and laser-focused, but this week has unlocked a relaxed side of her rarely seen by the public. She joked during final media commitments about flipping the table just to disrupt the monotony.
"Katie Taylor is one of the funniest people I've met. Unexpectedly funny. She's so strong and determined. But people who know, she's very jovial, she's got great energy and I think she's soaking all that up," Hearn adds.

From taxi drivers gridlocked in traffic to those pulling pints in Temple Bar, everyone across the capital is frantically seeking spare tickets.
But even with Taylor's popularity, selling out Croke Park is no easy feat. While she has a reputation for being fiercely zoned into her training rather than chasing the spotlight, she has put work into the promotion. And perhaps even enjoyed it.
Peters spearheaded an exhausting, 1,500-mile island-wide bus tour spanning all 32 counties, completing dozens of radio chats and community stops to promote the swansong.

"No-one works as hard as Katie," Peters says. "Those four days she did not stop working. These stadiums don't sell out on their own."
When thousands mobbed the gates at a Kilkenny stop on an unforgiving timetable, Taylor refused to turn a blind eye. "Ah Brian, we can't drive past them," Peters recalls Taylor insisting, pulling the vehicle over to take group photos.
That effort has helped turn Saturday into something bigger than a boxing event. About 80% of those inside Croke Park will be attending a live fight for the first time, while 65% of tickets were sold outside Dublin.
With the bout also being shown on free-to-air TV across Ireland, Taylor's farewell - which will include music from one of the nation's biggest pop groups, Westlife - has become a national celebration.

The undefeated challenger arrives with a 12-0 record and a hunger to create her own story.
"I have nothing to lose and everything to win," Pili, 29, said.
But with fight-week media commitments cleverly packed into the start of the week, Taylor has been given the space to get the tears and emotion out of her system.

Asked how she will feel when the dust settles on Sunday morning, Taylor says: "Probably a bit relieved - I don't have to take any more punches again."

Much has been said about Hong Kong’s vitality as a higher education hub. Yet, a radical rethink of our primary and secondary school system is equally necessary.

Eleven people sentenced to death in Vietnam drug trafficking case
- Published
Eleven people have been sentenced to death by a court in Vietnam in one of the country's largest drug trafficking cases, state media report.
They are among 227 people accused in total, with prison sentences ranging from 18 months to life behind bars.
Among those sentenced to death was the person purported to be the mastermind behind the drug trafficking network, Ha Danh Nam, who investigators said arranged for the drugs to be brought from France to Vietnam.
The case began in March 2023 when four Vietnam Airlines flight attendants - arriving in Ho Chi Minh City from Paris - were caught carrying more than 10kg of drugs in 157 toothpaste tubes.
Legal affairs newspaper Bao Cong Ly reported that authorities found the flight attendants - who were not prosecuted - had unknowingly transported the drugs, which included MDMA and ketamine.
Nam was found to have hidden the drugs inside consumer goods - including dietary supplements, laundry detergent, mouthwash and coffee - and then arranged for people in France to carry them in their luggage or transported via delivery service to Vietnam.
Nam targeted Vietnamese nationals living or studying in France to act as drug mules, local media report.
Prosecutors said those involved in this transnational drug trafficking network used encrypted messaging platforms and bank accounts registered under other people's names to facilitate their smuggling efforts.
Transactions linked to the network were worth nearly 29 trillion Vietnamese dong ($1.1bn; £815m), they said.
The court found the defendants played varying roles in the network - from leaders to accomplices - and penalties were imposed according to the seriousness of their involvement.
Around 20 others on trial were sentenced to life imprisonment for the illegal buying, selling, transporting and organising of drugs.
Vietnam is one of 54 countries that still have the death penalty, rights groups say.
The government does not publish how many people are on death row as that is considered a state secret, though human rights groups say there are more than 1,000 awaiting execution.
Last month, the Vietnamese government proposed abolishing the death penalty for six offences including drug trafficking. These proposed changes are yet to take effect.
The proposal follows changes to the criminal code in 2025 that removed the death penalty for eight offences - including embezzlement, espionage and overthrowing the government.
One of the most high-profile figures to be handed the death penalty was tycoon Truong My Lan, who was found guilty of embezzlement and sentenced to death in 2024.
The 2025 change in the law led to her death penalty being commuted to life imprisonment.

Steve Irwin's family celebrates 'superhero' dad, 20 years after shock death

Australian conservationist Bindi Irwin has marked the 20th anniversary of her famous father's death with a touching tribute to the man best known as the "Crocodile Hunter".
Steve Irwin died on 4 September 2006, aged 44, after a stingray fatally pierced his chest while he was underwater filming a documentary at the Great Barrier Reef.
Bindi, who was eight when her father died, called Steve a "superhero" in an online post on Friday, saying she has "watched the world mourn my dad with our family" for the past two decades.
"I always thought that my dad's legacy is wildlife conservation; it turns out, his legacy is love. For our planet and for each other," Bindi, 28, wrote on Instagram.
She described the impact of her father's death on her mother Terri and her younger brother Robert, 22.
"My mum lost the love of her life; my brother and I lost the greatest dad," she wrote. "Grief never truly leaves us; we walk alongside it every day."
Bindi also shared details on how her daughter connects with the grandfather she never got to meet.
"I have a 5-year-old daughter who watches his documentaries every morning. She feels utterly loved by her 'grandpa crocodile' without ever having met him."
Since Steve's death, the Irwins have continued to run Australia Zoo in Queensland.
"My dad left a lasting impact so poignant that it will ripple out for generations to come," Bindi wrote, saying his life and legacy were "worth celebrating".
She thanked Steve for being the family's "guardian angel" and signed off her message saying she loved him "with my whole heart".
Steve's wife Terri also took to social media to mark the day, posting an interview where the khaki-clad wildlife advocate recounted Bindi's birth and its impact on him.
"The most incredible wildlife encounter of my life was the birth of my daughter, Bindi," Steve says in the interview, with his signature enthusiasm.
The first time he held his newborn child, the inspiration for her name hit him.
"I was flabbergasted and it was then that her name evolved. I've gone, 'Bindi!' after my favourite crocodile, Bindi," he said, with a wide grin.
Robert Irwin also posted a tribute to his father, with a photo of Steve holding him when he was a baby, alongside the caption, "Your legacy is forever".
Last November, Robert was crowned the winner of US dance competition Dancing with the Stars, a decade after his sister won the same title.

The Apple Vision Pro was used for a successful hip surgery
Stryker says its SportSuite Vision software for the headset received De Novo authorization from the FDA in July.
Medical technology company Stryker announced this week that its Apple Vision Pro app has been used in a milestone surgery. Its SportSuite Vision app for the headset was part of a hip arthroscopy at Duke Health, marking the first time the software has been put into a real world practice. Stryker said it received De Novo authorization from the FDA for the software on July 17.
Since Apple first introduced its mixed-reality headset, we've had questions about who the device is intended for. The debut model was never going to reach a mainstream consumer audience, and neither was the beefier M5 version that we tried last year. But it has always seemed like the Vision Pro was pointing toward a very interesting hypothetical future and was just waiting for the right situation to come along.
A complex surgery is a good example of what that right situation could be. The mixed reality experience means that a medical professional can interact with the real world and a real patient while also easily seeing content or tools in the digital space. In the case of this inaugural SportSuite Vision operation, it gave the surgeon access to Stryker's orthopedic surgery planning tools, arthroscopic images and CT imaging while performing a hip arthroscopy.
"Using spatial computing enabled me to customize the placement of key clinical information to fit my workflow and access it within the sterile field," said Dr. Chad Mather III, the orthopedic surgeon at Duke Health who conducted the procedure with the Apple Vision Pro. "This helped create a more comfortable, streamlined OR setup while keeping the information I needed in view."
Considering the cost of the headset and the challenges of developing software for it, don't expect to see your primary care physician wearing one at your physical any time soon. It also doesn't bode well for the mainstream adoption of the device that Apple may have laid off quite a significant portion of its Vision Pro team last month. But as far as useful scenarios of mixed reality headsets go, this is the sort of creative application that could see the Vision Pro eventually reach its full potential.

Several videos have gone viral on social media following the devastating flash floods in Nepal on August 26, 2026. Some users shared a video claiming that after the disaster, the world’s largest Shaligram, said to be more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath.
In this context, Zee News put out a report with a screenshot from the viral video and, along with the hashtags #Nepal, #Flood and #Shaligram, wrote: “Viral Video: Floods have revealed a secret, a 170-million-year-old Shaligram has been found.”
Shaligrams are naturally formed stones traditionally found in Nepal’s Kali Gandaki River, and revered by Hindus as representations of the deity, Vishnu.
Right-wing X user Amitabh Choudhary (@MithilaWaaala), who has been found spreading misinformation and comminal propaganda several times in the past, shared a video and wrote: “Stone older than dinosaurs. Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal.”
Kisi ne sahi hi kaha hai, “शुरुआत भी वही, सफ़र भी वही, और अंत भी वही।”
Stone older than dinosaurs !!
Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal 🇳🇵 pic.twitter.com/GIv851LJbV
— Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala) August 29, 2026
X user Shashank Shekhar Jha, who claims to be a Supreme Court lawyer, and others such as @Nalanda_index, @CodexZeroTR, @Krishnavallabhi, @bhaktSenapati, along with several Facebook and Instagram users, too, shared videos and photos with similar claims.
Fact Check
To find out the truth behind the viral claim, we performed a relevant keyword search. This led us to reports published on June 30, 2026, by Himalaya Times and Online Khabar featuring images of the giant sculpture seen in the viral video.
The reports stated that a 22-foot-tall Shaligram sculpture in Nepal’s Mustang district was gradually becoming a centre of religious faith. According to the reports, sculptors from the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts carved a huge rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom in Gharpajhong rural municipality area and created the 22-foot-tall Shaligram replica between April 20 and May 4, 2026.
During our investigation, we found a report by a website called Desh Sanchar. According to the report, the 22-foot-tall sculpture had been unveiled on the evening of May 28, 2026, after religious rituals on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River.
We also located a video uploaded on April 23, 2026 on the Facebook page, Nepal Raibar, in which artists could be seen carving a rock to create a Shaligram statue.
We also geolocated the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video. It’s located on the Kali Gandaki River, opposite ‘Thakkhola Lodge & Jimihendrix Restaurant in Jomsom. When we compared Google Street View images from 2025 with the viral video, we found that the 2025 image only showed a large rock.
This makes it clear that the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video is not a natural or ancient stone. Rather, it is a statue created by carving a rock.
We also tried to look for the sources of all the variants of the now-viral visuals. We found the original version of the video and the screenshots shared by Zee News on the Instagram account of a user named Durga Prasad Poudel. It was posted on June 2, 2026.
View this post on Instagram
Similarly, we found the second viral video uploaded on June 30, 2026, on the Instagram account of a user named Rijan Dongol.
View this post on Instagram
The third viral video was shared on June 8, 2026, on the Facebook account of a user named Arjun Singh. Its caption reads: “A huge 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue is located on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom, Mustang. This monumental work, inaugurated by Jagadguru Shankaracharya Mahaswami Vidushekara Bharati, attracts a large number of pilgrims and stands as a major spiritual and cultural site in Nepal.”
Thus, all three viral videos featuring the Shaligram statue have been available on social media since June 2026. They have absolutely no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal in August.
Overall, the claim by Zee News and other users that after the recent disaster in Nepal, the world’s largest Shaligram, more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath is completely misleading. In reality, the 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue seen in the viral video was created by carving a rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Mustang district, during April–May 2026. The videos of the Shaligram statue circulating on social media are also from June 2026 and have no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal.

A devastating flash flood on Wednesday, August 26, near the Nepal-Tibet border, resulted in massive destruction in several districts of Nepal, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, with over 700 dead and over 2,500 people still missing. Reportedly, a glacial landslide of ice and rock caused the flash floods, which destroyed homes roads, bridges and power plants.
In the days following the catastrophe, social media was rife with video clips showing the extent of devastation — from gigantic waves of floodwater gushing through entire villages, to buildings collapsing, and people being swept away under the debris.
However, Alt News found that a large number of these videos circulating on social media were not authentic. Several of these videos were not from Nepal at all, but drawn from various other calamities which occurred across the world in the last few years.
Clip From 2025 Uttarakhand Floods
An X user, Said Ercan (@saidercan), posted a compilation clip on August 27 showing the havoc wreaked by large flood waves. The first clip shows a torrential river flowing through a mountainous area, and eventually sweeping through the houses on the banks, destroying them in an instant. The post has garnered over 5.8 million views and been reshared over 5,000 times at the time of publishing. (Archive)
To verify whether the video is of the Nepal floods, we broke it down into keyframes and ran a reverse image search. This led us to an Instagram post uploaded by The Times of India, on August 5, 2025, featuring the same footage.
View this post on Instagram
The caption states that the footage is of the Uttarakhand cloudburst havoc. “At least four people have died and many are feared missing after a devastating flash flood triggered by a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga river caused large-scale destruction in Dharali village in Uttarkashi district…,” read the caption.
A Dainik Bhaskar report also features the same video to show the scale of damage caused by the cloudburst in Uttarkashi. We ran relevant keyword searches, and found news reports from sources like Reuters, BBC, Al Jazeera, The Hindu, and others, that corroborated this finding. Thus, the video footage shared by the X user is actually of the 2025 Uttarakhand flash floods, and not of the recent Nepal havoc.
AI-generated Clip
In another instance, X user Ayesha Khan (@Ayesha0Khaan) posted a video clip, of huge waves sweeping away cars, building structures, and people. The clip received over 1 million views. (Archive)
X user Ravi Shankar Singh (@Ravishanka34381) also posted the clip with the same claim. However, we noticed some discrepancies in the video — for instance, around the 0:05 timestamp, a tree log appears out of nowhere in the debris flowing through the floodwater, indicating that the clip could be AI-generated.
We ran the video through Hive’s AI detection tool, which confirmed our suspicion, showing a 99.9% possibility of the video containing AI-generated content.
Clip From 2024 China Incident
News outlet Medya Post (@medya_post) uploaded a clip on X, which showed around 15 people getting swept away by powerful flood waves. The caption stated: “Tourists who wanted to take videos and photos during the flood disaster that occurred in Nepal were swept away by the current and disappeared.” The post had seen massive traction on social media, with over 1.5 million views. (Archive)
Two other X users with the handles (@JMNewsNetwork_) and (@redpillmd) had uploaded the same video, with the former having deleted it after it had been viewed over 45,000 times.
To verify the clip’s authencity, we ran a reverse image search, which led us to an X post, originally uploaded by an user with the handle (@Arab_Storms) on September 8, 2024.
التصوير اصبح اهم من الحياة #شاهد ❗️#الصين جرف المد القوي لنهر تشيانتانج العديد من الزوار الذين كانوا يحاولون التقاط صورة ،،،#Yagi pic.twitter.com/bdiEj7fk9b
— طقس_العالم ⚡️ (@Arab_Storms) September 8, 2024
According to the caption, the video had been taken in China, showing the powerful waves of the Qiantang River overpowering tourists on the shore who were clicking photos. The incident, which occured in the days following Asia’s most powerful storm in 2024, the Super Typhoon Yagi, had also been reported on by The Indian Express, and Newsflare.
Video From West Bengal Landslide
A news outlet TNT Media (@TNT_Media1) posted a clip which showed a mudslide from a vantage point. It also features the narrow escape of some vehicles and people gathered at the spot. The caption, written in Arabic, claims that horrifying scenes correspond to the recent Nepal flash floods. (Archive)
مشاهد مروعة من نيبال.. 😯😯 pic.twitter.com/N7f5jBl4i6
— 𝐓𝐍𝐓 (@TNT_Media1) August 26, 2026
We noticed that the car, visible in parts of the video, bears a number plate whose state code (WB) corresponds with that of West Bengal. Moreover, the recorder of the video, while shooting the clip, speaks in Bengali to warn people to get away from the waves.
A reverse image search on several keyframes of the video led us to this X post, uploaded by The Daily Jagran on August 17.
A biker had a narrow escape after a massive landslide struck the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district. Huge rocks, soil and debris suddenly came crashing onto the road as vehicles passed through.#Kalimpong #Landslide #WestBengal #Biker #ViralVideo #Monsoon pic.twitter.com/HgFLY7Dhjy
— The Daily Jagran (@TheDailyJagran) August 17, 2026
The caption states that the video shows a landslide in the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district, thereby proving that this video clip is not related to the Nepal flash floods.
Compilation Clip From Various Calamities
An X user named “Leonard Sardua $TOR” (@lsardua) posted a compilation of clips showing structures collapsing under the deluge, claiming they showed the devastation caused by the flash flood in Nepal. The clip garnered over 3.3 million views and 3,700 reshares. (Archive)
Two more users, “HadY Azmy” (@HadYAzmy1) and Ahmad Ansari (@Ahmadansari2233), amplified the same clip on August 27. The former video, which has now been deleted, had garnered over than 2.5 million views and over 3,000 reshares.
On running a reverse image search on one keyframe from the viral clip, we were led to an article published by The Times of India on July 21. The report shows the same building structure collapse under the force of floodwater, and states that the video was from the Budgam district of Jammu and Kashmir.
Another segment of the compilation shows a red building being engulfed by the gushing floodwater, sweeping away cars and other structures amid the debris.
Running a reverse image search on this keyframe, we found that the clip could be traced back to a mudslide in Japan’s Atami city from July 2021. An X user with the handle @d_t_dcg_sdh had uploaded several clips showing the mudslide sweeping away houses and vehicles. We also found news reports from Al Jazeera and Spanish news outlet La Nacion, corroborating that the clip was recorded during a mudslide in Japan in 2021.
The same compilation video also included a segment which showed a bridge being torn down by the raging floodwater.
This, we found, was in fact from an incident in Indonesia, showing the collapse of the wooden Molintogupo Bridge, owing to the overflowing of the Bone River. A video uploaded by Newsflare on Dailymotion, notes that the incident occurred on June 11, 2020. It was also reported on by VGTV.
Another segment of the same clip shows two men watching a bridge being dismantled and swept away by floodwater.
We found that this video was from Argentina. A reverse image search on a keyframe led us to this X post by AccuWeather on December 25, 2023, which shows a bridge in Argentina’s Catamarca being blown away by the turbulent floodwater.
A bridge was swept away in Catamarca, Argentina, on Christmas Day, leaving a city completely isolated.  pic.twitter.com/hVdwxmQ7QU
— AccuWeather (@accuweather) December 27, 2023
Another video, showing a white car being dragged along by the torrential flow of mud water, was also part of this compilation.
This, Alt News found, was originally from Islamabad, in Pakistan, dating back to a devastating flood that took place in July 2025.
Similarly, a segment showing a woman overlooking a building structure being swept away by flood water, was also part of this compilation, alleging that it was from Nepal.
A reverse image search proved that the image has existed on X since at least September 2024. On further investigation, we found that it showed the damage caused by Hurricane Helene in North Carolina, United States.
Don’t worry guys, weather modification isn’t real! It’s just a coincidence that Hurricane Helene is one of the most devastating “inland damage storms” in history and that hundreds of pro-Trump counties are being massively impacted during the most important election of our… pic.twitter.com/lyi8YZXB8A
— Matt Wallace (@MattWallace888) September 28, 2024
Another clip showing a submerged bus making its way through the floodwater was also featured in the compilation.
We found that this video was shot during a downpour in Pakistan’s Karachi, which left the city flooded and resulted in at least 16 deaths. Pakistani news media outlet 24 News HD, in their report on the flood dated March 19, used the same clip of the submerged bus.
Thus, the compilation clip uploaded by users “Leonard Sardua $TOR”, “HadY Azmy”, and Ahmad Ansari, with the claim that the footage depicts the havoc in Nepal is fake and misleading. The entire compilation stitches together footage from real calamities, occuring in various other parts of the world in the past few years, to wrongly claim that they are visuals from the Nepal flash floods on August 26.

“This circular is to notify all the Member Associations (MA) and stakeholders of the AIFF that a National Ban on the registration of new players has been imposed on the Club Churchill Brothers FC Goa, a club registered with the Goa Football Association,” the AIFF said in a letter dated September 2.
“Imposition of the ban will be effective immediately in accordance with the correspondence received from FIFA’s Head of Disciplinary dated 01 September 2026. ISRO's GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05 earth observation spacecraft takes off from Sriharikota
ISRO launched GSLV-17 carrying Earth-observation satellite EOS-05 from Andhra Pradesh at 2:55am IST, marking its second major launch attempt of 2026.
CHENNAI: A GSLV-F17 rocket carrying Earth observation satellite EOS-05 lifted-off from Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, Indian Space Research Organisation on Friday said.
After the conclusion of the 27.5 hour countdown, the 51.7 metre tall rocket, lifted off thunderously emanating bright orange colour fumes on its tail from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota at a pre-fixed time of 2.55 am at the spaceport, located about 135 km east of Chennai.
Also read: Isro returns to the launch pad: The satellite lost in 2021, and the second attempt at it
The satellite is expected to be placed in the sub-geosynchronous orbit by the GSLV rocket after a flight journey of 18 minutes,, which is dubbed to be 'eye in the sky' for its ability to monitor the Earth from an altitude of about 36,000 km.
The GSLV which has a lift off mass of 420.5 tonnes is a three-stage vehicle with a cryogenic upper stage.
"GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05 lifts off from Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota", ISRO said in a notification on Friday.
Today's mission is the follow-up to the GSLV-F10/Earth Observation Satellite-03 which was 'unsuccessful' as it suffered a cryogenic upper stage ignition failure after lift-off on August 12, 2021 at 5.43 am from Sriharikota.
Also read: ISRO begins countdown for GSLV-F17 launch with Earth observation satellite
The mission objective is to provide real-time imaging of large-area regions at frequent intervals for quick monitoring of natural disasters and episodic events, and to obtain spectral signatures for agriculture, forestry and waterbodies, ISRO said.
The Earth Observation Satellite would also share information for disaster warning, cyclone monitoring, cloudburst and thunderstorm monitoring, ISRO said.
Today's launch is also after a break of almost 8 months by Bengaluru-headquartered space agency.

Ferrari upgrade a step but not all we need - Hamilton
- Published
Lewis Hamilton says an upgraded Ferrari engine for this weekend's Italian Grand Prix is a "step forward but not the whole amount we need".
Ferrari are taking the opportunity of their home grand prix to introduce the second of the two upgrades they are permitted this year in the hope it will improve their chances of a win on the historic Monza track.
Ferrari have the fastest car in the corners on balance, but have been lagging on the straights so far this year.
"Every little helps. Until this point of the year, even last race, we were losing 0.4secs a lap (on the straights). We have carried that deficit," Hamilton said.
"This is a step forward. It is not the whole amount we need but we knew that was the case. I strongly believe we have what it takes to win."

Hamilton and team-mate Charles Leclerc have both won one race this season, with the Briton 59 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes.
"To win this weekend, the whole collective has to come together. Everything has to flow from the beginning," said Hamilton.
"There is a first ahead of me, in the sense of if I was to win I go into new territory winning for the first time in Ferrari at Monza. It would be phenomenal.
"The pressure's high. You want to do it for the team. Many of them will come to this race. The tifosi come out in huge numbers with a passion that's unmatched.
"And my mum's here. I don't think she's been to Monza, and certainly not (while I was) with Ferrari. I wanted her to experience this and bring any lucky dust she can bring."
Ferrari's hopes of a home victory are boosted by the fact that Italian Antonelli will have a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted number of engine parts and is likely to start at the back.
Hamilton said: "There is big gap between the top teams and the rest. Kimi will start from the back but with the power he has, and the performance he has, he should slide through that pack pretty easy and it's probably why they chose this race to do that.
"So achieving eighth or sixth should be relatively easy. We have to focus on maximising our weekend and try and take the energy from the tifosi to hopefully push us to the front."
Antonelli's grid penalty was inevitable at some point after reliability problems earlier in the year meant they would need to exceed his allowance of four engines for the season.
They chose this weekend because they calculated it was the most optimal race to do it, both in terms of the effect of a new engine on a track dominated by straights, and managing their engine pool through the rest of the year.
Team-mate George Russell will also have an engine penalty, most likely in Azerbaijan in two races' time.
Antonelli said: "I am very much looking forward to this weekend despite starting from the back. I will be able to enjoy it more than I did previously and hopefully we will still be able to have a good race.
"In some ways it helps to release pressure, although I would very much rather fight for pole and start at the front.
"It makes me a bit more relaxed going into the weekend. I think this track can be very good for us but we have to take into account that McLaren, Ferrari, even Red Bull can be good this weekend."
Hamilton arrived at Monza for media day on Thursday in his new Ferrari F40, an iconic 1980s supercar, which he described as "a dream car of mine".
He explained why the particular model he chose was so important to him, and a surprise resonance he discovered to his race number, which is 44.
The seven-time champion said: "I have been looking for one for a while. I wanted one with low mileage and a story behind it. Lots have come up at auction but not particularly special. Or the paint's been redone. I wanted to find the most authentic one.
"I found this one that a guy bought it and drove it 69km from Maranello to his home and parked it and never drove it again.
"Then the decision is, 'Do you keep it as an art piece, all dusty, or clean it up?' That took a while to decide.
"I might be wrong but none of the Ferrari drivers in history have ever arrived in the coolest car in history.
"When they were taking the car apart... it has 44 stamped on the engine. I couldn't believe it. So it feels very much fate."
He chose to drive it to the track, he said, "because I thought it was an opportunity to highlight the history of Ferrari in their own country and their race."

Having more than 150 non-human primates at a research center fall ill with diarrhea in a stomach-churning outbreak that flowed for over two years doesn’t sound much like good fortune. But for some scientists, it kind of was, providing a heaping pile of valuable data on how they might finally defeat a foul foe.
In a study published in the latest issue of Science Translational Medicine, scientist sifted through the dump of immunological data from the infections, logging new ways to train immune cells to defeat the bacteria behind the outbreak, a type of Shigella. Researchers were able to pluck out specific bits of the bacteria that the immune system could most effectively attack, linking specific target molecules to specific types of germ-busting immune responses. The researchers even precisely homed in on some of the tiny notches within those craggy target molecules where the most potent antibodies attached.
In all, the study “revealed unexpected features of the anti-Shigella antibody response in naturally infected [non-human primates] and represents a step toward the rational design of Shigella vaccine candidates,” the authors write.
Shigella is a gastrointestinal horror, striking more than 200 million people in the world each year and killing more than 200,000, mostly children. Those who survive typically develop some protective immune responses. But, given that there are various species and serotypes of Shigella, protective immune responses tend to only work against a narrow range of the bacteria’s family. And, on top of that, Shigella strains are only becoming more resistant to antibiotics.
The need for a Shigella vaccine—one that can combat the whole cruddy clan—is clear. As such, there are many vaccine development efforts underway. Still, scientists have been toiling without some of the detailed molecular and structural data needed to design a sophisticated vaccine. That’s where the outbreak came in.

A NY hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back
TROY, N.Y. — Like many residents of this aging industrial city on the Hudson River, Starletta Washington was stunned when she heard Troy's last remaining hospital planned to close its birthing center.
"It was devastating," said Washington, who heads the local YWCA. Washington was born at the hospital and had her children there. She couldn't believe families would now have to get to a hospital half an hour away or face the prospect of an emergency delivery.
"Nobody else was going to be born in the city of Troy unless they were born on a city bus, in the back of a cab, or, disgustingly, on the side of the street?" Washington said. "Blew my mind."
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Troy wasn't the first community to face this prospect. Since 2010, hospitals have closed hundreds of maternity units as cities and towns shrink and hospitals consolidate into larger systems.
Troy found a more hopeful ending.
Elected officials from both major parties joined patient advocates, mothers, midwives, doulas and community leaders like Washington to challenge Trinity Health, the large Catholic health system that owns Troy's hospital and birthing center. The campaign even united Planned Parenthood and the Catholic diocese.
"Whether you were Republican or Democrat, or if you didn't vote, it literally brought everyone together," said Carmella Mantello, the city's Republican mayor. "Everyone just said, 'We can't let this happen.'"
Throughout the country, healthcare remains a flash point as politicians square off ahead of November's elections. But in many places, Americans are also quietly finding common ground.
In this small city, citizens were brought together by frustration over large, corporate health systems that can seem to put profits over patients. And they resolved to work together to keep critical medical services in their community.
A community institution
Babies have been delivered at Samaritan Hospital on a hill above Troy since this city's once bustling factories produced most of America's shirt collars a century ago.
More recently, Samaritan's Burdett Birth Center had become a model for patient-focused care. Midwives and doulas work alongside OB-GYNs and support mothers who want to avoid a delivery by cesarean section unless necessary.
Patient safety advocates have pushed for years to reduce surgical deliveries, which can lead to complications. At Burdett, only about a quarter of newborns are delivered by C-section, compared with about a third statewide, according to 2025 hospital data. Burdett also had fewer preterm births and fewer babies with low birth weights.
"I wouldn't go anywhere else," said Lidia Zambrano-Madera, who gave birth to both her children at Burdett with the help of a midwife.
For Zambrano-Madera, who recently opened a children's play center in Troy, Burdett offered another advantage: It was just five minutes from home.
But three years ago, Trinity Health, a multibillion-dollar Michigan-based hospital system, said the birth center was losing money and would close.
Families from Troy and surrounding Rensselaer County would have to deliver at another Trinity hospital in Albany, up to a half-hour's drive away. The hospitals are branded under St. Peter's Health Partners in the Albany region.
"We've been frantic about trying not to cut the care at the bedside," said Steven Hanks, a physician who oversees Trinity hospitals in New York and New England. "But, you know, you get to a point where you can only consolidate so much. You can only spread people so thin, and then you have to start taking harder looks at your actual services."
Corporate backlash
Trinity's plans — news of which broke in a local newspaper — came without warning, surprising the obstetrical staff and community leaders. They set off a firestorm.
Within days, midwives, mothers, community leaders and politicians held a rally at the YWCA in downtown Troy. Others would follow. Volunteers led by doulas and midwives made T-shirts and handed out pink "Save Burdett" signs at the local farmers market.
Activists were outraged that the hospital hadn't adequately assessed the impact of the closure, particularly on low-income families. They conducted a community survey that found 1 in 4 Troy residents didn't have access to a car and would have trouble getting to Albany.
The campaign drew on deep connections that many residents had to Burdett. "They realized what a gem Burdett is, and what a great community service they provide," said Jessica Hayek, a doula and birth educator who helped lead the campaign.
Hayek and others also tapped into deep-seated frustration with Trinity, a healthcare behemoth that operates 91 hospitals and last year recorded more than $25 billion in revenue and a healthy operating margin that topped 5%.
"Trinity Health is in the Midwest, and they are not in the community," Hayek said. "So when you're looking at just the numbers from an office in the Midwest somewhere, they're not looking at the benefit that this place has on the community."
Hayek describes herself as a liberal Democrat. But Trinity's focus on its bottom line also irked many Republicans, including Mantello, who was the City Council president at the time.
"The whole hospital scene has changed," Mantello said. "It was very personable. You had nurses and doctors who were able to give more care and spend more time with patients." Now, by contrast, many hospitals have what she described as a "more corporate type of atmosphere."
Even the Catholic bishop decried the planned closure of the birthing center as out of step with the values of his faith and the hospital system's.
"Nothing is more central to the Catholic healthcare mission than supporting life and all those who bring it into the world," Bishop Edward Scharfenberger said after Trinity announced the closure plan. Scharfenberger has since retired.
A bipartisan solution
Despite the backlash, Trinity Health executives for months insisted they had no choice. The system even sued the state to push through the closure.
Ultimately, though, powerful state officials, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, joined the fight to save the birthing center, launching an investigation into the proposed closure and hosting a daylong hearing in Troy.
State Assemblyman John T. McDonald III, a Democrat who represents Troy, worked with Republican elected officials, including the county executive and the state senator representing Troy, to secure $5 million in state funding to help keep Burdett open.
"You had a Democrat and a bunch of Republicans all working together on the same issue," McDonald said, "because, at the end of the day, our job is to listen to what the public has to say."
Nearly a year after announcing the closure, Trinity reversed itself and said Burdett would remain open.
Lois Uttley, a New York City-based researcher and activist who has worked with communities facing hospital consolidation, said Troy's success reflects a growing bipartisan suspicion of big corporate healthcare organizations.
"The executives of these health systems will tell the community that joining a big health system will be good, that the quality of care will improve, that efficiencies will mean they can keep the costs low," Uttley said. "But what I have seen over the last 30 years of work is that those promises often are broken."
As hospitals close or downsize, she said, communities are catching on. "They're becoming more skeptical."
There's another, more hopeful lesson in Troy's success, said McDonald, the state assemblyman.
"If we take down our swords," he said, "and put out our arms, maybe we can get something done."

Hiker missing from B.C. gondola made call to 911 saying he's 'stuck on the mountain'
Stanislav Volo vanished on Sunday after going on a hike above the Sea-to-Sky Gondola
A new development has come to light in the search for a missing Squamish man who vanished while hiking by himself in B.C.'s Sea-to-Sky region.
Stanislav Volo got off at the top of the Sea-to-Sky Gondola, in Squamish, around 11:30 a.m. PT on Sunday, with plans to hike the Mount Habrich Loop, according to RCMP.
Dozens of volunteers from multiple search and rescue crews around the Lower Mainland have converged on the mountain above the gondola since to search for the missing 43-year-old.
Drones, helicopters, ground crews and police dogs have all been involved in the effort.
Volo’s sister, Ola Volo, said they received a new clue on Tuesday during the search.
“We recently got informed that he did make a phone call to 911,” Ola said. “He did say on the call that he was stuck on the mountain, but the call was very short.”
The call to 911 came through at around 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, search and rescue confirmed. 
Ola said the family listened to the phone call.
“It was definitely his phone number and his voice,” she said. “It was so brief that I just hold on to those seconds as much as I can.”
Mount Habrich Loop has limited cell service, which the family believes is the reason for the short phone call.
“We know he's out there and we know he's alive and he's doing everything he can to fight this weather and to stay warm and to stay with us,” Ola said.
Volo's cousin Yana Geng said there is a huge community of people who care about him.
“He is an amazing, hands-on, dedicated father to two beautiful children. He's a loving husband. He's a wonderful son, he's an awesome brother and an awesome cousin as well,” Geng said.
'Infinite number of places he could be'
Tyler Duncan, a search manager with Squamish Search and Rescue, said they believe Volo is still in the Habrich loop area.
“Due to the technical aspect of it, due to the countless number of gullies, little canyons, big boulder fields, there's literally an infinite number of places he could be,” Duncan said.
The area, while not geographically large, is challenging to search.
“When you actually get up there, and you look at pictures of the zone, you realize just how technical the terrain is and how varied and ledgy and stepped that terrain is,” Duncan said.
Weather complicated search efforts on Wednesday, and the search is resuming on Thursday morning for the fifth day.
On the day Volo went missing, other hikers believe they saw him on the Shannon Basin Loop, which leads to the hike he was expected to be on.
A section of the Mount Habrich Loop includes a series of fairly complicated cliff bands that stack on top of each other.
“Which is a very popular climbing area,” Duncan said. “There are some hiking trails that go up there, but it is technical, exposed alpine terrain, so not [a] beginner hiking zone.”
Duncan said there was also a missed call from Volo to his wife around 4:30 p.m. on Sunday.
“Our best theory is that he's down off the ridgeline somewhere and has lost service,” Duncan said.
Surveillance footage from Sunday shows Volo getting off the Sea-to-Sky Gondola at the top wearing a black T-shirt, black shorts and a black backpack.
Squamish RCMP are asking anyone who may have spotted Volo to contact them at 604-892-6100.

In Summary
- A decade ago, Indian brands commanded a large chunk of the Indian smartphone market. In Q2 2016, three of the top five smartphone brands were Indian ones.
- The arrival of Chinese brands and changes in the market led to the decline and exit of many Indian phone brands. Today, while brands like Lava and AI+ exist, their market shares are nothing compared to Indian brands of the past.
- Rising smartphone prices and memory costs seem to have opened the door for Indian smartphone brands, with new brands emerging and old ones looking to make a comeback, with encouragement and support from the Government. But is this just a temporary phase, or will Indian brands win back the market dominance they lost almost a decade ago?
When I first started covering technology, the Indian smartphone market looked extremely different from what it does today. Today, there are barely any Indian brands among the major smartphone brands in the Indian market – Counterpoint’s report on Q2 2026 showed not a single Indian brand among the top eight smartphone brands in the Indian market. Yes, some Indian smartphone brands do exist, such as the persistent Lava and the newcomer AI+, but they do not command significant market shares.
The story was extremely different a decade ago.
It may be hard to believe, especially for those who have started following smartphone trends in India since 2017, but in mid-2016, Indian tech brands were not just surviving but ruling the smartphone charts. IDC’s report for Q2 2016 placed three Indian brands in the top five smartphone brands in the country – Micromax, Intex and Reliance Jio (this was around the time of the 4G revolution).
And this was not because of a lack of competition. The Indian market was home to a number of high-profile foreign smartphone players like Apple, Samsung, HTC, BlackBerry, LG, Sony, and Motorola were very much present in the Indian market, and the likes of OnePlus, Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo had also arrived in the market. Still, Indian brands like Micromax, Intex, Spice, and Karbonn dominated sales charts for multiple and sometimes even consecutive quarters. In fact, in Q2 2014, Micromax even overtook Samsung to be the number one smartphone brand in the country in terms of shipments. It was a time when we carried a story on how Micromax deserved to be shown more respect.
Ghosts of the Indian smartphone market past: Why Indian brands ruled, and how the Chinese brands beat them
There was a reason for this dominance. At that point of time, Indian smartphone brands mainly catered to the budget segment, mostly under Rs. 15,000 (or even Rs 10,000), which comprised a large chunk of the smartphone market. While international brands had tried to enter this segment, they had very limited success, as they could not match the price-to-spec ratio that the Indian brands were offering. Big displays, big batteries, and decent processors (often from the more affordable MediaTek) and a small price tag made phones from the likes of Micromax, Intex, and Karbonn the perfect pick for anyone looking to pick up an entry-level smartphone. The likes of Apple, Samsung, HTC, Sony, and BlackBerry were largely operating in the mid/ upper mid and premium segment.
The tech climate changed as Chinese brands began to make their presence felt. Xiaomi, OnePlus, Vivo, and Oppo all stepped into the Indian market in 2014. Oppo and Vivo seemed to be playing in the premium segment, while brands like Xiaomi and OnePlus initially seemed to focus on flagship killers (a term OnePlus popularised). However, given India’s demography, it did not take a long time for these brands to realize that real numbers were actually in the budget and mid segment.
Even as Indian brands struggled with inventory issues as the 4G revolution hit India, the Chinese brands shifted focus and brought in smartphones with prices and spec combinations that matched and, in many cases, even eclipsed what Indian brands were offering. That was not all.
With the mobile Internet becoming more accessible thanks to extremely affordable 4G rates (pioneered mainly by Reliance Jio), these brands also opted for a very unconventional plan of action, going for flash sales, online only sales, often with little to no advertising in mainstream media, and building communities online. These not only cut expenses, but built greater brand loyalty (something Indian brands had been unable to do, as they had focused mainly on price). This combination of pricing and communications affected all the other brands in the market, but hit the Indian brands particularly hard, as it took away their biggest USP – a low price tag. The years that followed saw not just Indian brands fade, but even the likes of LG, Sony and HTC bid farewell to the Indian market.
The Indian Smartphone Market Today: Rocked by a steep price rise
In the last ten years, the Indian smartphone market has changed completely. Many Indian brands that had seemed almost invincible have packed their bags and left, although some like Lava have managed to stick around, in spite of not being the force they once were. But the tech stars in the tech universe move in different ways, and the way in which they have been aligning in recent times makes me think that the time is ripe for Indian smartphone brands to make a comeback in their own market.
Hear me out before you think I am talking through my hat. We have seen a very steady shift happening in the tech world in 2026. Many brands that earlier ruled the budget, mid, and lower-mid segments have been climbing up the price ladder for a while now, seeking larger profit margins. Indeed, the number of phones available in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment has been shrinking in recent times, with many brands seemingly inching towards vacating it altogether.
The likes of Motorola, OnePlus and Xiaomi are also no longer organizations with lean portfolios and small, focused teams but have become tech behemoths with large-scale operations, huge marketing budgets, multiple sub-brands and extensive product portfolios. This has, of course, affected their ability to offer the extremely competitive price-spec combo that made them popular in the first place.
The dramatic increase in the price of memory has now made it even more difficult for existing brands to offer good devices at lower price points. Devices with specs that used to be seen in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment are now being seen at prices in the range of Rs 25,000 or more. Options at lower price points are either vanishing or are coming with relatively modest specs.
And Indian brands are suddenly appearing on the horizon again.
Guess who’s back, back again… Indian smartphone brands
White Lava had never left; it seems to have got a new lease of life. AI+ is increasingly aggressive, and Fire-Boltt, a brand known more for its wearables and hearables, has entered the smartphone market. Even as this is being written, Mivi, a mainly audio brand, has announced plans for a smartphone with a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor for under Rs 15,000, and there is also talk of Micromax returning to the market, and Boat (which, like Fire-Boltt, is known mainly for audio and wearable products) is also planning to sail in smartphone waters. And from what we know, all these brands are targeting the sub-Rs 15,000 market, from which many brands have moved products to higher price points and/ or releasing new devices with much more modest specs in the past.
The Indian Government is also making efforts to build a smartphone brand that it can call its own. On August 21, it officially sent out a notification, as per which the Union Cabinet approved a budget of Rs. 62,500 crore for a Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) to build globally competitive, native smartphone brands. The scheme offers a number of incentives and rewards for Indian brands. To qualify, a company must be registered in India, keep its ownership and trademarks in India, have more than 51 percent Indian shareholding, be controlled in India, and have its products designed locally without outsourcing. This is a massive push and is likely to encourage more Indian entrepreneurs to enter the smartphone market.
Welcome back, Indian brands, but this time, please stay!
But making a comeback will not be enough. The smartphone world has changed a fair bit since the time Indian brands ruled the charts. And the new ones or those making a comeback would need to adopt a fundamentally different approach to ensure that the second innings of Indian brands in the smartphone market is a long one, and does not end as abruptly as the first. Being an ‘Indian brand’ has to have a different connotation than it did in the past.
Indian brands have struggled with offering good after-sales service and good software, and have tended to compete mainly on price and specs. That needs to change. The new and not-so-new native brands have to ensure they not just deliver a smartphone at a competitive price, but follow through on the whole process that comes after. Easy access to repairs and spare parts, timely OS updates, and improved, new-age marketing strategies are all necessities for these brands to actually establish themselves in this competitive market for the long run.
Native brands also need to shed their image of merely assembling and/or importing devices from outside and rebranding them for the Indian market. Authentic and good quality products backed up with a solid sales and service system are both needed to make consumers associate Indian brands not just with low prices, but also with high quality.
As of now, Indian brands are knocking on the door of their nation’s smartphone market once again. Just how well they will do, only time will tell. While I am hoping their second coming will be a successful one and they will win back lost ground (more local brands are always welcome in any market, and the big five out there need competition), there is no way of knowing how things will actually work out. Who knows, if I am still here, covering tech a decade later, I might be telling you a completely different story altogether.
A decade is a VERY long time in tech. Stay tuned.
